about_site_text: Robert Adam's neoclassical archive rises behind a screen of paired columns, its foundation stone laid on 27 June 1774 as the first building anywhere in Britain or Ireland purpose-built to store public records. Money ran dry more than once, and it wasn't fully finished until 1834 - sixty years after it began. At its heart sits the Adam Dome, a 50-foot-wide rotunda lit only by a central oculus and modelled on Rome's Pantheon.
interesting_fact: Adam worked small carved thistles into the dome's otherwise thoroughly Roman-inspired anthemion frieze, a quiet Scottish signature in an imported classical language. The building still does the job it was built for nearly 250 years later, holding centuries of Scotland's birth, marriage, death and court records, and remains the seat of the Lord Clerk Register and Lord Lyon King of Arms. It was actually judged too small before it was even finished - later architects Robert Reid and Archibald Elliot were called back in to extend it and dig further storage into the basement.

title: The Balmoral Hotel
about_site_text: A red sandstone clock tower rises 190 feet above Princes Street, its four 13-foot dials - made by Edinburgh jewellers Hamilton & Inches - visible across half the New Town. The hotel opened on 15 October 1902 as the North British Station Hotel, built directly above Waverley Station by the North British Railway to a design by William Hamilton Beattie. Sean Connery renamed it The Balmoral during a major 1991 refurbishment, and Rocco Forte Hotels has owned it since 1997.
interesting_fact: The clock has run three minutes fast since it first started ticking in 1902, a deliberate trick to help travellers dashing for their train actually catch it - it's only ever set right once a year, at midnight on Hogmanay. J.K. Rowling finished writing Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows in room 552 here on 11 January 2007, later signing a marble bust in the room with the date and a line from the book. The hotel became the first in Scotland to earn a five-star Forbes Travel Guide rating, and past guests have ranged from Laurel and Hardy in 1932 to Oprah Winfrey in 2010.

title: Waverley Bridge
about_site_text: Iron girders span the gap between Princes Street and Market Street below; lean over the parapet and you can see straight down into Waverley Station's platforms - this bridge doubles as the station's own roof. Built 1894-96 by engineers Blyth and Westland, it's Category A listed and one of three parallel crossings of this old loch-bed valley, alongside North Bridge and the Mound. Two carriageway ramps once let cars and taxis descend straight into the station concourse; that vehicle access closed in January 2014, leaving the ramps to pedestrians, cyclists and deliveries.
interesting_fact: Halfway across the bridge sits the former Waverley booking office - itself Category A listed - reborn in March 2016 as J D Wetherspoon's The Booking Office pub, so crossing today can mean stopping for a pint directly above the trains rumbling through the station underneath.

title: Edinburgh Waverley Station
about_site_text: Twenty platforms fan out beneath a vast glass roof here, Scotland's second-busiest railway station tucked into a valley the Old and New Town were built around rather than through. It formed in the 1860s when the North British Railway merged three rival Victorian stations that had grown up here since 1846 - North Bridge, General and Canal Street - under a name, 'Waverley', already used informally from around 1854 and borrowed from Sir Walter Scott's novels. The roof overhead was most recently reglazed with 370,000 square feet of clear panels between 2010 and 2012.
interesting_fact: A legal covenant dating back to the station's construction bans any building upward on the site, specifically to protect the view of Arthur's Seat from Princes Street above - one reason Waverley has always had to spread sideways and down into the valley rather than up, squeezed as it is between the Old and New Towns. Because it sits down in that valley, the station is almost entirely hidden from street level, with separate entrances dropping in from Waverley Bridge, Market Street and Princes Street on three different sides of the surrounding city blocks.

title: Waverley Market
about_site_text: This sunken plaza sits below street level by design - its roof was built deliberately flush with Princes Street to keep the classic view across to the Castle and Old Town unbroken. A Victorian fruit and vegetable market moved here in 1869 after the original marketplace under North Bridge was swallowed by the growing railway, and was roofed over in 1874 with an iron-and-glass hall that even had a rooftop garden for entertainment. That hall closed in November 1972 and was demolished the following year; the shopping centre here opened in November 1984 and was formally opened by the Queen on 25 July 1985.
interesting_fact: The centre has changed its name almost as often as its shop mix - Waverley Market, then Waverley Shopping Centre, then Princes Mall from 2004, then Waverley Mall from 2016 - before reverting back to its original name, Waverley Market, in a full-circle rebrand.

title: Fruitmarket Gallery
about_site_text: This building started out in 1938 as a genuine fruit and vegetable market, set right beside the railway that once carried the produce in - a working history still legible in its plain, functional brick. Founded as a gallery in 1974 and renovated by Richard Murphy Architects in 1994, it shows international and Scottish contemporary art free of charge, alongside talks and events. A £4.3 million expansion completed in 2021 converted a neighbouring former fruit warehouse - later the Electric Circus nightclub - into a second exhibition wing, roughly doubling the gallery's footprint.
interesting_fact: In 2011 the gallery commissioned Turner Prize-winner Martin Creed's marble reclad of the nearby Scotsman Steps - a free public artwork just round the corner, and the gallery's own contribution to that year's Edinburgh Art Festival.

title: Scotsman Steps
about_site_text: 104 stone steps spiral up inside an octagonal tower, climbing from Market Street and Waverley Station below to North Bridge above. Built between 1899 and 1902 as part of the same grand new headquarters going up next door for The Scotsman newspaper, the staircase spent decades afterwards as a dark, neglected shortcut, better known for litter and antisocial behaviour than for anything else.
interesting_fact: In 2011, Turner Prize-winning artist Martin Creed reclad every one of the 104 steps in a different marble drawn from quarries on every continent, a permanent public artwork titled Work No. 1059 and commissioned by the neighbouring Fruitmarket Gallery. Creed described climbing it as being 'like walking through the world' - and the £250,000 installation transformed the once-neglected passage into a genuine, free-to-visit piece of public art.

title: The Scotsman Hotel
about_site_text: Pinkish sandstone turrets and ornate baronial gables crown this Edwardian block, completed in 1902 to designs by Dunn & Findlay as headquarters for The Scotsman newspaper - then Scotland's leading national daily - and deliberately built to command the North Bridge skyline. Printing presses ran in the lower floors and editorial staff worked the middle ones, while, in a nod to older ways of getting news out fast, a pigeon loft once occupied the attic. Sitting right beside Waverley Station let finished papers reach the trains within minutes of coming off the press.
interesting_fact: The Scotsman finally moved out in 1999, and the building reopened in 2001 as a luxury hotel, keeping its oak-panelled Edwardian reception hall as a bar and turning the old basement printing-press room into a fitness suite - so guests now work out in the very room where the next day's headlines used to roll off the presses. A ceremonial staircase of Carrara marble still winds up through the building's core, unchanged from the newspaper's day.

title: Jinglin' Geordie
about_site_text: This close-hugging pub takes its name from George Heriot, the wealthy 16th and 17th-century Edinburgh goldsmith and moneylender nicknamed 'Jinglin' Geordie' for the coins that jingled in his pockets as he walked the Old Town. Heriot lived right here on Fleshmarket Close with his first wife, Christian Marjoribanks, and lent substantial sums to King James VI and Queen Anne. Inside, a long-case clock, stained-glass thistle and saltire windows, and old prints and photographs of Edinburgh keep the pub's history on show.
interesting_fact: When Heriot died in 1624 he left almost his entire fortune to found a hospital school for 'fatherless boys, freemen's sons of the town of Edinburgh' - a bequest that became George Heriot's School, still one of Edinburgh's best-known independent schools today, endowed by a goldsmith who once lived and worked just a few steps from where his namesake pub now stands. Three and a half centuries later, the pub kept far less pious company for a season: George Best is remembered as a regular here during his brief, chaotic stint playing for Hibernian in 1979-80, a flash of football glamour dropped into a pub otherwise steeped in 17th-century goldsmith history.

title: Halfway House
about_site_text: Widely reckoned Edinburgh's smallest pub, the Halfway House is tucked exactly halfway up the steep flight of steps that make up Fleshmarket Close, between Market Street and Cockburn Street. Squeeze inside and the tiny bar counter fits no more than about four people at once, with a couple more tables and booths wedged in around it, the walls hung with railway memorabilia fitting for a pub standing this close to Waverley Station.
interesting_fact: Despite its size it punches well above its weight: CAMRA named it Scottish and Northern Ireland Pub of the Year in 2005 and Edinburgh Pub of the Year in 2009. It takes cask ale seriously too, with four handpumps of guest beers rotating daily alongside its own house-label Tullibardine malt whisky behind the bar. It now operates as part of the Old Town Pub Co, one of fifteen Old Town venues run by Bruce Group Scotland, though it still trades and is reviewed as a genuine free house rather than a chain outlet.

title: Fleshmarket Close
address: Market St & Fleshmarket Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1DE
about_site_text: This steep, narrow medieval alley climbs from Market Street, just behind Waverley Station, up to Cockburn Street and the High Street above - and it earns its name honestly. Butchers once hung carcasses along this passage, with blood running down the slope toward the old Nor Loch that used to fill the valley now occupied by Princes Street Gardens. The flesh (meat) market had moved here from beside the Tron Kirk by the late 17th century, and the close remains one of the most-used routes between the railway station and the Old Town today.
interesting_fact: It lent its name to Fleshmarket Close, the fifteenth Inspector Rebus novel by Edinburgh crime writer Ian Rankin, published in 2004, and long housed the Jinglin' Geordie pub, once a favourite haunt of journalists from the Evening News and The Scotsman until both papers moved out to Holyrood in 1999. More recently, in June 2025, the close was used to film J. J. Abrams's The Great Beyond, starring Glen Powell, Jenna Ortega, Emma Mackey and Samuel L. Jackson.

title: The Booking Office
about_site_text: This single-storey building began life as Edinburgh Waverley's original booking office, built by the North British Railway Company as the station was rebuilt through the 1890s. Passengers bought tickets here until the office became the station's parcels office around 1984, after which its timber-panelled counters were cleared out. Grade A listed and sitting directly above the station concourse - forming part of Waverley's own roof - the building later passed through spells as licensed premises and a restaurant before J D Wetherspoon opened The Booking Office here in March 2016.
interesting_fact: The pub's entrance floor carries a replica of the mosaic that once covered the real Victorian booking hall nearby, showing the North British Railway Company's coat of arms - the original, laid between 1892 and 1902, was ripped out with the old wood-panelled ticket counters in 1970. Photographs on the walls recall the station's steam-age heyday: the Flying Scotsman at the platform, 1945 refreshment trolleys, and the sleek 1960s Elizabethan express, alongside fragments salvaged from the very booking office the pub now occupies.

title: The Edinburgh Dungeon
about_site_text: Sunk down in the valley behind Waverley Station, this Category B listed row of buildings at 31-39 Market Street makes a fittingly gloomy, half-underground setting for what's inside. Opened in 2000 by Vardon Attractions (now part of Merlin Entertainments, which also runs the original London Dungeon), it takes visitors through roughly 500 years of Scotland's darker history using live actors, sets and special effects rather than static displays - eleven shows and a ride, staffed by around fifteen actors, spread through the building's vaulted rooms.
interesting_fact: The cast of characters leans into Edinburgh's grislier past: Burke and Hare, the 1820s body-snatchers-turned-murderers who sold corpses to anatomists; Agnes Finnie, tried as a witch in 1644; and the legend of Sawney Bean, Scotland's supposed cannibal cave-dweller. The finale is the Drop Ride to Doom, a free-fall drop staged as a mock execution. A £500,000-plus refit in November 2016 rebuilt the Witch Hunt show around a new steel structure and an effects combination Merlin billed at the time as a world first for the format.

title: City Art Centre
about_site_text: Nine iron-framed storeys clad in restrained Beaux Arts stone, built 1899-1902 by architects Dunn and Findlay - the same firm and years as The Scotsman Hotel further up North Bridge - originally as an extension of the newspaper's works before it became part of Edinburgh's wholesale fruit and vegetable market. The City of Edinburgh Council converted it into a public gallery in 1980, a scheme by City Architect Brian Annable that won a RIBA Award for Architecture in 1983, and a 1990s expansion opened it out into six full floors of neutral, flexible gallery space.
interesting_fact: The council's own collection here runs to around 4,800 works of Scottish art from the 17th century to today - paintings, photography, sculpture and contemporary media by names like J.D. Fergusson, Joan Eardley and Eduardo Paolozzi - though with no permanent display, what's actually on the walls changes with each exhibition. A 1961 bequest from Edinburgh resident Jean Watson has quietly funded more than 900 acquisitions to the collection since, still shaping what turns up on show today.

title: Metal Thistle Sculpture
about_site_text: Officially titled 'Blawn Wi' The Wind' (Scots for 'Blown with the Wind'), this hand-forged thistle sculpture stands outside the Market Street Hotel at 6 Market Street, its heads and leaves bent and rippling as though genuinely caught mid-gust. It's the work of blacksmith and metalwork artist Kev Paxton and his team at ArtFe, based in Ratho just outside Edinburgh, who built it from mild steel and reclaimed scrap - old farmers' fencing wire and parts salvaged from past exhibition stands among it - forged into Scotland's national flower.
interesting_fact: After dark the sculpture is lit from below in purple LED, the thistle's traditional colour, making it glow against the surrounding stonework. Paxton has described the piece as a nod to the plant's old reputation for a 'don't mess with me' resilience - its spiked defiance standing in for courage and determination. Getting a permanently lit sculpture fixed into a public footpath inside a UNESCO World Heritage Site was its own undertaking: architects Leask, working alongside Paxton, had to navigate the 'complexities of consents, permits and logistics' the site demanded before it could go in.

title: Waverley Steps
about_site_text: This broad stairway down from Princes Street into Waverley station's concourse first opened in 1902, built alongside the North British Hotel next door - now the Balmoral - by the same North British Railway Company that owned them both. Flanked by original 1902 shopfronts to the east and Waverley Market to the west, the steps stayed largely unchanged for over a century until Network Rail rebuilt them in 2010-2012: a new escalator and lift were added for accessibility, all sheltered under a glass-and-steel canopy by Jefferson Sheard Architects, its frameless glass panels held up on branching steel 'tree' columns running down the centre of the stairs.
interesting_fact: Before the canopy, older Edinburgh residents remember the open steps as one of the windiest spots in the city centre - a funnel between the valley and Princes Street catching gusts from every direction. The £7 million rebuild had to satisfy tight heritage constraints: Waverley is a Grade A listed station inside a UNESCO World Heritage Area, so every part of the new structure needed sign-off before a single glass panel went up. The steps can still be gated shut at the top today, whenever the station closes for the night.

title: Cockburn Street
about_site_text: Curving stone tenements in the Scots Baronial style, crow-stepped gables and turrets catching the light, line a street that has no business existing in a medieval street plan - and that's exactly the point. Cockburn Street was cut through the Old Town's solid tenement blocks between 1856 and 1864, curving from the High Street down to Market Street to ease the gradient for carriages heading to the new Waverley Station below. It was built by the High Street and Railway Station Access Company under the Railway Station Acts of 1853 and 1860. Most of its ornate buildings went up under architects Peddie & Kinnear between 1859 and 1861, and if you look closely at the stonework you'll spot their trademark carved 'PK' monogram worked into gables and window surrounds along the street. It took its name from Henry, Lord Cockburn, an Edinburgh judge and early defender of the Old Town's character, who died in 1854 before construction began.
interesting_fact: The street's gentle S-curve and shallow gradient - about 1-in-14 - were deliberately engineered so horses and carriages could manage the climb from Waverley Station up to the Old Town, cutting straight through several of the Old Town's historic closes to do it. Lord Cockburn never saw the street bearing his name, and the irony runs deeper: shortly before his death he'd campaigned loudly against exactly this kind of Old Town 'improvement' scheme. Its curving pavement today is known for something else entirely - independent shops selling records, comics, tattoos and vintage clothes, a countercultural reputation quite different from the grand retail parade its builders had in mind.

title: Craig's Close
about_site_text: Barely wide enough for two people to pass, Craig's Close is one of the Old Town's oldest, its stone walls closing in as you head down from the High Street. It's named after John Craig, a burgess who acquired the land through marriage, and for two centuries this cramped passage was a hub of Edinburgh printing: Andro Hart printed an influential Scottish edition of the Bible from a house at its head around 1610, and Edinburgh's first regular newspaper, the Edinburgh Courant, rolled off presses here from 14 February 1705. Its original High Street entrance, once almost directly opposite the Mercat Cross, was sealed off in 1932 when the council's municipal offices were extended; today the close survives only as a short passage between Cockburn Street and Market Street.
interesting_fact: Andro Hart's press wasn't always so devoutly employed: in 1596 he was among the leading participants in a riot in which an armed mob besieged King James VI inside the Old Tolbooth, and by February 1597 he'd been marched off as a prisoner to Edinburgh Castle alongside two other booksellers for his part in it - the future Bible-printer as rabble-rouser, more than a decade before his best-known edition ever went to press. A plaque near the foot of the close's steps commemorates a later chapter in its literary history: poet Robert Fergusson's membership of the Cape Club, a boisterous eighteenth-century dining and drinking society for Edinburgh's writers and artists. Barely wide enough for two people to pass, the close is easy to miss entirely from Cockburn Street, yet across two centuries it printed some of the earliest scripture and news ever set in type in Scotland.

title: Old Fishmarket Close
about_site_text: Old Fishmarket Close plunges steeply from the High Street down to the Cowgate, cobbles slick underfoot, named for a fish market once held partway down its length; its earliest recorded name, Swift's Wynd, dates back to 1427. During the 'Lang Siege' of 1573 the close was bombarded along with much of the Royal Mile, and in April 1585 a girl working here became the first recorded victim when plague reached Edinburgh. George Heriot, the goldsmith later famous for endowing George Heriot's School, lived in the close in 1586. In 1705 a Dutchman named Abraham Sever reportedly kept a touring elephant in a flat here, to the fury of a baker below whose ovens suffered from the animal's droppings.
interesting_fact: The close has been renamed repeatedly over the centuries: Home Close in 1707, Gourlay's Close in 1756, and Carmichael's Close in 1722, before finally settling on 'Old Fishmarket Close' for the market once held partway down its slope. A quirky cast-metal sign of leaping fish, in silver and bright pink, still swings above its High Street archway today, keeping the old market's memory alive long after the last stall closed.

title: Anchor Close
about_site_text: Split neatly in two when Cockburn Street was carved through its middle in the 1850s, Anchor Close still runs from the High Street down toward Market Street much as it did when first recorded in 1714, its name taken from a tavern that once stood at its head. Its most notable resident was printer William Smellie, who ran his press from the close and produced the first edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica between 1768 and 1771, as well as the first Edinburgh-printed volume of Robert Burns's poems in 1787. Sir Walter Scott's parents lived in the close until 1771, not long before the novelist was born nearby - a single close that, within two decades, helped print both the world's first encyclopaedia and Scotland's national poet.
interesting_fact: Smellie also founded the Crochallan Fencibles, a rowdy Edinburgh drinking club that met in a tavern in the close, taking its odd name from 'Crodh Chailein' (Colin's Cattle), a favourite song of the landlord, paired with 'Fencibles', the term for home-defence militia regiments. Robert Burns was introduced to the club by Smellie in 1787 and became a member, reportedly composing some of his bawdier verses purely for the group's private amusement - verses later gathered into The Merry Muses of Caledonia, a collection of ribald Scots song and poetry too explicit for respectable publication in his lifetime. It circulated only privately for decades after his death, its connection to Scotland's national poet an open secret nobody wanted to put their name to.

title: Tron Kirk Market
about_site_text: Gothic tracery windows and a slender spire still anchor this stretch of the Royal Mile, though the church beneath them hasn't held a service in over seventy years. The foundation stone was laid on 4 March 1637, commissioned by Charles I after St Giles' up the street became Edinburgh's cathedral and its displaced parish needed a church of its own. Master mason John Mylne designed it, blending Gothic tracery with Dutch-influenced classical detailing, though construction dragged into the 1640s because of the Wars of the Covenant. Its original steeple burned down in the Great Fire of Edinburgh in 1824; the current spire, by R. & R. Dickson, replaced it in 1828. The congregation held its final service here in 1952, thinned by decades of Old Town depopulation, and merged with St Giles'. The kirk's name comes from the tron, a weighing beam that stood outside until around 1800, taxing goods sold nearby.
interesting_fact: Restoration in the 1970s uncovered the cobbled surface of Marlin's Wynd beneath the floor, a paved street thought to be among the oldest in Scotland, named after mason Walter Merlioun who lived there around 1500; part remains visible under glass panels today. After decades as a heritage centre, the building reopened in July 2022 as Tron Kirk Market, run by the Scottish Design Exchange, where local makers sell jewellery, art and craft from stalls inside the old nave.

title: The Milkman
about_site_text: The Milkman occupies one of Cockburn Street's most photographed corners: a slender stone tower wedged onto a genuinely triangular plot, its steeply pitched roof narrowing up to a single ornamental point. The shop itself is barely wider than its own doorway, its floor plan following the wedge of ground it sits on so tightly that there's room for little more than a till and a handful of customers. It's part of a Baronial-style terrace built in 1859, the same construction wave that cut Cockburn Street through the Old Town - its deliberate curve engineered to disguise the fact it slices diagonally across the medieval street pattern above it.
interesting_fact: Before it sold coffee, the building was a confectioner's - a hand-painted fascia sign uncovered during a 2016 restoration still reveals that former trade. Edinburgh World Heritage contributed more than £6,000 toward the project, which repaired the shop's original timber shutters (still slid into slots beneath the windows each night) and the antique lettering, carried out in partnership with shop owner Mark Donald.

title: Sir Chris Hoy Gold Post Box
about_site_text: An ordinary Victorian pillar box, painted gold almost overnight in August 2012, still stands on this Hunter Square corner - one of two in Edinburgh honouring Sir Chris Hoy after his double gold-medal haul at the London Olympics, this one marking his win in the men's keirin, with a second box on Hanover Street for his team sprint gold. Royal Mail repainted a post box gold in the hometown of every British Olympic and Paralympic gold medallist that summer, the first time in modern history the colour of the country's post boxes had ever changed from their traditional red.
interesting_fact: Hoy's two London 2012 golds weren't even his best Games: at Beijing 2008 he won three - team sprint, keirin and individual sprint - the first British man to take three golds at a single Olympics since 1908, and still Scotland's most successful Olympian outright.

title: Adam Smith Statue
about_site_text: Ten feet of bronze on a tall stone plinth, this is the world's first major public monument to Adam Smith, the Kirkcaldy-born economist whose 1776 book The Wealth of Nations helped found modern economics. Sculpted by Alexander Stoddart, Scotland's leading monumental sculptor, and funded entirely by private donations gathered by the Adam Smith Institute, it was unveiled on 4 July 2008 by Nobel laureate economist Vernon L. Smith, on the very stretch of the Royal Mile Smith himself lived just off, further down toward the Canongate.
interesting_fact: Stoddart packed the statue with symbolism: a plough behind Smith represents the agrarian economy his ideas displaced, a beehive in front stands for the industriousness he saw as progress's engine, and a globe sits half-hidden beneath his gown-covered hand, angled toward Leith's harbour and his native Fife. His clothing deliberately borrows from America too - the neckwear modelled on Thomas Jefferson's, the wig on George Washington's - a nod to Smith's advocacy of free trade with the American colonies.

title: Mercat Cross
about_site_text: A market cross first recorded in a charter of 1365, historically the spot from which Edinburgh's royal proclamations were read and, for centuries, the symbolic heart of the burgh's civic and trading life. The medieval cross was demolished in 1756; its carved shaft was eventually salvaged and re-erected at Drum House in Gilmerton, while five of its eight heraldic panels were bought by Sir Walter Scott for Abbotsford. In 1885 the old shaft and its unicorn were reunited here in Parliament Square on a new octagonal base, paid for personally by former Prime Minister William Gladstone, whose family hailed from Edinburgh.
interesting_fact: Proclamations were the cross's respectable side; for a century and a half it was also Edinburgh's scaffold. Between 1564 and 1710, well over a hundred people were beheaded here by the Maiden, an early Scottish guillotine now on display at the National Museum of Scotland, among them James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, executed by the very device he is sometimes wrongly credited with inventing.

title: Edinburgh City Chambers
about_site_text: This grand 18th-century quadrangle was never meant to become Edinburgh's town hall. Built from 1753 as the Royal Exchange - designed by John Adam, with amendments by John Fergus, funded by public subscription and opened by Lord Provost George Drummond in 1760 - it was meant to lure the city's merchants off the street and into proper trading rooms. It never really worked: merchants kept right on doing business at the Mercat Cross outside, so the Town Council gradually took the building over instead, buying its north range as council offices in 1811 and the rest by 1893. It has served as Edinburgh's seat of local government - Town Council, Corporation, District Council and now City of Edinburgh Council - ever since.
interesting_fact: Because the site drops steeply toward the Cowgate, the Royal Exchange's builders simply built over the top of an entire buried close of existing tenements rather than levelling it first - the mostly intact 17th-century street now survives sealed beneath the building as Real Mary King's Close. Category A listed since 1970, the Chambers' quadrangle has also stood in for other cities on screen, doubling as Stirling in Braveheart (1995) and appearing in the TV series Belgravia (2019).

title: Real Mary King's Close
about_site_text: A genuine 17th-century Old Town street, sealed beneath Edinburgh's Royal Exchange when it was built over from 1753 rather than being demolished outright. Below street level, Mary King's Close - named for a prominent 17th-century fabric merchant who traded here - survives largely intact, its tenement walls, fireplaces and cobbled surface preserved in the dark exactly where the builders left them. The close, and the plague and poverty its former residents lived through, opened to the public as a heritage attraction in 2003 and now draws around a quarter of a million visitors a year.
interesting_fact: The close's reputation for hauntings partly rests on a very ordinary cause: escaping biogas from old drains and the buried Nor Loch marshland below is thought to have produced eerie lights and possibly hallucinations for past visitors. Its best-known ghost has a gentler origin, though - after a Japanese psychic named Aiko Gibo sensed a distressed little girl asking after a lost doll during a 1990s TV documentary, she left a doll behind for her, naming her 'Annie'. Visitors have been leaving toys and gifts in the room ever since. Real history supplied its own grim figure too: the close's plague doctor, George Rae, treated victims of the 1645 outbreak wearing the now-iconic beaked leather mask stuffed with herbs believed to filter the 'bad air' thought to spread infection, lancing and cauterising his patients' plague boils with a heated iron. He was one of the few to survive an epidemic that killed between a fifth and a half of Edinburgh's population - but the town council owed him for the dangerous work, and he reportedly spent years fighting them for his unpaid salary before he died, still out of pocket.

title: Parliament House
about_site_text: Built between 1632 and 1640 to a design by James Murray, the Crown's Master of Works, this was the world's first purpose-built parliament building, raised so Scotland's Parliament, Court of Session and other courts could finally leave their cramped, shared quarters inside St Giles' and the old Tolbooth. Its centrepiece, Parliament Hall, is a vast 122-by-49-foot chamber roofed with an elaborate oak hammerbeam structure carved by master wright John Scott in 1637. Scotland's Parliament sat here for the last time on 28 April 1707, ratifying the Union with England; the building has housed the Court of Session, Scotland's supreme civil court, ever since.
interesting_fact: For generations, advocates without a case to argue simply paced the length of Parliament Hall to pass the time and be seen - a custom Robert Louis Stevenson described in 1878 as governed by 'ferocious custom', noting some men walked there 'daily for ten or twenty years without a rag of business or a shilling of reward'. Lawyers still discuss cases while walking its length today, partly because pacing up and down makes it harder for eavesdroppers to follow any one conversation.

title: St Giles' Cathedral
about_site_text: The High Kirk of Edinburgh has stood on this site since at least 1124, though the present Gothic building mostly dates from the 14th and 15th centuries, crowned by a distinctive open crown steeple built around 1460-1467 - one of only two such medieval crown spires surviving in Scotland. John Knox, leader of the Scottish Reformation, preached here from 1559 until his death in 1572 and is buried, rather incongruously, beneath what is now a numbered parking space outside. Despite its popular name, St Giles' has only ever briefly been a true cathedral - the seat of a bishop - during two short-lived Stuart attempts to impose bishops on the Church of Scotland.
interesting_fact: On 23 July 1637, the introduction of a new prayer book here supposedly triggered a riot when market trader Jenny Geddes hurled her folding stool at the Dean's head rather than hear him read from it - a protest, if it happened as told, that helped spark the National Covenant and eventually the Wars of the Three Kingdoms. Two-and-a-half centuries later, the ornate Thistle Chapel was added in 1911 for the Order of the Thistle, Scotland's highest order of chivalry, designed by Robert Lorimer and opened by King George V.

title: Signet Library
about_site_text: Home to the WS Society (Writers to the Signet), Scotland's oldest body of solicitors, whose role keeping the monarch's private seal traces back to 1594. The current building was begun in 1810 to designs by Robert Reid, with William Stark responsible for its two great libraries: a Lower Library finished in 1815 and, above it, an Upper Library completed in 1822 in time for a royal visit that would define its reputation. William Playfair and William Burn later carried out further alterations, and the building has been Category A listed as a classical masterpiece ever since.
interesting_fact: When George IV toured Edinburgh in August 1822 - the first reigning monarch to visit Scotland in nearly two centuries - he was shown into the newly finished Upper Library ahead of that evening's state banquet next door in Parliament Hall, and reportedly declared it 'the most beautiful drawing room in Europe'. Records of the Writers to the Signet themselves stretch back even further, to 1369, making the society considerably older than the grand rooms it eventually built to house its library - and its ranks over the centuries included some unexpected names. Sir Walter Scott himself trained as a Writer to the Signet, apprenticed to his father's law firm years before he ever published a novel, one of many prominent Edinburgh figures who passed through the Society on their way to making their name doing something else entirely.

title: Heart of Midlothian Mosaic
about_site_text: A heart shape picked out in coloured granite setts, set into the pavement outside St Giles' to mark the site of Edinburgh's Old Tolbooth - a squat, forbidding 15th-century building that served over the centuries as council chamber, courthouse and prison before it was finally demolished in 1817. The mosaic itself only dates from 1860, decades after the building it commemorates disappeared, but it has kept the Tolbooth's memory fixed firmly in the pavement ever since. Walter Scott had already sealed the building's grim reputation in his 1818 novel The Heart of Midlothian, and Edinburgh's Heart of Midlothian Football Club later borrowed both the name and the heart shape for its own crest - though the club's own origin is even more roundabout, growing out of a Victorian dance club called the Heart of Mid-Lothian Quadrille Assembly, itself named after Scott's novel, when it turned to football in 1874.
interesting_fact: Locals still spit on the heart as they pass, a habit usually explained today as a superstition for good luck or a promise to return to Edinburgh - though it most likely began as a much less friendly gesture of contempt for a building where prisoners were tortured and hanged. The Tolbooth stood so close to St Giles' that it partly blocked the church's main door, and its demolition in 1817 was reportedly cheered by the crowds who came out to watch it come down.

title: Brodie's Close
about_site_text: A narrow close on the Lawnmarket, opening almost opposite Deacon Brodie's Tavern and named for the family of William Brodie, the respectable cabinet-maker and city councillor secretly running a double life as a burglar by night. The close itself is older than its famous name suggests: it was built around 1570 by Edinburgh magistrate William Little as Little's Close, only becoming known as Brodie's Close in the 18th century once the Brodie family - William's mother among them, recorded as head of household here in 1774 - had lived there long enough for the name to stick. The mansion at its foot was demolished around 1835 and now lies beneath Victoria Terrace.
interesting_fact: Brodie grew up here as the son of a cabinet-maker before rising to become Deacon of the Incorporation of Wrights and Masons - the respectable public face that hid his secret career as a burglar. For the full story of his crimes, capture and execution, see Deacon Brodie's Tavern, just across the street.

title: Deacon Brodies Tavern
about_site_text: The building at 435 Lawnmarket dates from the early 18th century, standing at the junction of the Lawnmarket and Bank Street, close to where William Brodie himself lived and kept his cabinet-making workshop. Its ground and first floors were converted into a public house by architect P. L. Henderson in 1894, with further alterations by Robert Hurd in 1950; it has been protected as a Category A listed building since 1970. Many tourist guides give 1806 as the tavern's founding date, though the listing record's account of a much later 1894 conversion suggests the pub in its current form may be somewhat younger than that popular figure.
interesting_fact: William Brodie (1741-1788) was a respected Edinburgh cabinet-maker, locksmith and city councillor - Deacon of the Incorporation of Wrights and Masons - who led a secret double life as a burglar, using his legitimate trade to take wax impressions of clients' keys before a botched 1788 raid on the Excise Office saw him caught, tried and hanged. Local legend holds he had once helped design the very gallows used to hang him. The stark contrast between his respectable daytime reputation and his criminal nightlife is widely credited as an inspiration for Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde - Stevenson grew up with a cabinet Brodie had built in his family home.

title: Statue of Walter Francis Montagu Douglas Scott
about_site_text: Unveiled on 7 February 1888 in Parliament Square, this bronze by Sir Joseph Edgar Boehm shows Walter Francis Montagu Douglas Scott, 5th Duke of Buccleuch and 7th Duke of Queensberry, robed in the Order of the Garter and looking out over the High Street from beside St Giles'. Its hexagonal pedestal, designed by Sir Rowand Anderson, carries three tiers of bronze decoration: a top gallery of huntsmen and hounds chasing a stag, a middle tier pairing scenes from the Duke's own life with allegorical 'Virtue' figures by William Birnie Rhind, and a lower tier of larger reliefs recounting Scott family history, guarded at its corners by rampant stags holding shields.
interesting_fact: One lower relief shows Sir Walter Scott of Buccleuch and Branxholm's failed 1526 attempt to rescue the teenage James V from his Douglas captors, another the burning of the family's Catslack Tower by English raiders in 1548. The Duke was himself a descendant of Charles II's illegitimate son James Scott, Duke of Monmouth - so his statue and Charles II's, standing a few strides away in the same square, quietly represent opposite ends of the same illegitimate royal line.

title: Robert Burns House Plaque
address: Lady Stair's Close & Lawnmarket, Edinburgh EH1 2NT
about_site_text: This plaque on the Lawnmarket, above the entrance to Lady Stair's Close, marks the site of Baxter's Close - demolished long ago - where Robert Burns took lodgings on 28 November 1786, his first winter in Edinburgh. Newly arrived from Ayrshire on the strength of his Kilmarnock-printed poems, he shared a single room at Mrs Carfrae's flat with his friend John Richmond, a law clerk already living there; when Burns moved in, the rent rose from Richmond's usual two shillings and sixpence a week to three, for a chaff bed, a sanded floor and a deal table between them.
interesting_fact: Sparse as it was, this was the room Burns wrote from at the height of his sudden fame, freshly hailed by Henry Mackenzie as a 'heaven-taught ploughman'. Richmond later recalled Burns kept 'strict sobriety' throughout their year together here - before moving out to lodge with William Nicol. Baxter's Close itself is long gone; its site now lies beneath Deacon Brodie's Tavern, a few steps further along this route.

title: Makars' Court
address: Makars' Court, Lady Stair's Close, Edinburgh EH1 2PA
about_site_text: Just off the Lawnmarket in Lady Stair's Close, beside the Writers' Museum, this courtyard has had quotations from Scottish writers carved into its paving stones since 1997, when the Saltire Society chose the first twelve makars - the Scots word for poets or authors, literally 'one who fashions or makes'. Ronald Harwood, then president of International PEN, unveiled the first slab; the poet Iain Crichton Smith unveiled the rest, and further stones have been added at intervals ever since. The collection now runs to more than forty writers spanning the 14th century to the present, inscribed across Gaelic, Scots, English and Latin.
interesting_fact: The lines underfoot range from John Barbour's 1375 'Fredome is a noble thing' to Robert Louis Stevenson's verdict that 'there are no stars so lovely as Edinburgh street lamps'. Robert Burns has a slab too, quoting 'man to man the world o'er shall brithers be for a' that' - just steps from the close where he actually lodged.

title: The Writers' Museum
address: Lawnmarket, Lady Stair's Close, Edinburgh EH1 2PA
about_site_text: Down the turnpike stair of this turreted 1622 townhouse - its crow-stepped gables and conical-roofed turret typical of the fortified townhouses once lining this stretch of the Lawnmarket - sits the Writers' Museum. Built for the merchant Sir William Gray, it was renamed after Elizabeth Dalrymple, Dowager Countess of Stair, who bought it in 1719. Town planner Patrick Geddes prompted the 5th Earl of Rosebery to buy and restore the crumbling house in 1895, with architect George Shaw Aitken carrying out the work, and Rosebery gifted it to the city in 1907 as a free museum devoted to Robert Burns, Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson.
interesting_fact: Among the cases are Scott's own chess set and his dining table from 39 Castle Street, Burns's draft of Scots Wha Hae, and Stevenson's wardrobe - built, fittingly, by Deacon William Brodie, the respectable cabinetmaker-by-day and burglar-by-night whose double life partly inspired Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde. Elsewhere in the cases are quieter, more personal relics of Stevenson's last years in Samoa: his riding boots and a ring given to him by a Samoan chief, brought back across the world after his death there in 1894 to the Edinburgh he'd left as a sickly young man.

title: Gladstone's Land
about_site_text: Gladstone's Land is a surviving six-storey Old Town tenement on the Lawnmarket, its earliest recorded building dating to 1501. In 1617 the prosperous merchant Thomas Gledstanes and his wife Bessie Cunningham bought and rebuilt it, raising it to its present height and completing the work by 1620 with elaborate painted ceilings, later hidden under plaster and only rediscovered decades on. By the mid-1800s the Old Town's wealthier residents had long since decamped to the New Town, leaving the building to decline until the National Trust for Scotland rescued it from demolition in 1934, restoring it as a house museum reopened after a further £1.5 million refurbishment in 2021.
interesting_fact: The reconstructed timber-fronted shopfront on the ground floor recreates the arcaded booths once common along the medieval Royal Mile, almost all demolished elsewhere by later street widening. Above the door hangs a gilt-copper hawk with outstretched wings, a punning shop sign on the family name: 'gled' is the old Scots word for a kite or hawk. Past residents ranged from cloth merchants to an episcopalian minister of St Giles', and the museum still draws well over a quarter of a million visitors a year.

title: The Hub
about_site_text: This dark neo-Gothic building on the corner of Castlehill and Johnston Terrace was built in 1842-1845 as Victoria Hall, a joint design by Scottish architect James Gillespie Graham and the English Gothic Revival architect Augustus Pugin, meant to give the Church of Scotland's General Assembly a proper meeting hall. Queen Victoria laid its foundation stone in 1842. From 1929 it served as Highland Tolbooth St John's Church, holding services in both Gaelic and English, until its congregation united with Greyfriars Kirk in 1979 and the building closed, standing disused for over a decade. A five-year, £7.5 million conversion led by architect Benjamin Tindall - one of the most complex conservation projects ever undertaken in Scotland, involving more than 1,000 contributors - reopened it in 1999 as The Hub, home of the Edinburgh International Festival.
interesting_fact: At 71.7 metres, The Hub's spire is the tallest point in central Edinburgh, visible for miles across the city skyline. Queen Elizabeth II formally reopened the building in 1999, and despite its new life as a festival venue, cafe and box office, the Church of Scotland's General Assembly still returns to meet inside it every May, keeping alive the very purpose the hall was built for over 180 years ago.

title: Camera Obscura & World of Illusions
about_site_text: Edinburgh's camera obscura began life on Calton Hill in 1835, built by Maria Theresa Short around a telescope she inherited from her father, instrument-maker Thomas Short. When the city demolished her observatory there in 1851, she relocated the whole operation here to Castlehill, buying a townhouse and opening it in 1853 as Short's Observatory, Museum of Science and Art. After her death in 1869 her husband kept it running until 1892, when the pioneering town planner Patrick Geddes took over, renaming it the Outlook Tower and using its floors to display the world, Europe, Scotland and Edinburgh in ascending order, with the camera obscura crowning the summit.
interesting_fact: Category A listed since 1970, it claims to be the oldest purpose-built visitor attraction in Edinburgh and one of the oldest in Britain. The original camera obscura, a rotating mirror projecting a live moving image of the city onto a table below, still operates on the top floor exactly as it did in Short's day, now beneath five further floors of the World of Illusions' mirror mazes and vortex tunnels. Geddes later built a second Outlook Tower in Montpellier, France, since absorbed into the Scots College there.

title: The Witchery by the Castle
about_site_text: The Witchery occupies Boswell's Court, a merchant's townhouse built in 1595 for Thomas Lowthian - its own naming story, and the literary visitors it drew a century and a half later, are told next door at Boswell's Court itself. By the 1970s the building had fallen into disrepair, serving latterly as Church of Scotland committee rooms, when 20-year-old chef James Thomson bought it in 1979, becoming Scotland's youngest licensee at a time when the Royal Mile was considered a poor location for a restaurant. In 1989 Thomson expanded into the former Castlehill School playground next door, creating the candlelit Secret Garden dining room, and later added nine Gothic-styled hotel suites above.
interesting_fact: The restaurant takes its name from the hundreds of men and women burned as witches on Castlehill during the 16th and 17th centuries, reputedly more than anywhere else in Scotland under James VI - a small bronze fountain, the Witches' Well, marks the spot just up the street. Local folklore holds The Witchery is itself haunted by one of the condemned, and its candlelit Gothic suites, one entered through a hidden bookcase door, have since hosted guests including Jack Nicholson and Andrew Lloyd Webber. The ghost stories have been good for business too: what began in 1979 as one man's punt on an unfashionable stretch of the Royal Mile has grown into an operation employing more than 70 staff, marking its 45th anniversary in 2024 by opening its own luxury goods shop next door.

title: The Scotch Whisky Experience
about_site_text: Opened on 5 May 1988 as the Scotch Whisky Heritage Centre, this attraction occupies a former Victorian school building immediately beside the Castle esplanade. It was the brainchild of Alastair McIntosh, a managing director at whisky blender William Muir Ltd, who persuaded nineteen Scotch whisky companies to put up £2 million so visitors unable to reach the Highlands could still learn the spirit's history. The original tour carried guests through 300 years of whisky-making in mock oak barrels past thirteen theatrical sets, designed by Heritage Projects, the team behind York's Jorvik Viking Centre. A £3 million renovation in 2023 replaced the barrel ride with three new galleries: Origins, The Art of Whisky Making and Maturation.
interesting_fact: Since 2009 the centre has housed the Diageo Claive Vidiz Whisky Collection, 3,384 bottles gathered over 35 years by a single Brazilian enthusiast and unveiled by then First Minister Alex Salmond - it's certified by Guinness World Records as the largest Scotch whisky collection on Earth, and its oldest bottle, a Buchanan's blend, dates back to 1897. Downstairs, the Amber restaurant and whisky bar stocks more than 420 single malts, blends and liqueurs, and the attraction has now welcomed more than 8.5 million visitors since it first opened its doors in 1988.

title: Tartan Weaving Mill
about_site_text: This building began as Castlehill Reservoir, built between 1849 and 1850 to supply the New Town with water, on a site that had earlier held a small 1755 reservoir and, before that, Christ Church chapel - demolished so its stone could help build the Tron Kirk. The huge cistern could hold two million gallons and discharge it at 5,000 gallons a minute; workmen digging the foundations reportedly found human remains and black oak coffins beneath the site. The reservoir was finally drained in 1992, opened briefly to public tours during the 1993 Doors Open Days, then bought and converted between 1995 and 1997 into the Old Town Weaving Company, later rebranded the Tartan Weaving Mill and Exhibition.
interesting_fact: Category B listed since 1987, the building still carries the Witches' Well, a small cast-iron fountain fixed to its outer wall commemorating those burned as witches nearby on Castlehill. Inside, a viewing window over the basement workshop lets visitors watch a working heritage loom weave tartan cloth in real time, a rare working link to the site's water-powered industrial past.

title: Cannonball House
about_site_text: Built in 1630 for furrier and skinner Alexander Mure and his wife Margaret Niellems - their initials and the date still carved above the door as 'AM MN 1630' - this Category A listed townhouse stands at the top of Castlehill, right by the entrance to the Castle esplanade. A 1913 restoration for the Edinburgh School Board converted it into an annex of the neighbouring Castlehill School, removing the narrow Blair's Close that had run through the building, though salvaged architectural fragments were reused elsewhere in the city. After the school closed in 1951 the building housed the Castlehill Urban Studies Centre and later a base for Edinburgh Festival walking tours, before becoming a restaurant under the Contini family in 2014.
interesting_fact: The house takes its name from the iron cannonball still lodged in its west-facing wall. Popular legend claims it was fired from the Castle's Half Moon Battery at Bonnie Prince Charlie during the 1745 Jacobite rising, but the more likely explanation is far less dramatic: engineers are thought to have fixed it there around 1675 to mark the exact gravitational height needed for Edinburgh's first piped water supply, drawn from springs at Comiston, to reach this point by gravity alone.

title: Ramsay Garden
about_site_text: Ramsay Garden takes its name from the poet and wigmaker Allan Ramsay the Elder, who built an octagonal house nicknamed 'Goosepie House' for its odd roofline here in 1733, later joined by a short Georgian terrace called Ramsay Street in 1760. Its present striking form dates from 1890-1893, when the pioneering town planner and biologist Patrick Geddes redeveloped the site as part of his wider campaign to regenerate Edinburgh's decaying Old Town, deliberately mixing university students, working artisans and wealthier residents in one community. Architect Stewart Henbest Capper designed the sixteen-apartment complex, with Sydney Mitchell completing construction after Capper's health failed. Today it remains private residential apartments and cannot be entered or accessed by visitors - it's best appreciated from the street outside, where its towers and balconies are clearly visible.
interesting_fact: Built in ornate Scots Baronial style, with red ashlar stonework beneath white harled upper storeys, towers and prominent balconies, Ramsay Garden is one of the most photographed silhouettes on the Edinburgh skyline, clearly visible from Princes Street far below. Geddes himself was fond enough of the result to call it 'the seven-towered castle I built for my beloved'. Past residents have included Ramsay's own descendants and the Royal Scottish Academy artist George Clark Stanton.

title: Castle Esplanade
about_site_text: The broad flat esplanade in front of Edinburgh Castle was created in 1753 as a military parade ground, built up using spoil excavated from the foundations of the Royal Exchange down on the High Street, then widened and given its present north wall and railings in 1816. Free to enter without a castle ticket, it offers sweeping views north to the Firth of Forth and south to the Pentland Hills. Since 1950 it has hosted the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo every August - the first show had just eight items and drew 6,000 spectators, compared with the roughly 10,000-seat temporary stadium built and dismantled here each summer today.
interesting_fact: Statues of Robert the Bruce and William Wallace flank the Castle's gatehouse at the esplanade's western end, while scattered across its edges are a small bronze Witches' Well commemorating those executed for witchcraft nearby, commissioned by Patrick Geddes in 1894; a memorial to the 78th Highlanders topped by an elephant, remembering a regimental mascot said to have enjoyed the soldiers' beer; a statue of Prince Frederick, Duke of York, of nursery-rhyme fame; and the grave of dragoon Charles Ewart, who captured a French army standard at Waterloo in 1815. The esplanade has hosted more than monuments and graves, though: since 1950 it has been transformed each August for the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, and that first, modest show - just eight items, watched from simple benches and scaffolding around three sides of the esplanade - still drew a combined audience of around 100,000 people across its 20 performances, an early sign of an appetite for the Tattoo that's never really let up since.

title: Edinburgh Castle
about_site_text: Edinburgh Castle sits on Castle Rock, the plug of an extinct volcano that has made this one of the most defensible sites in Scotland since at least the Iron Age, when it held a hillfort roughly 3,000 years ago. It became a royal residence under King Malcolm III Canmore in the 11th century and went on to be besieged more often than almost any other fortress in Britain, including a celebrated night raid in 1314 - led by Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, nephew of Robert the Bruce - that recaptured it from English hands by scaling the crag under cover of darkness. Today it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site holding the Honours of Scotland (the country's crown jewels) and the Stone of Destiny, used for centuries in the coronation of Scottish monarchs.
interesting_fact: Tucked within the walls, St Margaret's Chapel is the oldest surviving building in Edinburgh, built around 1130 by King David I and named for his canonised mother; barely large enough for a handful of people, it is still used today for small weddings and christenings. Every day at 1pm (except Sundays, Good Friday and Christmas Day) a gun fires from Mills Mount Battery - a tradition begun in 1861 so ships out in the Forth could set their chronometers even when fog hid the Nelson Monument's time ball on Calton Hill. The castle's most famous object has an even more eventful history than its oldest building: the Stone of Destiny, taken from Scone by Edward I in 1296 and built into the English coronation throne at Westminster Abbey, was stolen right back in 1950 when three Scottish students broke in and smuggled it home, eventually leaving it on the altar at Arbroath Abbey before authorities returned it south. It came to rest permanently at Edinburgh Castle only in 1996, carried down the Royal Mile past a crowd of around 10,000 people.

title: The Witches' Well
about_site_text: Set into the wall at the foot of Castle Esplanade, this small cast-iron drinking fountain marks the site of Edinburgh's principal witch-burning ground. It was commissioned in 1894 by town planner Sir Patrick Geddes and designed by his friend John Duncan, a leading figure of the Scottish Celtic Revival, and fixed to the outer wall of the newly built Castlehill Reservoir - the same building that later became the neighbouring Tartan Weaving Mill. A plaque explaining its symbolism was added in 1912. Roman numerals worked into the bronze relief, 1479 and 1722, bracket the two and a half centuries during which Scotland's Witchcraft Act sent an estimated 300 people to their deaths on this spot alone.
interesting_fact: The relief pairs a serene face with a wicked one, both entwined by a serpent coiled around Hygieia, Greek goddess of health, and her father Asclepius, god of medicine - a reminder that the same knowledge could heal or condemn its holder. A sprig of foxglove beside them makes the same point twice over: it is both a heart medicine and a poison. Scotland executed an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 people for witchcraft between the 16th and 18th centuries, a rate of persecution proportionally far higher than the more famous Salem trials three thousand miles away.

title: The India Cross
about_site_text: This sandstone Celtic cross, raised on Castle Esplanade in 1862, commemorates 256 officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 78th Highlanders - the Ross-shire Buffs - who died relieving the besieged British garrison at Lucknow during what an on-site Historic Environment Scotland panel now terms the Indian Rebellion or Mutiny of 1857-8. Indian soldiers had risen against British rule and besieged the city that June; when the 78th fought through the rebel lines to relieve it that September, the whole regiment was voted the Victoria Cross by ballot - a mechanism reserved for collective acts of gallantry too widespread to credit to one man - and the relieving commander General Henry Havelock is said to have declared he had 'never seen better conduct,' adding, 'I am not a Highlander but I wish I was one.'
interesting_fact: The regiment's elephant badge dates to the Battle of Assaye in 1803 and is carved into the cross itself. Around thirty years later the 78th brought a real elephant back to Edinburgh Castle - the animal reportedly led parades through the city, drank beer poured through the soldiers' canteen window, and was stabled alongside the regiment's horses. The 78th's lineage continues today within the Highlanders battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland.

title: Scottish Horse Memorial
about_site_text: This granite Celtic cross on Castle Esplanade was unveiled in 1904 to the men of the Scottish Horse, a yeomanry regiment raised in 1900 to fight in the Second Boer War. Two regiments were recruited that year from Scotland, Australia and South Africa to help Britain annex the South African Republic and Orange Free State, and the volunteers fought a brutal guerrilla campaign of night raids and farm-burning against Boer commandos. The design is credited to William Tait-Conner, with the granite carved by the firm Stewart McGlashan & Son; the regiment itself was disbanded at Edinburgh Castle in 1902, its lineage carried on today by the Scottish and North Irish Yeomanry.
interesting_fact: An identical memorial was unveiled the same year on Caledonia Hill in Kensington, Johannesburg, where it later became the official war memorial of the Transvaal Scottish regiment. Both crosses commemorate several Zulu scouts who served and died alongside the Scottish Horse - a rare instance of Black South African soldiers being formally named on a colonial-era war memorial - though sources disagree on the exact number honoured: Edinburgh's own on-site panel says three, while an account of the Johannesburg original says four.

title: The Afghan Needle
about_site_text: Known locally as the Afghan Needle, this pink Peterhead granite obelisk on Castle Esplanade was raised in 1882-83 by public subscription to the 105 officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 72nd Duke of Albany's Own Highlanders who were killed in action or died of wounds and disease during the First and Second Anglo-Afghan Wars of 1839-42 and 1878-80. Standing 3.5 metres tall behind iron railings and designed by the Aberdeen firm MacDonald, Field & Company, its base carries every name, rank and regiment, grouped by how each man died. It is listed Grade II* by Historic Environment Scotland.
interesting_fact: The 72nd amalgamated with the 78th Highlanders - commemorated by this leg's own India Cross a few steps away - to form the Seaforth Highlanders in the army reforms of 1881, only a year or two before this memorial itself went up. Both regiments' lineage now continues together within the Highlanders battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, so the esplanade's two 19th-century war memorials effectively honour the same modern regimental family.

title: The Gatehouse
about_site_text: The Gatehouse forming Edinburgh Castle's main entrance looks centuries old but is a Victorian addition, built in 1886-88 in Scots Baronial style to give the fortress a grander, more romantic approach befitting its status as a national monument - reportedly designed in some secrecy, since military authorities feared a cosmetic addition to a still-functioning garrison might draw public criticism. Flanking the archway in twin canopied niches, added decades later in 1929 to mark the 600th anniversary of Robert the Bruce's death, stand bronze statues of Bruce and William Wallace; the drawbridge and portcullis groove above the arch are both still in working order.
interesting_fact: Though it looks centuries old, the Gatehouse itself wasn't the work of a romantic castle architect: records credit its design to R. Lawson Scott of the Royal Engineers Department in London, drawn up in the same secretive spirit that kept the whole scheme out of public view until the stonework was already going up. The bronze figures flanking its arch - added four decades later - have their own separate stories, told at Robert the Bruce and William Wallace nearby.

title: Princess Louise's Fountain Memorial
about_site_text: A weathered stone memorial drinking fountain built into the Castle Esplanade's wall, its worn central panel carries a royal crown, a row of smaller crowns and an entwined monogram above twin round drinking basins, one on each side, their bronze fittings now dry and green with age. An inscription across its base names 'THE PRINCESS LOUISE'S ARGYLLSHIRE HIGHLANDERS', commemorating the regiment formed in 1881 when the 91st (Argyllshire Highlanders) amalgamated with the 93rd (Sutherland Highlanders) to become the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, styled 'Princess Louise's' after their royal colonel-in-chief. It stands among a cluster of esplanade memorials from the same turn-of-the-century era, including the nearby Scottish Horse Memorial.
interesting_fact: Princess Louise, Queen Victoria's fourth daughter and Duchess of Argyll by marriage, lent her name and patronage to the regiment for decades. An identical South African War memorial to the same regiment stands on Stirling Castle's esplanade, the regiment's other historic depot - suggesting this fountain also dates from just after the Second Boer War (1899-1902). No dedicated modern source records this specific fountain's exact unveiling date or sculptor, so its own worn inscription remains the clearest record of what it commemorates.

title: Robert the Bruce Statue
about_site_text: Standing in a canopied niche to the left of Edinburgh Castle's Gatehouse, this bronze figure of Robert the Bruce was sculpted by Thomas J. Clapperton and unveiled on 28 May 1929, the 600th anniversary year of the king's death. Bruce is shown crowned and armoured, gripping a battleaxe in one hand and a heraldic shield in the other - the pose recalling his decisive personal combat with Sir Henry de Bohun on the eve of Bannockburn in 1314, when he split the English knight's skull with a single axe blow while mounted on a small palfrey rather than a war-horse. The statue, and its companion figure of William Wallace on the Gatehouse's other side, were funded by a bequest from Captain Hugh Reid and chosen through a public design competition that proved surprisingly divisive, sparking heated debate in the Scottish press throughout 1928 and 1929 over how the nation's two great medieval heroes should be portrayed.
interesting_fact: Bruce seized the Scottish throne in 1306, was excommunicated and hunted as a fugitive - the source of the famous, probably apocryphal, tale of a spider inspiring him to try again after defeat - before his victory at Bannockburn in 1314 secured Scotland's independence in fact if not yet in law. He died in 1329, reputedly of leprosy, and asked that his heart be carried on crusade after his death; it was eventually brought home and is buried at Melrose Abbey, while the rest of him lies at Dunfermline Abbey.

title: William Wallace Statue
about_site_text: A matching niche to the right of the Gatehouse archway holds this bronze William Wallace, sculpted by Alexander Carrick and unveiled alongside its Robert the Bruce counterpart on 28 May 1929. Wallace is shown in chainmail and a plaid, gripping a claymore, with a helmet resting at his feet - both statues share niches designed by the architect Sir Robert Lorimer and were funded by the same Hugh Reid bequest that paid for the Bruce figure opposite.
interesting_fact: Wallace led the rebel Scottish army to victory over a much larger English force at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in September 1297 and was appointed Guardian of Scotland, but was defeated the following year at Falkirk. Betrayed and captured in 1305, he was taken to London and executed as a traitor to a crown he had never sworn allegiance to - his death only hardening Scottish resistance that culminated in Bruce's victory at Bannockburn sixteen years later. Braveheart (1995) popularised his story worldwide but takes wide liberties with the history; the real Wallace, for instance, almost certainly never wore a kilt, which did not yet exist in his lifetime.

title: Ensign Ewart Memorial and Grave
about_site_text: Charles Ewart, a sergeant in the Royal North British Dragoons - the regiment later known as the Royal Scots Greys - captured the eagle standard of the French 45th Regiment in brutal hand-to-hand combat at the Battle of Waterloo on 18 June 1815, fighting off a standard-bearer, a lancer and an infantryman in quick succession before carrying the eagle clear of the fighting. He was promoted to Ensign in reward and became a minor celebrity in Scotland, reportedly acquainted with Sir Walter Scott, though by his own account he shunned the attention. Ewart died in 1846 near Manchester and was buried in Salford, where his grave was later paved over and forgotten.
interesting_fact: His remains were rediscovered in the 1930s and reburied here on the Castle Esplanade, with a granite memorial unveiled at an official ceremony on 16 April 1938, attended by a guard of honour and the regimental band of the Royal Scots Greys. His own account of the fight survives almost word for word: 'I took the eagle from the enemy... he made a thrust at my groin; I parried it off and cut him down through the head.' In his memory, the Royal Scots Greys - and the Royal Scots Dragoon Guards that succeeded them - still wear an eagle badge today.

title: Johnston Terrace Wildlife Garden
about_site_text: Wedged onto a slope of the Old Town barely 50 metres from the Castle esplanade, this postage-stamp garden holds far more history than its size suggests. It began as the site of a medieval chapel, was later turned into a children's growing garden for fruit and vegetables under the influence of town planner Patrick Geddes, did service as a military post during the Second World War, and has at various points also worked as a playground and an outdoor cafe. Since the Scottish Wildlife Trust took over the adjoining office in 1982, the plot - at just 0.07 hectares, the smallest of the Trust's 123 Scottish nature reserves - has been managed as a tiny urban haven for wildlife, its broken-up concrete replaced with two ponds, a wildflower meadow and a stone wall, tucked in among the tenements along Johnston Terrace.
interesting_fact: Despite sitting in the shadow of one of Scotland's most fortified sites, the reserve now supports frogs, bumblebees and butterflies, with grey herons occasionally spotted overhead - proof that even a garden smaller than a tennis court, wedged into the Old Town's steepest stairway, can function as a genuine wildlife habitat.

title: The Vennel and Flodden Wall
about_site_text: Squeezed between tenement walls at the south-west corner of the Grassmarket, The Vennel is a steep, roughly 70-step stairway climbing to Lauriston Place above - and one of Edinburgh's most photographed spots, framing the Castle rising directly above the rooftops as you climb. Partway up, the path runs alongside a genuine surviving stretch of the Flodden Wall, thrown up in a panic after Scotland's catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Flodden in 1513 left the capital fearing an English invasion. Near the top of the steps, where Brown's Place meets the Vennel, the older wall gives way to the Telfer Wall, a westward extension enclosed between 1628 and 1636 after the merchant George Heriot donated land to the city - the surviving Flodden Tower bastion here still shows its distinctive crosslet gunloops, an early defensive answer to cannon fire.
interesting_fact: Despite being built to keep an army out, the wall never actually faced a siege - the English invasion Scotland feared after Flodden never came - so what survives today is less a monument to a battle fought than to a capital city bracing, at real expense, for one that never arrived. The name 'Vennel' itself comes from the French 'venelle', meaning a narrow lane or alley - a leftover of Scotland's centuries of trade and cultural ties with France, layered onto a stairway now better known for one of the most-photographed Castle views in the city.

title: Tanner's Close, West Port
about_site_text: Just off the Grassmarket, the run-down lodging houses of West Port's Tanner's Close became the base of operations for William Burke and William Hare, whose eleven-month, sixteen-victim killing spree in 1827-28 remains Scotland's most notorious murder case. Rather than robbing graves like the "resurrectionists" of popular imagination, the pair smothered vulnerable lodgers, drinking companions and acquaintances outright, then sold the fresh bodies to Robert Knox, a prominent Edinburgh anatomist who asked no questions about where his specimens came from. Hare turned King's Evidence and walked free; Burke was hanged in 1828 before a crowd of tens of thousands and, in a fitting final twist, was publicly dissected himself at the university where his victims had ended up. Tanner's Close itself was demolished in 1902-03, and the site today sits beneath the unremarkable office block Argyle House - nothing on the building marks what happened here.
interesting_fact: Burke's skeleton is still kept by the University of Edinburgh's Anatomical Museum, and a section of his skin was reportedly used to bind a small book, now held by Surgeons' Hall Museum - making him almost certainly the only Edinburgh murderer whose remains ended up on public display in two separate collections.

title: Beehive Inn
about_site_text: One of the Grassmarket's oldest surviving pub sites, the Beehive Inn traces its trade back to a coaching inn that once stood here, when mail coaches and travellers arriving from the south would have stabled their horses right outside. Robert Burns is said to have stayed next door during his 1786-87 visits to Edinburgh and to have watched cockfights held inside the inn - a blood sport common in Scottish taverns of the period. Today the pub is best known as the starting point of the Edinburgh Literary Pub Tour, launched here in 1996 as the city's first tour of its kind: two professional actors lead visitors between a handful of historic pubs, dramatising the lives and rivalries of Scottish writers from Burns and Sir Walter Scott through to Robert Louis Stevenson, Muriel Spark, and the generation of Rebus and Harry Potter. Behind its three-storey frontage, the pub also opens onto an extensive, tiered beer garden with views up toward the Castle - one of the largest outdoor drinking spaces in the Old Town.
interesting_fact: The tour still begins in a private function room on the Beehive's third floor before spilling out onto the Grassmarket - meaning most nights of the week, this centuries-old coaching inn is quietly hosting a two-hour dramatised argument about which Edinburgh writer deserves the last word. Upstairs on the first floor hangs a genuinely grim relic: the actual door from the condemned cell at Calton Jail, Edinburgh's former prison on Regent Road, long since demolished - a stray piece of the city's execution history that ended up decorating a pub built for drinking and theatre rather than punishment.

title: White Hart Inn
about_site_text: Parts of the White Hart Inn date back to 1516, making it a strong contender for the oldest continuously operating pub in Edinburgh's city centre - and, by its own reckoning, the most haunted. Its guest list includes Robert Burns, recorded staying here in 1791, and William and Dorothy Wordsworth, who lodged at the inn in 1803 during their tour of Scotland. Less welcome visitors reportedly included the body-snatchers Burke and Hare, said to have used the pub as a hunting ground for future victims among its clientele, and, in April 1916, a German Zeppelin: a bomb dropped during one of the first air raids on Britain detonated nearby, and an inscribed flagstone outside still marks the spot where it fell.
interesting_fact: The Zeppelin raid of 2-3 April 1916 killed 13 people and injured two dozen more across Edinburgh that night - making the bomb that fell close to the White Hart Inn's door part of the earliest aerial attack the city ever endured, a strange piece of 20th-century wartime history layered onto a pub already three centuries old.

title: Petit Paris
about_site_text: Gingham tablecloths and whitewashed walls give Petit Paris the look of a Left Bank cafe that wandered off course and settled in the Grassmarket - fitting, since it opened in 1998 in a space vacated by one of the original branches of Pierre Victoire, the budget French bistro chain that collapsed into receivership that same year amid allegations its founder had quietly siphoned company funds. Where that empire crashed, its former waiter thrived: Philippe Bachelet, originally from Orleans, had worked at Edinburgh's first Pierre Victoire since 1989 and later ran two Chez Jules franchises with his wife, Nathalie, before striking out alone on this same stretch of the Grassmarket. Bachelet bought the building's freehold in 2004 and completed a self-funded refurbishment in 2011, fitting bespoke oak units while keeping the gingham and whitewash that give the place its old-fashioned Parisian feel. Nearly three decades on, it remains an independent, family-run bistro serving classic French dishes such as coq au vin, with a 4.5-star average across thousands of reviews and a regular place on Tripadvisor's list of Edinburgh's best French restaurants.
interesting_fact: The Grassmarket square below Petit Paris's outdoor tables has been a marketplace since a 1477 royal charter and, for over a century from around 1660, the city's main site of public execution - the Covenanters' Memorial nearby marks exactly where the gallows stood. Diners here look straight up at Edinburgh Castle on its rock above the square, one of the more dramatic backdrops for a plate of moules frites anywhere in the city.

title: Patrick Geddes Steps
about_site_text: This flight of stone steps drops from Johnston Terrace down through Castle Wynd South to the Grassmarket, just a stone's throw from Edinburgh Castle's esplanade. Long a functional Old Town shortcut, the stairway was formally renamed the Patrick Geddes Steps in honour of the Scottish biologist-turned-town-planner who made this exact corner of the city his life's work. Geddes arrived in Edinburgh in 1884 and spent decades regenerating its decaying Old Town tenements, most visibly a few steps up the hill at Ramsay Garden, which he redeveloped into student and family flats between 1890 and 1893. At the top of these steps, a scrap of waste ground he once cleared survives today as the Johnston Terrace Wildlife Garden, still tended in his conservation-minded spirit.
interesting_fact: A small sign partway down the steps carries Geddes's own emblem: three doves representing 'hand, heart and head' - the trio of practical skill, feeling and thought he believed any real work of civic improvement had to combine, a motto he applied everywhere from his Old Town tenement plans to his university teaching.

title: Covenanters' Memorial
