about_site_text: At the east end of the Grassmarket, this low circular memorial marks the site of Edinburgh's public gallows, where more than 100 Covenanters - Presbyterians who refused to accept the crown's authority over the Church of Scotland - were hanged between 1661 and 1688, most during the 'Killing Time' of the 1680s. Erected by public subscription in 1937, the monument's cobbled surface is laid with a cross of differently coloured stone marking out the shadow the gallows themselves once cast across the square. A bronze band running around its rim carries the memorial's dedication, and an adjoining plaque names many of those who died here - one of them, the ordinary criminal Margaret 'Maggie' Dickson, is remembered today not on this stone but a few doors along, at the pub that still carries her name.
interesting_fact: The last Covenanter martyr executed here was James Renwick, hanged on 17 February 1688 - just two days after his 26th birthday - for refusing to swear an oath acknowledging the king's authority over the Church. His death came only months before the Glorious Revolution swept away the religious policy he had died opposing, one of the era's starker examples of a cause won just after its believers had already been executed for it.

title: W. Armstrong & Son (Armstrongs Vintage)
about_site_text: Racks of military surplus, kilts and ballgowns spill from every corner of this red-fronted shop at 81-83 Grassmarket, the original home of W. Armstrong & Son, a vintage clothing emporium trading under the family name since 1840. What began as a single Grassmarket outfitter has grown into a small Edinburgh institution with sister shops on Cockburn Street, Teviot Place and Clerk Street - the last of which now serves as the business's head office - stocking everything from cashmere to decades of retro fashion. Locals and regular customers still rate the original Grassmarket store as the pick of the four branches, prized for its size and the sheer depth of stock built up over nearly two centuries on the same spot.
interesting_fact: Armstrongs' enormous stock of genuine vintage military surplus and old uniforms, built up across generations rather than bought in for effect, has made it a go-to source for film and TV costume designers working in Edinburgh - on top of its everyday trade fitting festival-goers, students and fancy-dress shoppers from the very same rails.

title: Portsburgh Stone
about_site_text: This weathered, rounded boulder sitting beneath a tree in the small walled garden off West Port is known as the Portsburgh Stone, believed to be a glacial erratic dragged here during the last Ice Age - possibly from the Corstorphine quarries on the far side of the city, though an older, more fanciful theory once suggested it might be a fallen meteorite. It originally stood in Portsburgh, the burgh of barony that grew up just outside the city walls here after 1649, before being built into the perimeter wall of a Salvation Army hostel (now part of Edinburgh College of Art) alongside two smaller companion stones. When that stretch of wall was cleared in 1905, the stone was moved into the garden itself, where it has sat ever since.
interesting_fact: Of the stone's two smaller Ice-Age companions, only one survives today, still visible built into a wall of the college building nearby - the other has gone missing somewhere in more than a century of construction work since. The garden itself belongs to Edinburgh College of Art and has historically been open to the public only on Sundays, so this glacial visitor is easy to miss the rest of the week.

title: The Last Drop
about_site_text: A blunt, double-edged name hangs over this Grassmarket pub: for over a century a gallows stood right outside, and 'the last drop' is thought to mean either the condemned prisoner's final drink here before execution or the drop of the hangman's noose itself. Public hangings ran in the Grassmarket from 1660 until 4 February 1784, when a man named James Andrews became the last person executed on the site - practically on the doorstep of where you're standing now. The current building was rebuilt using original 17th-century stone salvaged from the historic tenements that once stood here, keeping something physically continuous with the executions the name still commemorates.
interesting_fact: Staff and regulars have long reported the pub is haunted by the ghost of a small girl in old-fashioned, medieval-style clothing, seen both in the cellar and around the bar - an oddly gentle haunting for a building named after mass public execution. The pub sits only a short walk from the Covenanters' Memorial and the cobblestone pattern marking the actual site of the gallows, so drinkers here are, quite literally, having a last drop where condemned prisoners once had theirs.

title: Maggie Dicksons
about_site_text: Margaret 'Maggie' Dickson lends this pub both her name and one of the Grassmarket's most retold escapes: a fishwife hanged here on 2 September 1724 for concealing a pregnancy after the death of her newborn son. Her coffin was loaded onto a cart bound for burial in Musselburgh, but when the driver stopped for lunch at the Sheep Heid Inn along the way, he discovered Maggie was still alive inside it. Under Scots law a death sentence carried out and survived could not lawfully be repeated, so 'Half-Hangit Maggie' walked free - and, according to local legend, went on to live for decades afterwards, eventually running a pub of her own on this same stretch of the Grassmarket.
interesting_fact: The pub that carries her name today leans fully into the gothic backstory, decorated with dark wood panelling, exposed brick and a skeleton locked in a set of stocks by the door. It stands only metres from the Covenanters' Memorial marking Grassmarket's old execution site, meaning Maggie's own brush with the noose happened almost exactly where her namesake pub now pours pints.

title: Candlemaker Row
about_site_text: Tallow and wick smoke once filled this row's air: Candlemaker Row takes its name from Edinburgh's candlemaking trade, banished here from the cramped closes of the Old Town after a fire that broke out in a candle workshop killed the Deacon of the Bonnetmakers' Guild. Pushed out to what was then open ground near the old Bristo Port and town wall, the Incorporation of Candlemakers of Edinburgh built a proper guild hall on the row in 1722 to hold its meetings, its doorway carved with a shield and the date, marking the trade's new, safer home away from the tightly packed tenements above.
interesting_fact: That 1722 hall, a four-storey block with two square stair towers, still stands on Candlemaker Row today - restored in 1979, it's the only incorporation hall left standing anywhere in Edinburgh out of the city's many historic craft guilds. The candlemakers' Latin motto, 'Omnia manifesta luce' ('All things are revealed by light'), was a fitting boast for tradesmen whose entire business was keeping Edinburgh's nights lit before gas or electric lighting ever existed.

title: The Elephant House
about_site_text: The Elephant House opened as a cafe on George IV Bridge in 1995 and became world-famous as one of the places J.K. Rowling wrote parts of the early Harry Potter novels between about 1996 and 1999, drawn in by cheap coffee, long communal tables and a back-room view over Greyfriars Kirkyard. A devastating fire in a neighbouring property in August 2021 gutted the cafe, and the closure dragged on for more than four years once the building's owner went into liquidation; it finally reopened on 29 December 2025, its refurbished back room renamed the Writers' Room and hung with portraits of Rowling alongside fellow Edinburgh writers Ian Rankin, Alexander McCall Smith and Irvine Welsh. The original table Rowling wrote at was salvaged from the wreckage and sits back in place for visitors today.
interesting_fact: The cafe's own Harry Potter fame is often tangled up with a separate, much-repeated legend from just over the kirkyard wall: that a gravestone belonging to one Thomas Riddell inspired Voldemort's birth name. That story properly belongs to Thomas Riddell's Grave itself, a short walk away in Greyfriars Kirkyard - the Elephant House's real, well-documented connection to Rowling is this room and that table, not the headstone.

title: George IV Bridge
about_site_text: Nine semicircular stone arches carry George IV Bridge across the deep Cowgate valley - though only two are visible today, the rest buried beneath the shops, tenements and even a festival venue built directly on top. Architect Thomas Hamilton designed the crossing to carry a new road from the Old Town's South Side up to the Lawnmarket, its ceremonial foundation stone laid on 15 August 1827. Funding shortfalls and disputes with the Edinburgh Improvement Commissioners dragged construction out for nearly a decade - Hamilton himself resigned from the project in 1834 - and the bridge wasn't finally finished until 1836.
interesting_fact: Building the bridge meant demolishing two historic streets outright, Old Bank Close and Libberton's Wynd, taking with it John Dowie's Tavern - a tiny, much-loved 18th-century howff where Robert Burns was a regular, favouring its smallest snug, nicknamed 'the coffin', which sat only four or six people at a squeeze.

title: National Library of Scotland
about_site_text: The National Library of Scotland traces its roots to the Advocates Library, founded in the early 1680s and formally opened in 1689, which gained the right to a free copy of every book published in Britain under the Copyright Act of 1710. It only became a national institution in its own right in 1925, when an Act of Parliament formally established it, backed by a £100,000 endowment from Sir Alexander Grant, managing director of the biscuit firm McVitie & Price. Grant later matched that with a further £100,000 toward a purpose-built home on George IV Bridge, designed by Reginald Fairlie from 1934 and finally completed in 1956 after wartime delays halted construction for years.
interesting_fact: Legal deposit still applies today: by law the library is entitled to a copy of virtually everything published in the UK and Ireland, in print or online, and its holdings have grown to somewhere in the region of 30 million items - one of the largest research collections in Europe, sitting almost next door to Edinburgh's own public library on this same short stretch of George IV Bridge.

title: Edinburgh Central Library
about_site_text: Designed by George Washington Browne in an ornate French Renaissance style, Edinburgh Central Library opened on George IV Bridge in 1890 as the city's first public library. The building drops away below street level, with further storeys descending through the gorge towards the Cowgate. It stands on the site of a 1616 townhouse belonging to Sir Thomas Hope, whose carved stone lintel - inscribed 'TECUM HABITA 1616' - was preserved and set into the new building.
interesting_fact: The library was paid for by the Scottish-American steel magnate Andrew Carnegie, who doubled his original offer of £25,000 to £50,000 after being shown the site. Carnegie insisted the words 'Let there be Light' be carved above the entrance of every library he funded, and they appear above the door here too. He wasn't present when Lord Rosebery officially opened the building on 9 June 1890 - instead a telegram from Carnegie was read out, hoping 'that this Library is to grow in usefulness year after year.' Edinburgh is still the only local authority in the UK that classifies its adult library collection using the Library of Congress system rather than Dewey Decimal.

title: Victoria Street
about_site_text: Victoria Street curls in a single elegant bow from the Grassmarket up to George IV Bridge, its rainbow-painted shopfronts making it one of the most photographed streets in Scotland. It began life as the West Bow, a notoriously crooked and dangerous medieval route linking the Grassmarket to the Royal Mile, until architect Thomas Hamilton - the same man behind George IV Bridge itself - swept much of it away between 1827 and 1834 as part of Edinburgh's Improvement Act works. Renamed in 1837 to mark Queen Victoria's accession, the street's two-tier design left an upper walkway, Victoria Terrace, running along its northern side above the shops.
interesting_fact: The street is widely credited, if unofficially, as an inspiration for Diagon Alley in the Harry Potter books - J.K. Rowling worked for years at the Elephant House on George IV Bridge, a few minutes' walk from its top end, and would have passed this way often. Its older name, West Bow, has darker associations too: in 1670 a respected Edinburgh soldier named Major Thomas Weir confessed on his deathbed to decades of black magic, and was executed as the self-styled 'Wizard of the West Bow'.

title: The Red Door Gallery
about_site_text: One of the shopfronts most responsible for Victoria Street's rainbow reputation, the Red Door Gallery trades behind its namesake scarlet doorway at number 42, carrying work from around 150 UK and Scottish artists. Inside, contemporary screenprints and giclee art prints sit alongside designer jewellery, enamel pins, knitwear and handmade greetings cards - independent, small-run work rather than mass-produced tourist stock. Trading from this address since 2003, it's one of dozens of small, owner-run shops that have filled Victoria Street's curved Georgian frontages since the street's 1830s construction, keeping independent retail alive on one of the most photographed streets in Scotland.
interesting_fact: The gallery is open all seven days of the week, year-round - a rarity among small independent Old Town shops, and a reflection of just how much passing footfall Victoria Street's photogenic curve now draws.

title: Victoria Terrace
about_site_text: Reached by a narrow flight of steps just off Victoria Street, Victoria Terrace is the surviving upper deck of Thomas Hamilton's 1827-34 rebuilding of the old West Bow - an iron-railed balcony walkway laid along the rooftops of the buildings below, lined with its own small row of shops and cafes, and giving uninterrupted views down over Victoria Street's curved, candy-coloured shopfronts to the Grassmarket beyond. It mirrors, on a smaller scale, the same trick Hamilton pulled off with George IV Bridge a few streets over: a street built up on hidden lower levels, so what looks like solid ground is really a bridge or terrace over the buildings and streets below.
interesting_fact: From the terrace's railing, the view stretches from Victoria Street's coloured rooftops below all the way up to Edinburgh Castle on its rock - one of the few places in the Old Town where you can look straight down onto a whole street from a walkway built directly above its shops.

title: Greyfriars Hall
about_site_text: Rising above the Cowgate with a Gothic tower and pointed windows, Greyfriars Hall began life around 1861 as Cowgatehead Church, one of several 19th-century churches built to serve Edinburgh's crowded Old Town parishes. The congregation eventually moved on and the building passed out of religious use, standing empty for years before being restored as part of Virgin Hotels Edinburgh, which opened across three linked historic buildings on the site in 2022. The old nave's vaulted ceiling and stone tracery survive intact inside, now used as an event space seating up to 150, while a new glass-fronted extension - visible right beside the old tower - was built onto the church to house the hotel's modern guest floors.
interesting_fact: The hotel's design team, led by Edinburgh-based ICA Studio, first sketched the plan to link the old church with its neighbouring buildings back in 2013 - meaning the glass-and-stone building visible today took the better part of a decade to go from an architect's sketch to a finished hotel.

title: Tomb of John Bayne of Pitcairlie
about_site_text: Built into the boundary wall of Greyfriars Kirkyard, this weathered stone mausoleum commemorates John Bayne of Pitcairlie, a writer to the signet (a senior class of Edinburgh lawyer) who died in 1681. Bayne made his name and fortune supervising the building contracts for Charles II's 1670s renovation of Holyrood Palace, working alongside architects Sir William Bruce and Robert Mylne on major Edinburgh projects including Canongate Kirk and the Tron Kirk. His widow, Eupham Aikman, won permission from the Town Council in 1684 to raise this monument in his memory; masons Philip Alisone and Patrick Hunter built it, and James Andersone painted and gilded the carved surface, which still carries a long Latin inscription.
interesting_fact: Carved into the statue's hand is a purse holding the royal signet - a nod to Bayne's own career - while the tomb's sheer opulence reflects a wider shift in the kirkyard after 1660, when burial inside the church itself was outlawed and wealthy Edinburgh families began competing instead to build the grandest possible monument out in the yard.

title: Greyfriars Kirk
about_site_text: Standing at the edge of its own kirkyard just off George IV Bridge, Greyfriars Kirk was Edinburgh's first church built after the Reformation, opening on Christmas Day 1620 on land that had belonged to a Franciscan friary until Reformers destroyed it in 1559. A gunpowder explosion in 1718 - stored in the tower during a siege - wrecked much of the structure, and the church was later split into two separate congregations, Old and New Greyfriars, that worshipped side by side until reuniting in 1929. It remains an active Church of Scotland parish today, its plain harled walls and squat tower giving little outward hint of the momentous scene that unfolded just outside its door in 1638.
interesting_fact: The National Covenant - a mass declaration against royal interference in Scottish worship - was laid out on a flat tombstone in the churchyard on 28 February 1638 for signing, and within weeks copies had circulated the country so widely that tens of thousands of Scots had added their names, some reputedly signing in their own blood.

title: Greyfriars Kirkyard
about_site_text: Table tombs, wall monuments and grand mausolea crowd every path through Greyfriars Kirkyard, together forming one of the richest collections of post-Reformation funerary architecture in Scotland. The ground has served as one of Edinburgh's main burial grounds since 1562, when Mary Queen of Scots granted the town council land that had previously belonged to a Franciscan friary - the 'grey friars' whose robes gave the site its name. With the Old Town's older kirkyards long full, it became the resting place for generations of merchants, lawyers and reformers. Notable residents include James Craig, the young architect who won the competition to design Edinburgh's New Town but died in poverty in 1795 and was buried here in an unmarked grave, since given a memorial noting his legacy. Just inside the main gate on Candlemaker Row is also the small headstone marking where Bobby, the loyal terrier commemorated by the statue at this leg's end, was buried in 1872.
interesting_fact: By the early 1800s the kirkyard was so tempting a target for body-snatchers supplying the city's anatomy schools that grieving families began fitting heavy iron cages called mortsafes over freshly dug graves - several can still be seen bolted in place near the kirkyard's boundary walls today.

title: Covenanters' Prison
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard (Forrest Road side), Edinburgh EH1 2QL
about_site_text: In the southeast corner of Greyfriars Kirkyard, behind a locked iron gate off Candlemaker Row, lies the walled enclosure known as the Covenanters' Prison. After the Covenanter army was crushed at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge in June 1679, around 1,200 prisoners were marched to Edinburgh and held here in the open air for more than four months, each allotted just four ounces of bread a day. Dozens died of exposure and starvation before winter set in; others were tried and executed, escaped, or bought freedom by signing a bond renouncing the Covenant. In November 1679 some 257 survivors, sentenced to transportation to the American colonies, were marched to Leith and put aboard a ship called the Crown. It wrecked off Deerness, Orkney on 10 December during a storm; by one survivor's account, the crew battened the hatches to stop the prisoners escaping the sinking ship, and nearly all of them drowned, still shackled below deck.
interesting_fact: The grand mausolea now crowded inside the enclosure mostly date from after 1705, when the ground was formally laid out for burials - meaning almost none of the monuments a visitor sees today existed when the Covenanters were actually confined here in the open air in 1679.

title: The Black Mausoleum
about_site_text: Tucked against the southern boundary wall of Greyfriars Kirkyard, this domed classical mausoleum was built for Sir George Mackenzie of Rosehaugh, the King's Advocate who prosecuted the Covenanters imprisoned metres away in 1679 and earned the nickname 'Bloody Mackenzie' for the executions he ordered during the period later known as the Killing Time. Designed by architect James Smith and completed shortly before Mackenzie's death in 1691, its drum-shaped, colonnaded form was unusual for Restoration-era Scotland. Mackenzie was also a founding force behind the Advocates' Library, later absorbed into the National Library of Scotland just up the street.
interesting_fact: Local legend holds that a homeless man sheltering inside the mausoleum in December 1998 fell through a collapsed floor into an underground burial vault full of disturbed remains, triggering the 'Mackenzie Poltergeist' - years of reported scratches, bruises and fainting among visitors that made this one of the most-investigated 'haunted' sites in Britain, and led the kirkyard's keyholder to have the tomb locked and exorcised in 1999. Tour guides and Harry Potter fan sites also point to the mausoleum's poltergeist as a possible inspiration for Hogwarts' own mischievous poltergeist, Peeves - a comparison Rowling has never confirmed and that appears to rest on general atmosphere rather than any documented naming link.

title: Greyfriars Bobby's Bar
about_site_text: This Category B listed pub occupies the ground floor of a row of early Georgian houses at the foot of Candlemaker Row, built as part of the same 1720s development as the neighbouring Candlemakers' Hall next door. Long a Candlemaker Row tavern under other names, it was renamed Greyfriars Bobby's Bar after the small Skye terrier whose statue - cast by sculptor William Brodie and unveiled in 1873, the year after the dog's death - stands on the pavement just outside its door. Inside, dark wood panelling and old photographs of the real Bobby lean into the legend, while the pub's position squarely between the kirkyard gate and the statue makes it one of the most-photographed backdrops on this stretch of the walk.
interesting_fact: The famously shiny nose and paws visitors pause to rub for luck belong to the bronze dog on the pavement outside, not to the pub itself - see the Greyfriars Bobby Statue for that story, including the city council's occasional re-gilding of the worn bronze to stop generations of polishing from eating into the metal.

title: Bedlam Theatre
about_site_text: A short walk past Greyfriars, this red sandstone Gothic building at the corner of Forrest Road and Bristo Place was built in 1848 as the New North Free Church, designed by Thomas Hamilton, one of the architects behind the Scott Monument and the Royal High School. The congregation left in 1941, and after decades as a University of Edinburgh chaplaincy and storeroom, students converted the deconsecrated church into a theatre in 1980-81, keeping its steep gabled roof and lancet windows intact. Today the Bedlam Theatre is the oldest continuously running student theatre in Britain, staging around forty University of Edinburgh Theatre Company productions a year and packing in up to eight separate Fringe shows a day every August.
interesting_fact: The theatre takes its name not from the church but from the area's earlier history: this stretch of Forrest Road once stood beside Edinburgh's 'Bedlam', a poorhouse and asylum, where the poet Robert Fergusson - a major influence on the young Robert Burns - died in 1774 at just twenty-four.

title: Sandy Bell's
about_site_text: A fiddle tune spilling onto Forrest Road most evenings is usually the first clue you've found Sandy Bell's - a pub that began life as an ordinary grocery shop, its narrow, oddly proportioned interior still giving the game away. It was already a bar by the 1920s, run by an owner named Mrs Bell, before regulars started calling it simply 'Sandy Bell's' - a nickname that stuck for over fifty years before it ever appeared on a sign. From the 1960s, under landlord Jimmy Cairney, it became one of the true engine rooms of the Scottish folk revival, hosting nightly sessions and after-hours 'kitchen ceilidhs' that drew players from across the city and abroad. Hamish Henderson, the poet and folklorist often called the father of that revival, held informal court here for years; a small bust of him still watches over the bar today. It only adopted 'Sandy Bell's' as its official name in the early 1990s.
interesting_fact: Musicians who passed through its sessions include Barbara Dickson, Billy Connolly, Gerry Rafferty, Aly Bain, Johnny and Phil Cunningham, and Dick Gaughan - and the influential folk group Jock Tamson's Bairns formed out of chance meetings at the bar. Traditional Scottish and Irish sessions still run here most nights, making it one of the longest continuously running folk-music pubs in the country.

title: Bristo Port (Flodden Wall)
address: Forrest Road (between nos. 5 and 7), Edinburgh EH1 2QQ
about_site_text: A small marker and a line of dark cobbles (setts) set into the pavement here trace the course of Edinburgh's Flodden Wall, the town's defensive perimeter begun in fearful haste after the catastrophic Scottish defeat at the Battle of Flodden in 1513. This spot marks the site of the Bristo Port - also called the Greyfriars or Society Port - a fortified gateway built around 1515 where the wall crossed what became Bristo Street, controlling movement in and out of the walled burgh. The gate itself vanished long before Forrest Road was cut through the area in the 1860s to link George IV Bridge with the university quarter, so almost nothing survives above ground; walk between numbers 5 and 7 today and the gap in the modern paving is essentially all you'll find of it.
interesting_fact: Bristo Port was a comparatively late addition to the Flodden Wall circuit, added as the built-up area crept south toward Greyfriars decades after the original wall line was hurriedly laid out in 1513 - a reminder that the 'town wall' visitors picture as one single ring was actually extended and patched piecemeal over more than a century.

title: Teviot Row House
about_site_text: Opened on 19 October 1889, Teviot Row House is generally reckoned to be the oldest purpose-built students' union building in the world - earlier student societies had simply borrowed rooms elsewhere, but this was designed and built from scratch for the job. Architects Sydney Mitchell and Wilson gave it a Scots Baronial look, with pinnacled drum towers and crow-stepped gables echoing the royal palaces at Holyrood and Falkland, built in warm Hailes sandstone. It was extended westward in 1902-05 to add a dining hall and further bars, then again with a plainer rear block in 1962. The site has older roots too: it once held a townhouse belonging to Lord Ross, later a lying-in hospital that operated here between 1793 and 1842, before the union building replaced it. Push through the doors today and you'll find a few in-jokes layered onto all that history, not least a mounted moose head presiding over one of the archways.
interesting_fact: A mounted moose head hangs over one of Teviot's archways under a long-running student tradition: any group that can remove it and prove - with photographic evidence - that they've carried it more than a mile from the building gets their names added to a plaque installed beside it. It has apparently never been successfully retrieved for good.

title: Reid Concert Hall
about_site_text: Funded by the bequest of General John Reid, a British Army officer, flautist and composer who endowed Edinburgh University's Chair of Music, Reid Concert Hall opened on 14 February 1859, designed in an Italianate neoclassical style by the Scottish architect David Cousin. Its intimate 218-seat auditorium sits beneath a richly coffered, tunnel-vaulted ceiling, with a 1978 organ built by the German firm Jurgen Ahrend against the east wall. For well over a century the building also housed a remarkable museum gallery of historic instruments, assembled by Professor John Donaldson and long considered the oldest purpose-built musical instrument museum in Europe. Sit in the stalls on a concert night and the hall's original purpose is still obvious - it was built purely for the sound to carry, not for spectacle.
interesting_fact: That instrument collection moved out in 2017, relocating to St Cecilia's Hall on the Cowgate to form a single 5,000-object collection - so the display cases here stand empty today, though the hall still hosts concerts, including an annual Reid Concert every 13 February marking General Reid's birthday and his gift to the university. During the Festival Fringe it becomes 'The Cowbarn', an Underbelly comedy venue.

title: McEwan Lantern Pillar
about_site_text: Standing at the edge of Bristo Square opposite McEwan Hall's entrance, this tall tapering pillar of Portland stone was designed by Robert Rowand Anderson - the same architect responsible for McEwan Hall itself - and erected around 1890. It combines a decorative lamp standard with carved detailing, including the McEwan family coat of arms, and was presented to the City of Edinburgh by the brewer and Liberal MP William McEwan alongside his much larger gift of the Hall, which opened a few streets away on 3 December 1897. McEwan had left school at fourteen to work in his uncle's brewery and built it into one of Scotland's largest, later ploughing a fortune into university buildings across the campus that still bear his name.
interesting_fact: Despite being a Category B listed structure in its own right - officially catalogued by Historic Environment Scotland as the 'Corporation Lamp', a nod to its status as a civic gift rather than purely a university one - the lantern pillar is easy to walk straight past, with most visitors' eyes going straight to the huge domed hall behind it. That's a fitting fate for a monument to William McEwan, who spent his career building one of Scotland's largest breweries only to become, in later life, an active member of the Temperance Society campaigning against alcohol - an irony that had little visible effect on the flow of McEwan's beer, or on the university buildings his fortune paid for across the campus around this pillar.

title: The Next Big Thing is a Series of Little Things
address: Bristo Square, Edinburgh (paving between the Dugald Stewart Building and McEwan Hall)
about_site_text: Easy to miss underfoot, this artwork by artist Susan Collis consists of around 1,600 small bronze dots set into the paving of Bristo Square, meandering roughly 68 metres from near the Dugald Stewart Building across to the entrance of McEwan Hall. Titled 'The Next Big Thing is a Series of Little Things', the piece resembles a trail of dripped paint spilled carelessly across the stone - a playful, almost invisible companion to the grand Victorian architecture surrounding the square that most people cross a dozen times before they ever notice it underfoot. It was installed as part of a wider redevelopment of the square that also brought in new paving, seating and lighting for the university's central plaza.
interesting_fact: Collis designed the dots to change with use rather than stay fixed: as thousands of students' feet cross the square every day, the bronze studs slowly polish up brighter than the stone around them, so the artwork is quite literally still being finished by the people walking over it, years after it was installed - a fitting twist on a title that plays on the cliche 'the next big thing', suggesting grand ambitions are really just an accumulation of small, easily overlooked details, much like the dots themselves. It was the University's first major public art commission in years, cast by the Powderhall Bronze Foundry and installed over about three weeks as part of the wider redevelopment of McEwan Hall and Bristo Square, with the trail of drips starting from McEwan Hall's original main doorway - so it traces, roughly, the route generations of graduates have walked away from their own graduation ceremony.

title: Old Medical School
about_site_text: This vast red sandstone complex, designed by Robert Rowand Anderson after he won an 1874 architectural competition, opened through the 1880s in a Northern Italian Renaissance style, with palazzo-style frontages and a corbelled stair turret that still catches the evening light along Teviot Place. It was built to give Edinburgh's rapidly growing Medical School - founded back in 1726 and previously squeezed into Old College - room to expand, and its footprint is enormous: the complex runs the entire length of the block from Teviot Place down the top of Middle Meadow Walk. Integral to the new building was a purpose-built Anatomical Museum, which opened in 1884 and still holds the university's historic anatomy and pathology collections today. The courtyard at its heart was officially renamed the Elsie Inglis Quadrangle in 2017, and its walls are lined with blue plaques to the school's most influential figures.
interesting_fact: Along the quad's walls: Sir James Young Simpson, who discovered chloroform's anaesthetic properties in 1847 after testing it on himself one evening; Joseph Lister, whose antiseptic techniques transformed surgical survival rates; Sir Robert Sibbald, the school's 17th-century founding professor; James Lind, whose 1747 trial proved citrus cured scurvy; Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, a medical graduate who based Sherlock Holmes's deductive method on one of his own professors here; physiologist Sir Edward Sharpey-Schafer, a pioneer of hormone research; and three trailblazing women - Sophia Jex-Blake, one of the 'Edinburgh Seven' who fought to open medical education to women; Elsie Inglis, the WWI medical pioneer the quadrangle is now named after; and Mary Pickford, who became the school's first female professor in 1966.

title: George Heriot's School (Main Building)
about_site_text: George Heriot, court goldsmith and moneylender to James VI, picked up the nickname 'Jinglin' Geordie' from the coins and jewels that rattled in his pockets as he did business around the city - and left just over £23,625 on his death in 1624, worth several million pounds today, to found a charitable hospital school for 'poor fatherless bairns'. Its foundation stone was laid in 1628, with master mason William Wallace leading construction until his death in 1631, succeeded by William Aytoun and then John Mylne; Sir William Bruce later added the distinctive central tower between 1676 and 1693. Building work was interrupted when Oliver Cromwell's occupying troops used the half-finished quadrangle as a barracks, reportedly stabling horses in what would become the chapel. It finally opened in 1659 with thirty pupils, converted to a fee-paying day school in 1885, and admitted girls for the first time in 1979.
interesting_fact: Generations of pupils have nicknamed the building 'the Wark' - simply 'the works' - out of grudging local affection for what's widely considered one of the finest examples of Scottish Renaissance architecture in the country, its quadrangle also holding the more sombre distinction of being the first large building constructed outside Edinburgh's old town walls. Heriot's own fame outlived him by two centuries: Sir Walter Scott turned him into a character, the kindly goldsmith 'Geordie Heriot', in his 1822 novel The Fortunes of Nigel, lending a real King James VI moneylender's fortune to help a fictional young lord out of debt - a portrayal that did as much as anything to fix the 'Jinglin' Geordie' nickname in popular memory.

title: Middle Meadow Walk
address: Middle Meadow Walk, Edinburgh (northern end, near Teviot Place)
about_site_text: This tree-lined path began taking shape in 1722, when Thomas Hope of Rankeillor leased the old, boggy bed of the drained Burgh Loch and set about turning it into an ornamental park with formal walkways. In 1737 the Town Council granted a strip of land across George Heriot's Hospital's own grounds to extend the route north toward Forrest Road, and it opened fully to the public in 1743 once a gap was cut through the old city wall at its head. It was formally relaid in the 1850s after a Town Council design competition, gaining stone gatepiers whose carved unicorns - added in 1850 by sculptor Alexander Handyside Ritchie, one bearing Edinburgh's own coat of arms and motto and the other Scotland's royal one - replaced the original wooden posts marking the walk's north end.
interesting_fact: For roughly 170 years, Edinburgh's civic authorities and residents fought off repeated attempts to open this route to wheeled traffic - documented campaigns in 1864, 1871, 1873-74, 1876, 1879, 1885, 1892, 1895, 1915, 1919, 1921-22, 1928, 1931, 1935-36, 1946 and 1962 all failed, several defeated by public meetings thousands strong. The only concession ever won was a cycle lane added in 1983, meaning this has remained a pedestrian route in substance for very nearly three centuries.

title: Lister Housing Co-operative (Georgian Tenements)
about_site_text: This block of Georgian tenements, built between 1816 and 1824 around Heriot Place, Keir Street and Lauriston Place, had fallen into serious disrepair by the 1970s. Rather than see it demolished, residents formed one of Edinburgh's early tenant-led housing co-operatives, taking ownership of the buildings and securing government funding for a full rehabilitation carried out between 1978 and 1982 - work that went on to win a Saltire Award. Part of the funding came through the Lister Trust, set up in memory of Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery, whose old Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh stands directly across Lauriston Place.
interesting_fact: In the mid-1980s the co-operative expanded again, taking on a U-shaped tenement across the road that the Royal Infirmary itself had earmarked for demolition. The 1990-92 rescue created 50 new flats at a cost of £5.5 million, making it the highest-value housing project in Scotland at the time. The co-operative has since paid off every loan it took out and now owns all of its properties outright, a rare outcome for a scheme of this size and age.

title: Greyfriars Bobby Statue
address: Corner of George IV Bridge & Candlemaker Row, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ
about_site_text: A small bronze dog perches above a granite drinking fountain at the corner of George IV Bridge and Candlemaker Row, facing Greyfriars Kirkyard's gate across the street. The statue commemorates Bobby, a Skye terrier said to have belonged to John Gray, a nightwatchman with the Edinburgh City Police. When Gray died of tuberculosis in 1858 and was buried in the kirkyard opposite, tradition holds that Bobby kept vigil at his grave for the next fourteen years, becoming so well known around the Old Town that Edinburgh's Lord Provost, Sir William Chambers, personally paid for the dog's licence in 1867 and had him fitted with a collar, now on display in the Museum of Edinburgh. Sculptor William Brodie cast the memorial from life not long after Bobby's own death in 1872, and English philanthropist Baroness Angela Burdett-Coutts funded its unveiling on 15 November 1873.
interesting_fact: Generations of visitors touching Bobby's nose and paws for good luck have rubbed them to a bright, polished shine - so much wear that Edinburgh City Council has had to regild the discoloured bronze more than once to keep the polishing from eating into the metal itself. Despite being barely knee-high, the statue and its fountain became a Category A listed structure in 1977, reputedly Edinburgh's smallest; the water itself stopped flowing in 1975 after a health scare, leaving what was once a two-level trough - a basin for horses above, a lower one for dogs - purely decorative ever since.

title: Greyfriars Bobby's Grave
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (just inside the main gate)
about_site_text: Just inside Greyfriars Kirkyard's main gate, close to the George IV Bridge/Candlemaker Row entrance, a small red granite headstone marks the traditional burial spot of Greyfriars Bobby, the loyal terrier who is said to have kept vigil at his master John Gray's grave for fourteen years. The stone itself is much newer than the 1872 burial it commemorates: it was erected by the Dog Aid Society of Scotland and unveiled by His Royal Highness The Duke of Gloucester on 13 May 1981, more than a century after Bobby's death. Bobby's own grave lies around seventy-five yards from Gray's, since dogs could not normally be buried within the kirkyard itself - a small, unofficial exception made for the city's most famous mourner.
interesting_fact: Not everyone accepts the loyal-vigil story at face value. Historian Jan Bondeson's 2011 research argued that Bobby was more likely a stray, encouraged to stay around the graveyard by kirkyard staff and a nearby restaurant owner keen to draw visitors, and kept fed to hunt rats rather than to mourn at any particular grave - he may even have been two different dogs, the original dying around 1867 and a younger animal carrying on the routine for the rest of the fourteen-year vigil. Bondeson points to more than sixty similar 'faithful graveyard dog' stories recorded elsewhere in 19th-century Europe as evidence the tale follows a familiar folk pattern rather than a one-off event.

title: Thomas Riddell's Grave
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (southern yard, near the boundary wall)
about_site_text: A weathered sandstone marker toward the back of Greyfriars Kirkyard's southern yard carries two names: Thomas Riddell Esq., who died in Edinburgh on 24 November 1806 aged 72, and a Thomas Riddell junior beside him. Little else about either man survives in easily available records - what has made the stone famous is a name, not a biography. Fans and tour guides have long argued it's the source of Tom Riddle, the birth name J.K. Rowling gave Lord Voldemort, whose fictional middle name Marvolo lets the full name anagram into 'I am Lord Voldemort'. The theory gained extra traction because the grave sits only a short walk from the Elephant House, the cafe overlooking the kirkyard where Rowling wrote much of the early books. Rowling herself has never confirmed drawing the name from this specific stone: in a March 1999 Barnes & Noble web chat she said only that she collects names generally, including from gravestones and other sources, and she has separately recalled one of her own children coming home from a Greyfriars tour with a Riddell-grave theory that was, by her account, news to her rather than something she had deliberately planted. Greyfriars Kirk's own visitor materials now formally list the stone among the yard's stops as the 'Tom Riddell Gravesite' regardless, reflecting how firmly the site has been absorbed into the kirkyard's modern identity, whatever the truth of its literary connection.
interesting_fact: Fan traffic has been heavy enough that the grave is now fenced off with iron railings to keep visitors from touching or entering the plot directly - an unusual protective measure for what is, on its own documented terms, an obscure 18th-century family burial with no literary history of its own.

title: Captain John Porteous's Grave
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (near the west wall)
about_site_text: Near the west wall of the original kirkyard lies the grave of Captain John Porteous of the Edinburgh City Guard, buried here on 9 September 1736 - two nights after a mob dragged him from the Tolbooth and lynched him at Hunter's Close in the Grassmarket, in revenge for his having ordered his men to fire into a crowd there that April and then receiving a royal reprieve from execution for it. See Hunter's Close, passed earlier on this walk, for the full story of the riot itself.
interesting_fact: For more than two hundred years his grave carried only a small square stone marked with the single letter 'P' and the date 1736. In 1973 a biographer paid to replace it with a proper headstone reading 'John Porteous, a Captain of the Edinburgh City Guard, murdered 7 September 1736 - All passion spent'. Unlike several neighbouring graves, no tour guide or fan source consulted for this entry claims any Harry Potter connection for the Porteous name - his story appears on kirkyard tours purely for its own dramatic history.

title: The Potter Grave (Anne and Robert Potter)
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (near the main entrance)
about_site_text: Close to Greyfriars Kirkyard's main George IV Bridge entrance stands a family headstone inscribed to Anne and Robert Potter. As with many of the yard's more modest 18th- and 19th-century burials, no further biographical detail about the two survives in the sources checked - the stone itself, and its surname, are essentially the whole of what is documented about them today.
interesting_fact: Tour guides and fan blogs widely cite this as the grave that gave J.K. Rowling her hero's surname, since it sits only steps from the Elephant House cafe where she wrote. Rowling has given a different account herself, though: in a March 1999 Barnes & Noble web chat she said 'Potter was the name of a brother and sister who I played with when I was very young. We were part of the same gang and I always liked that surname' - crediting childhood friends rather than this or any other headstone.

title: The Scrymgeour Gravestone
about_site_text: Greyfriars Kirkyard holds at least one Scrymgeour family monument, though sources disagree on exactly which stone tour guides mean: some point to a memorial for Margaret Louisa Scrymgeour Wedderburn, others to a separate stone for a Daniel Scrymgeour standing near the Potter family grave. Either way, the Scrymgeours were a genuine, long-established Scottish family - the name is also historically borne by the Royal Standard Bearers of Scotland - rather than an invention for the tour.
interesting_fact: The surname is popularly said to have inspired Rufus Scrimgeour, the gruff Minister of Magic introduced in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows - the spelling shifts slightly from 'Scrymgeour' to 'Scrimgeour'. As with the other kirkyard names on this leg, Rowling has never confirmed the connection; she has said more generally that she has 'got names from saints, place-names, war memorials, gravestones' over the years.

title: John Gray's Grave
about_site_text: John Gray arrived in Edinburgh around 1850 with his wife Jess and son John, and, unable to find work as a gardener, joined the Edinburgh City Police as a night watchman. He died of tuberculosis on 15 February 1858 and was buried here in Greyfriars Kirkyard - an ordinary working man whose own grave carries none of the fame later attached to the small dog who, by tradition, would not leave it.
interesting_fact: That dog, Bobby, is said to have kept vigil at Gray's grave for the next fourteen years, a story already covered by this leg's separate Greyfriars Bobby-related POIs. No Harry Potter connection has ever been claimed for the name Gray at this kirkyard - unlike several neighbouring stones, it appears on tourist itineraries purely for the Bobby legend rather than any Rowling naming theory.

title: John Watson's Grave
about_site_text: John Watson, an Edinburgh Writer to the Signet, died in 1762 (one source gives 1759) and left the residue of his estate, around 2,000 pounds, for charitable use in the city - specifically, according to his will, to found a hospital aimed at 'preventing child murder', a starkly worded 18th-century way of describing support for destitute and abandoned infants. The Society of Writers to the Signet administered the growing fund for decades and later erected a monument to him here in Greyfriars in his honour.
interesting_fact: That bequest eventually funded John Watson's Institution, a Stockbridge school for orphaned children designed by William Burn and opened in 1828; it became John Watson's School before closing in 1975, and the building now houses the Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art (Modern One). No source consulted for this entry links the name Watson to any Harry Potter character - unusually for this leg, his grave is included for his own genuine philanthropic legacy rather than any claimed literary connection.

title: Elizabeth Moodie's Gravestone
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (near the Flodden Wall)
about_site_text: Near the Flodden Wall inside Greyfriars Kirkyard stands a weathered stone bearing the name Elizabeth Moodie. As with several of the yard's less prominent burials, no biography of her beyond the name and approximate location on the stone appears to survive in the sources checked - she is one of many otherwise-unrecorded Edinburgh residents whose only public trace today is this single gravestone.
interesting_fact: Tour guides and Harry Potter fan sites frequently cite this as the source of Auror Alastor 'Mad-Eye' Moody's surname, one more entry in the kirkyard's informal list of character-name graves alongside Riddell, Potter, Scrymgeour and McGonagall. As with the others, Rowling has never confirmed drawing the name from this or any specific stone here.

title: William McGonagall's Tombstone
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (near the Flodden Wall, by George Heriot's School gate)
about_site_text: William McGonagall (c.1825-1902) is widely regarded as the worst poet in the English language, best remembered for verse such as 'The Tay Bridge Disaster' and 'The Famous Tay Whale', written with total sincerity and no apparent awareness of how badly they scanned. He died in poverty in Edinburgh in 1902 and was buried in a communal pauper's grave in Greyfriars Kirkyard; the exact plot was never recorded, so in 1999 well-wishers installed a memorial plaque near the Flodden Wall, inscribed with a line from his own poetry describing himself as 'the poor poet that lives in Dundee'.
interesting_fact: This is one of the few kirkyard 'Harry Potter grave' claims Rowling has actually addressed directly: on the official Wizarding World site she said there was 'something irresistible' about his name and 'the idea that such a brilliant woman [Professor Minerva McGonagall] might be a distant relative of the buffoonish McGonagall' - a deliberate, acknowledged piece of wordplay rather than the unconfirmed rumour attached to most of the other names on this leg.

title: Adam Family Mausoleum
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (south division, near the Heriot's School gate)
about_site_text: This small classical temple-fronted mausoleum was designed in 1753 by the young Robert and John Adam - later two of Britain's most celebrated architects - to hold the tomb of their father, William Adam (1689-1748), the leading Scottish architect of his own generation, responsible for buildings including Hopetoun House and the original Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh. Later inscriptions inside record other family members, including a descendant, John Adam, acting Governor-General of India, who died at sea in 1825.
interesting_fact: Despite its imposing, gothic-adjacent silhouette among the kirkyard's other grand tombs, no source checked for this entry claims any Harry Potter naming connection for the Adam family. It stands here purely as a genuine piece of Edinburgh architectural history: one dynasty of architects building a monument to the father who trained them.

title: James Hutton's Grave
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard (Covenanters' Prison enclosure), Edinburgh EH1 2QL
about_site_text: Inside the walled Covenanters' Prison enclosure at the south end of Greyfriars Kirkyard lies the grave of James Hutton (1726-1797), a farmer turned naturalist widely called the father of modern geology. Observing how ordinary processes like erosion and sediment deposition worked in the Scottish landscape around him, he argued that the same slow forces, acting over immense stretches of time, had shaped the entire Earth - a theory of 'deep time' that upended the far shorter Biblical timelines then generally assumed. He presented his Theory of the Earth to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1785, publishing it in 1788 and an expanded two-volume edition in 1795.
interesting_fact: Because the Covenanters' Prison enclosure is normally kept locked to the public, Hutton's grave tablet - a century after the Covenanters' own confinement here - is usually visible only during the kirkyard's annual Doors Open Days each September, or by special arrangement with Greyfriars Kirk's own guides. No Harry Potter connection has been claimed for Hutton or his grave in any source checked for this entry.

title: Little Free Library
about_site_text: This small, hand-built book box on Forrest Road is one of dozens of 'Little Free Libraries' scattered across Edinburgh - miniature street-corner bookcases where anyone can take a book or leave one behind, no library card or fee required. The movement in Edinburgh was kickstarted by the Edinburgh Tool Library, a community group better known for lending tools rather than books, which built the city's first one in the Stockbridge Colonies in 2016. Demand for book-sharing grew sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the network has since expanded across the city through a mix of the Tool Library's own volunteer makers and independent residents building their own from public plans.
interesting_fact: Each Little Free Library costs roughly £250-300 to build and install, and every one needs a named local 'custodian' who volunteers to keep it stocked, tidy and in good repair - meaning this small box on Forrest Road, sitting almost exactly between Greyfriars Bobby's statue and the university's Bristo Square quarter, only survives because someone nearby keeps quietly looking after it.

title: Alexander and Bucephalus Statue
address: City Chambers Courtyard, High Street, Edinburgh EH1 1DF
about_site_text: This ten-foot bronze group in the City Chambers courtyard shows Alexander the Great taming his wild horse Bucephalus, sculpted by Sir John Steell. It was Steell's first major work, begun in 1829 soon after he returned from studying in Rome, and modelled that same year - but Edinburgh council was slow to pay him, and the piece wasn't actually cast in bronze until 1883, over fifty years later. Presented to the city by public subscription in 1884, it originally stood in St Andrew Square before being moved to this High Street courtyard in 1916. Steell went on to become one of Scotland's most celebrated sculptors, appointed Sculptor in Ordinary to Queen Victoria in Scotland in 1838, and later cast the equestrian Duke of Wellington statue you may have already passed on Princes Street, this leg's own starting point.
interesting_fact: Look closely at the horse's ears - local legend has it that Steell took revenge on the council for the decades-long delay by giving Bucephalus a pair of pig's ears instead of a horse's, a small act of sculpted protest hidden in plain sight above one of Edinburgh's busiest courtyards.

title: Hugh Miller Plaque
about_site_text: A plaque at 297 High Street marks the former offices of The Witness, the Free Church of Scotland's newspaper, where the geologist and writer Hugh Miller worked as editor from 1840 to 1856. It was in The Witness that Miller first serialised much of his groundbreaking geological writing, including The Old Red Sandstone (1841), turning a religious newspaper into an unlikely platform for popular science and reaching a far wider readership than a scientific journal ever could have.
interesting_fact: Miller began working life as a stonemason, not a scholar - it was cutting into Old Red Sandstone rock that first sparked his fascination with the fossils inside it. Entirely self-taught, he went on to pioneer the field of palaeoecology and correspond with the leading geologists of his day, though he remained a fierce religious opponent of Darwin's theory of evolution right up to his death by suicide in 1856, worn down by years of mental illness and overwork.

title: General Stanislaw Maczek Statue
address: City Chambers Courtyard, High Street, Edinburgh EH1 1YJ
about_site_text: This bronze statue in the City Chambers courtyard honours General Stanislaw Maczek (1892-1994), commander of the 1st Polish Armoured Division, who Winston Churchill entrusted with defending Scotland's east coast against invasion during the Second World War. Maczek's division went on to play a decisive role in the 1944 Battle of Normandy, helping close the Falaise Gap, before liberating parts of France, Belgium and the Netherlands, including the Dutch city of Breda, which still marks the anniversary of its liberation by Polish troops every year. Sculpted by Bronislaw Krzysztof, the statue was unveiled here on 3 November 2018.
interesting_fact: After the war, Poland's postwar communist government stripped Maczek of his citizenship and his war pension in punishment for having fought alongside the Western Allies. Unable to return home, he settled permanently in Edinburgh and, to support his family, spent years working as a barman at the Learmonth Hotel - a decorated wartime general pulling pints just a few streets from where his own statue now stands.

title: The News Steps
about_site_text: This 124-step stairway drops from St Giles Street, just off the High Street, down to Market Street near Waverley Station, one of the Old Town's steepest shortcuts to the New Town below. The steps take their name from the Edinburgh Courant, one of Britain's earliest regional newspapers (founded 1705), whose printing house once stood near St Giles Street - papers fresh off the press were rushed down these steps to reach Market Street and the trains at Waverley. Today the railings are covered in hundreds of padlocks, left by couples and visitors in a homegrown 'love lock' tradition - nobody official put them there, and the council has never endorsed them, but new ones keep appearing.
interesting_fact: From the top there's a genuine 'two levels of the city' view, framed right through the padlocks: North Bridge overhead, the Balmoral Hotel's clock tower across the valley, and rooftops spilling down the slope alongside you - a compact demonstration of how the Old Town was built to stack one street directly above another, the same trick you'll have already seen at Scotsman Steps and Fleshmarket Close earlier on this walk. The Edinburgh Courant that gave these steps their name was Scotland's first regional newspaper, first printed in 1705 - and one of its early editors was Daniel Defoe, sent north by the English government to report on, and quietly shape opinion around, the 1707 Union, years before he made his name writing Robinson Crusoe.

title: The Caledonian Hotel
about_site_text: Red sandstone quarried at Locharbriggs and Corncockle in Dumfriesshire rises above this corner of Princes Street, hauled north on the Caledonian Railway Company's own trains to build its grand terminus hotel between 1899 and 1903. Inside, marble columns and gilded ceilings once greeted arriving passengers, who could step straight from the platforms of Princes Street Station through three archways into the hotel itself - 205 guest rooms waiting on the other side. Long known simply as "The Caley", it outlived the station by decades: passenger trains stopped running from Princes Street in September 1965 and the tracks were lifted, but the hotel above kept operating, still the grandest address at the west end of Princes Street.
interesting_fact: The Caledonian's engineers once piped waste steam from locomotives at the adjoining station straight into the hotel's boilers to help heat its water - a literal recycling of the railway's own exhaust. Its corridors are noticeably wide, reputedly built generously enough for two Edwardian ladies in full hooped skirts to pass without their dresses touching. Over the twentieth century its guest book filled with the famous - Charlie Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, Elizabeth Taylor, Bing Crosby, Gene Kelly, who is said to have danced down the main staircase, and Sean Connery, a regular guest over the decades until his death in 2020. More recently Taylor Swift stayed here during her 2024 Eras Tour dates in Edinburgh.

title: View Down Frederick Street to St Stephen's and the Kingdom of Fife
address: Frederick Street at George Street, Edinburgh
about_site_text: From this point at the top of Frederick Street, the New Town's dead-straight grid opens onto one of Edinburgh's most celebrated views: the street runs directly downhill for half a mile, closing on the tower of St Stephen's Church in Stockbridge before the view carries on past it, across the Firth of Forth, to the hills of Fife beyond. William Playfair designed St Stephen's, built in 1827-28, specifically to terminate this vista - its tower rising 162 feet to dominate the skyline exactly where Frederick Street, Howe Street and St Vincent Street all converge below.
interesting_fact: St Stephen's clock, fitted by James Ritchie & Son in 1828, carries the longest pendulum of any public clock in Europe - 60 feet long, swinging with an 8.6-second period inside the tower. The far shore on a clear day is Fife, still known traditionally as "the Kingdom of Fife" from its days as a distinct Pictish territory rather than part of mainland Scotland proper. St Stephen's stopped holding regular Church of Scotland services decades ago and became Saint Stephen's Theatre; in 2026 the building itself went up for sale, its spire still framing the same view Playfair intended two centuries earlier.

title: Dean Ramsay Memorial
address: St John's Episcopal Church, Princes Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EP
about_site_text: This soaring Celtic cross, over 8 metres of Shap granite on three broad steps, stands in the graveyard of St John's Episcopal Church at the west end of Princes Street, commemorating Edward Bannerman Ramsay, the church's minister for over 40 years and Dean of Edinburgh from 1841 until his death in 1872. Designed by the architect Robert Rowand Anderson and erected in 1879, the cross carries a set of bronze relief panels cast by F. A. Skidmore of Coventry, depicting scenes from Christ's Passion, the Resurrection and Ascension alongside six acts of charity - fitting for a man remembered as much for his philanthropy as for his ministry.
interesting_fact: Dean Ramsay's lasting fame rests less on his sermons than on a single book: "Reminiscences of Scottish Life and Character", a collection of anecdotes and observations on the Scottish national character first published in 1858. It became one of the runaway publishing successes of Victorian Scotland, running through 22 editions by the time of his death in 1872 alone, and it stayed in print well into the 20th century. Ramsay was also a co-founder of Glenalmond College, one of Scotland's leading independent schools, and served as minister of St John's - the church whose churchyard this cross now stands in - from 1830 right through to his death.

title: Hard Rock Cafe
about_site_text: Behind the neon sign sits a Georgian townhouse dating from George Street's original 1780s development as one of the New Town's grand residential streets. By 1882 the building had become Dowell's Rooms, a well-known Edinburgh auction house, before a later spell as a public house. Hard Rock Cafe took over the premises in 1998, adding its trademark gold guitar logo to a facade that had already lived through a century of very different Edinburgh trades - a pattern repeated up and down George Street, where grand Georgian frontages now house everything from banks to bars behind their original stonework.
interesting_fact: The "Love All, Serve All" motto worked into the doorway lettering here is the same one displayed at every Hard Rock Cafe worldwide, dating back to the very first branch, opened in London in 1971 by two young Americans, Isaac Tigrett and Peter Morton, who wanted an American-style diner that welcomed absolutely everyone. That founding philosophy of inclusivity is also why Hard Rock cafes fill their walls with rock memorabilia rather than velvet ropes; Edinburgh's own collection has included Ringo Starr's leather jacket and a guitar once played by Red Hot Chili Peppers.

title: The Standing Order
about_site_text: This grand banking hall, all soaring columns and coffered ceiling, was built in 1874-78 as the Edinburgh headquarters of the Union Bank of Scotland, designed by the noted Scottish architect David Bryce and completed after his death by his nephew John Bryce. Grade A listed, it's one of George Street's most imposing former banks - a street that was lined with them in the Victorian era - and Wetherspoon converted it into a pub while keeping much of the original interior intact, including the vast scale and detailing that once signalled a bank's solidity and trustworthiness to its customers.
interesting_fact: The pub takes its name, "The Standing Order", from banking terminology as a nod to the building's past - and that past is still visible throughout. One of the dining areas contains an original Chubb vault, its markings inside dated 1968, while a bronze statue nicknamed "Money, Money, Money" - a bank manager offering up a case of cash - watches over the main hall, a wry piece of commentary on the building's former trade planted right in the middle of what's now one of Scotland's best-regarded Wetherspoon pubs.

title: The Alexander Graham Bell
about_site_text: This corner pub occupies a pair of classic Georgian townhouses on George Street dating from around 1785, though a carved lintel over one doorway carries a much older inscription: "God bless the baxters of Edinburgh who built this house 1675", a reference to the city's medieval baker's guild and a much earlier building on the site. The premises traded for years as the Ivory Lounge before JD Wetherspoon took it over in May 2010, renaming it in honour of the world-famous inventor said to have been born just around the corner.
interesting_fact: Alexander Graham Bell, inventor of the telephone, was born at 16 South Charlotte Street - a walk of only a few minutes from this pub's front door, and this tour's own route passes his birthplace separately elsewhere on leg 3. Bell emigrated to Canada and then the United States as a young man, patented the telephone in 1876 while teaching at Boston University, and kept his ties to his native city throughout his life, returning on visits and eventually being made a Freeman of Edinburgh in 1920, over four decades after the invention that made him famous.

title: Mather's Bar
about_site_text: This single-room corner bar occupies the ground floor of a five-storey building put up in 1900 by the architects Sydney Mitchell & Wilson for the National Commercial Bank of Scotland. Wine merchant Hugh Mather took over the ground floor in 1902 and established the licensed premises the following year, giving the pub its name, which still runs in gold lettering across the frontage: "Wines. H.P. Mather. Spirits." Inside, the pub has changed remarkably little in well over a century - high ceilings with ornate plasterwork, a large stained-glass window, floor-to-ceiling tiling in the porch, and an original bar counter and half-height panelling.
interesting_fact: CAMRA (the Campaign for Real Ale) has identified Mather's as having a nationally important historic pub interior, one of a small number in Scotland to earn that distinction - meaning the fixtures and layout are protected as being of outstanding historic value, not just an old-looking pub but a genuinely preserved one. Tucked just off the west end of Princes Street, it's long been a classic "old man's bar" popular with people passing through on their way to the trams, buses, or the theatre nearby, rather than a tourist destination in its own right.

title: Statue of Sir James Young Simpson
about_site_text: This seated bronze figure in academic robes, book resting on one knee, was erected by public subscription in 1877 and designed by the sculptor William Brodie. It commemorates Sir James Young Simpson, professor of midwifery at Edinburgh University, who in November 1847 became the first doctor to demonstrate chloroform's use as an anaesthetic - testing it first on himself and two colleagues at his own dinner table before adopting it in his obstetric practice. The discovery transformed surgery and childbirth almost overnight, sparing patients an era of fully conscious operations.
interesting_fact: The breakthrough came the hard way, by trial and error on willing volunteers. On the evening of 4 November 1847, Simpson and two assistants sat at his dinner table inhaling sample chemicals one by one, hunting for something better than ether. Chloroform knocked all three clean off their chairs — one kept laughing helplessly, another's voice cracked into a falsetto, and Simpson himself came round on the floor under the table, delighted rather than alarmed, and pronounced on the spot that they'd found their answer. He put it to clinical use within days, but the drug faced fierce religious objection at first — some clergy argued that easing the pain of childbirth defied the biblical curse on Eve — until Queen Victoria herself was given chloroform by her own physician during the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853, an endorsement that ended the controversy overnight. Simpson became one of the most celebrated Scots of his era: knighted in 1866, the first doctor in Scotland to receive the honour, and when he died in 1870 more than 100,000 people are said to have lined Edinburgh's streets for his funeral procession to Warriston Cemetery.

title: Thistle Street Bar
about_site_text: This snug traditional pub occupies a building put up around 1775-80 on Thistle Street, often reckoned the oldest street laid out in Edinburgh's New Town - a narrow service lane running parallel to George Street, originally intended for tradesmen's workshops and stables rather than grand frontages. True to that humble origin, the building itself started out as a cow shed before its later life as licensed premises; today it's known for a proper cask-ale selection from independent Scottish breweries and regular live folk music sessions.
interesting_fact: In the late 1970s and early 1980s the pub traded as Marr's Bar, named for its then-landlord Archie Marr - an original member of the Bay City Rollers who played keyboards on the band's first single, a cover of "Keep on Dancing", released in October 1971, before Edinburgh's own "Rollermania" peak with tartan-clad fans queuing for hours at record-shop signings. Marr was long gone from the band's classic mid-70s line-up by the time the hysteria hit, in keeping with a group whose membership churned constantly through its early years - even its own name is said to have been picked at random by throwing a dart at a map of North America, landing near Bay City, Michigan.

title: Fishers in the City
about_site_text: Fishers in the City occupies a converted warehouse on Thistle Street, opened in 2001 as the second branch of a Leith seafood institution that's been family-run since 1991. The menu leans hard into the classics - chowder, fishcakes, fish and chips, and a rotating shellfish selection - alongside meat and vegetarian dishes given equal attention, served in a warm, contemporary dining room built for long, unhurried lunches as much as celebratory dinners.
interesting_fact: The original Fishers restaurant still operates a few miles away on the historic waterfront at The Shore in Leith, inside a striking round stone tower built in 1685-86 by the architect Robert Mylne as a windmill, later stripped of its sails and topped with battlements in 1805 to serve as a harbour watchtower. This Thistle Street branch doesn't share that landmark building - its own premises are a plainer former warehouse - but the family recipes and seafood sourcing carry over directly. Now in its third generation of family ownership, Fishers has grown from that single Leith address, opened in 1991, into one of Edinburgh's most consistently well-regarded seafood groups.

title: Cafe Marlayne
about_site_text: This intimate French bistro on Thistle Street opened its doors on 27 February 2000, founded by Islay Fraser and Marcelline Levicky, who blended their two names to create "Marlayne". The menu draws its inspiration from the bistros and brasseries of Marcelline's hometown, Lyon, reworked with the best Scottish produce available - classic French cooking served with the kind of care and precision that's kept the small, lively room busy for a lunch crowd by day and a more romantic dinner trade after dark.
interesting_fact: Cafe Marlayne became successful enough to open a second branch on Old Fishmarket Close, just off the Royal Mile - a location that's since moved again, now trading at the top of Leith Walk, while this original Thistle Street bistro remains the flagship. More than two decades after opening, it's still independently and personally run by its founders rather than having expanded into a wider chain, something diners and reviewers regularly point to as central to its lasting appeal.

title: The Cambridge Bar
about_site_text: This two-storey Georgian corner bar on Young Street has become known across Edinburgh for its craft beer selection and gourmet burgers, made with locally-sourced ingredients and served in an L-shaped downstairs bar full of wooden alcoves, low tables and leather benches, with an upstairs room used for private functions and overflow dining. Young Street itself was originally laid out as the westernmost stretch of Thistle Street before being renamed after an early New Town developer - one of the many quiet service lanes tucked just behind George Street's grander frontages.
interesting_fact: The Cambridge Bar shares Young Street with an even more famous neighbour just a few doors along: the Oxford Bar, the unpretentious real-ale pub made internationally known as detective John Rebus's regular haunt in Ian Rankin's bestselling crime novels. The two pubs, named after Britain's oldest rival universities, sit on the same short Edinburgh lane by coincidence rather than design - though it makes for a natural point of comparison between the Oxford's famously spartan, traditional interior and the Cambridge's more contemporary craft-beer-and-burgers approach.

title: Old Waverley Hotel
about_site_text: This seven-storey Victorian building on Princes Street, opposite the gardens and Waverley Station, dates from 1848 and was designed by the architect John Armstrong for the hotelier Robert Cranston. With 86 rooms, it was one of the largest hotels on the street when it opened, and it kept the Cranston family's management for decades, giving the building its long-standing local nickname long before "Old Waverley" became its formal name.
interesting_fact: For almost 25 years the hotel operated as "Cranston's Temperance Hotel" - the first temperance hotel in Scotland, serving no alcohol at all at a time when the temperance movement was a serious social and political force across Victorian Britain. Robert Cranston was a committed temperance campaigner as well as a hotelier, and his teetotal Princes Street establishment became a well-known statement in a city otherwise thick with taverns and licensed hotels, before the business eventually dropped the temperance policy and became the more conventional hotel operating under the Old Waverley name today.

title: North Bridge
about_site_text: Cross this bridge and you're walking on the reason the New Town exists at all: without a crossing here, linking the medieval Old Town to the ridge of Georgian development rising to the north, that whole elegant grid could never have been built where it is. The first North Bridge opened for pedestrians in 1765, but was still incomplete when disaster struck: on the evening of 3 August 1769, its south abutment gave way without warning and part of the structure collapsed, killing five people. An inquiry blamed rushed construction and shallow foundations dug into loose earth - the very ground where the Old Town had been dumping its excavation spoil for generations. Rebuilding cost £18,000, almost double the original budget, and the bridge didn't fully reopen until 1772. That first North Bridge stood until 1896, by which point it could no longer cope with the growing city. The bridge beneath your feet now, its blue ironwork trimmed in red and gold, was built in two stages between 1894 and 1897, engineered to span directly over the platforms of Waverley Station below, and formally opened on 1 September 1897 by the Lord Provost, Sir Andrew McDonald.
interesting_fact: The bridge's ironwork was fabricated by Sir William Arrol & Co, the Glasgow firm responsible for two of Britain's most famous Victorian engineering landmarks: the Forth Bridge, opened in 1890 as the first major crossing built entirely of steel, and London's Tower Bridge, which opened the same year North Bridge's construction began, in 1894. From this spot the view takes in the turreted Balmoral Hotel, the Palladian front of General Register House, and - across the valley - the unfinished columns of the National Monument and the Nelson Monument crowning Calton Hill.

title: Advocate's Close
about_site_text: One of dozens of narrow closes branching off the Royal Mile, Advocate's Close drops steeply from the High Street down toward Market Street and Cockburn Street, its masonry dating back to at least 1544. It takes its name from Sir James Stewart of Goodtrees, Lord Advocate of Scotland (1692-1709 and 1711-13), who rebuilt the house here after 1688 and lived in it until his death - one of many distinguished residents in an era when these closes housed everyone from the city's elite to its poorest tenement dwellers, stacked together in the same tight wynds.
interesting_fact: Glance back up the close toward the Royal Mile and you'll catch one of Edinburgh's most photographed accidental views: the Gothic spire of the Scott Monument, perfectly centred at the far end, with Princes Street and the New Town beyond. That view survives today thanks to a 2014 restoration by Morgan McDonnell Architecture, which won the close Scotland's £25,000 Doolan Prize for building of the year, beating competition that included Glasgow's Hydro arena - a striking turnaround for a passage that had stood semi-derelict for decades. The work also turned up a genuine surprise: a Latin and English inscription over an old doorway, reading 'Blessed be God and all his gifts,' unnoticed for so long it wasn't rediscovered until 2009.

title: Warriston's Close
about_site_text: A steep flight of some 120 stone steps drops from the Royal Mile down to Cockburn Street through Warriston's Close, one of the steepest and most physically dramatic of the Old Town's closes. It takes its name from Sir Archibald Johnston, Lord Warriston, a prominent 17th-century lawyer and Covenanter who lived here.
