As with many closes, the buildings visible today were rebuilt on top of much older structures - the lower levels of the original medieval street survive beneath, buried and preserved rather than demolished when later buildings went up above.
interesting_fact: Archibald Johnston was one of the principal authors of the National Covenant of 1638 and a leading figure in Scotland's Presbyterian resistance to royal religious policy, rising as high as a seat in Oliver Cromwell's own parliament. After the Restoration of Charles II in 1660 he fled abroad, was tracked down in France, and eventually brought back to Edinburgh, where he was hanged in 1663 - just yards from this close, near the Mercat Cross on the Royal Mile, for his earlier anti-Royalist activities. His punishment didn't end with the noose: Johnston's head was struck off and displayed on a spike at the Netherbow Port, the Old Town's main city gate, before eventually being taken down and buried with the rest of him in Greyfriars Kirkyard - the fate handed to several Covenanter leaders executed in Edinburgh during the Restoration crackdown on Presbyterian dissent.

title: The Doric Bar
about_site_text: Edinburgh's oldest gastropub by its own reckoning, the Doric occupies a corner of Market Street in the shadow of North Bridge and Waverley Station - a building dating to the 17th century that was adapted into a pub in the 18th, even if what you see today looks more late-Victorian than truly ancient. A traditional ground-floor bar - stocked with more than fifty single malt whiskies - sits below a first-floor bistro serving fresh, locally sourced food cooked to order, a split-level format that's let it run as both a proper pub and a serious dining room for decades.
interesting_fact: The name likely nods to "Doric," the term for the broad, characterful dialect of North-East Scotland - as well as, coincidentally, one of the three classical orders of Greek architecture, the plainest and sturdiest of the three columns. Tucked into the tangle of streets and closes below the Royal Mile near Waverley Station, the pub sits within a few minutes' walk of several of the Old Town's most atmospheric closes, making it a natural stopping point on a route through the historic heart of the city.

title: Old Saint Paul's Scottish Episcopal Church
about_site_text: The congregation here traces back to 1689, when Bishop Alexander Rose, ousted from St Giles' Cathedral after the Scottish Episcopal Church lost its status as the national church, set up worship in a converted wool store in nearby Carrubber's Close. Episcopalians paid for that split for decades afterward: their clergy and congregations were persecuted under law through the Jacobite Risings, and it took the death of Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1788 to finally loosen the association between Episcopacy and Jacobite politics. The current building, designed by Hay & Henderson and completed in 1883 at a cost of £3,500, was formally named "Old" St Paul's to distinguish it from a separate, newer St Paul's that had opened in the New Town. A war memorial chapel and a dramatic 33-step Calvary Stair, added in 1926, connect the church down to its Jeffrey Street entrance.
interesting_fact: Despite its unassuming entrances - one via the steep Calvary Stair from Jeffrey Street, another through Carrubber's Close off the Royal Mile - the church opens into a surprisingly large, richly decorated interior that gives little away from outside. As one of Scotland's original 17th-century Episcopalian congregations, it represents a direct thread back to the years just after the 1689 Revolution, when Presbyterian church government was re-established and Episcopalian worshippers like Rose's displaced congregation had to find new, often improvised, places to meet.

title: Margaret Tait Filmmaker Plaque
about_site_text: This blue plaque, part of the "MT100" trail marking the centenary of filmmaker Margaret Tait's birth, records one of her own sound recordings made at this very spot: "13 Jan, 4.30-5pm, 1963: 'record' startings under the North Bridge on a Sunday afternoon - a little traffic and not very much other noise." Tait, born in Kirkwall, Orkney in 1918, trained as a doctor at Edinburgh University and served with the Royal Army Medical Corps in India during the Second World War before turning to filmmaking, studying in Rome and founding her own studio, Ancona Films, in Edinburgh.
interesting_fact: Tait's painstaking sound recordings, capturing the precise ambient noise of specific places at specific moments, were made to be edited separately into the soundtracks of her own 16mm films - part of a working method built around close, patient observation rather than conventional narrative filmmaking. In 1992, at the age of 74, she became the first Scottish woman to direct a feature-length film, Blue Black Permanent, capping a career of more than 30 largely self-financed short films that went largely unrecognised in her lifetime but are now seen as foundational to Scottish independent cinema.

title: Sir Robert W Philip Plaque
about_site_text: This blue plaque near The Mound commemorates Dr Robert William Philip, who in 1887 founded the Victoria Dispensary for Consumption and Diseases of the Chest nearby - the world's first clinic dedicated specifically to fighting tuberculosis. Rather than simply treating patients as they arrived, Philip pioneered what became known as the Edinburgh Scheme: tracing a disease back through a patient's household and social circumstances, examining infected families, and working to contain outbreaks at their source, treating tuberculosis as a public health problem to be managed at population scale rather than case by case.
interesting_fact: The plaque itself was erected in 1957, the centenary of Philip's birth, by the National Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis, and quotes his own confident prediction that mankind would eventually master the disease. His dispensary model - combining outpatient treatment, home visits, and a linked sanatorium and after-care colony - was so influential it was copied around the world and became the template for modern tuberculosis-control programmes, decades before antibiotics existed to actually cure the disease he spent his career trying to contain.

title: The Scotsman Picturehouse
about_site_text: Tucked into a previously disused room inside the former Scotsman newspaper building, this 48-seat boutique cinema opened on 9 August 2019 after a multi-million-pound refurbishment - a rare new addition to a building otherwise defined by its Edwardian past. Rather than rows of standard cinema seats, bespoke red leather and velvet armchairs and sofas, each with its own table lamp, sit beneath the original ornate cornice-work and wood panelling that survive throughout the wider hotel.
interesting_fact: The opening night doubled up two very different films back to back: the Elton John biopic Rocketman, followed by Yesterday, the Danny Boyle-directed musical fantasy built around The Beatles' songbook. It's a fittingly theatrical launch for a cinema built inside a building that spent a century as a working newspaper office - printing presses once ran in the floors below, and editorial staff worked just above where audiences now settle in with a drink to watch a film, one more layer in the building's long history of repurposing.

title: O'Neill's Bar
about_site_text: Five storeys of Grade A listed sandstone rise above Hunter Square at what's now O'Neill's, built in 1788-90 by the Edinburgh Merchant Company as its Merchants' Hall, designed by John Baxter. The Company moved out to Hanover Street in 1879, after which the ground floor was substantially altered - most notably in 1894, when the Royal Bank of Scotland relocated the entrance from its original central position to one at the side. The building later fell into disrepair before a full restoration between 1991 and 1996 brought its five floors, including a basement, back into active use.
interesting_fact: Before becoming this branch of the O'Neill's Irish pub chain in 2025, the premises traded for years as The Tron, named for its position right beside the Tron Kirk a few steps up the Royal Mile. The building's long list of past occupants - merchants' guild, bank, restaurant, and now an Irish theme pub - is a fairly typical Old Town story: a grand 18th-century civic building repeatedly repurposed as the institutions that first used it moved on, while the structure itself, protected by its listed status, has stayed largely intact.

title: The Inn on the Mile
about_site_text: A giant Doric portico and Greek key cornice give this High Street corner the gravitas of a Victorian bank, because that's exactly the effect its builders wanted. Built in 1923 at the peak of the British Linen Bank's success, this grand Greek Revival building served as the bank's Royal Mile branch, an expansion beyond its original headquarters in St Andrew Square. Its Classical facade - complete with copper anthemion ornament and an ornate stone crest carved into the stonework above - was crafted to project exactly the solidity and permanence a bank wanted its customers to feel.
interesting_fact: The British Linen Bank's fortunes declined through the two world wars, and it was eventually absorbed by the Bank of Scotland in the 1970s. The building passed through further ownership changes before its rebirth as The Inn on the Mile, now a nine-room boutique hotel and pub that has kept the original ceiling cornice moulding and exposed brickwork inside, pairing them with contemporary interiors - a High Street landmark that's spent a century as a monument to banking respectability and only recently become somewhere to actually stay the night.

title: Landy's Fish and Chips
about_site_text: Landy's opened in December 2024 in a grand corner unit on North Bridge, formerly a Byron Burger, giving the Old Town a proper seaside chippy on a genuinely lavish scale: 7,000 square feet across two floors, with room for around 200 diners. It's run by the Crolla family's Vittoria Group, an Edinburgh institution that traces back to 1970, when the family opened its first restaurant in Leith. From that single venue they built up a small stable of Italian-influenced restaurants and cafes across the city, and Landy's marked their first venture into the classic fish supper - a nod to their own seaside roots and the fish-and-chip tradition long associated with Scottish-Italian families, many of whom, like the Crollas, ran chip shops and cafes across Edinburgh through the 20th century.
interesting_fact: The £2 million fit-out created 70 new jobs, and the menu leans into nostalgia as much as tradition: alongside classic battered haddock, sausages, haggis and black pudding suppers, it offers a vegan fish and chips and a deep-fried Mars Bar for dessert.

title: Bain's Retro Sweets
about_site_text: Jars stacked to the ceiling behind a bright yellow-and-blue frontage, Bain's Retro Sweets has traded from this Grassmarket shopfront for over twenty years, run as a genuine family business built around old-fashioned confectionery rather than modern chocolate-bar brands. Inside, the shop stocks the sweets many Scottish visitors remember from childhood corner shops: cola cubes, black jacks, mint crispettes and Chelsea whoppers alongside Scottish specialities like tablet, Edinburgh rock and the traditional toffee tins that come with their own little hammer. It sits in a stretch of the Grassmarket that has been a market and trading place since medieval times, giving a shop built entirely on nostalgia a suitably old setting to trade from.
interesting_fact: Bain's homemade tablet is what regulars come back for specifically, and the shop's shelves mix genuine vintage British sweets with imported American candy, making it as much a stop for curious tourists as for locals chasing a specific childhood favourite.

title: Hunter's Close
about_site_text: This narrow arched close at the southeast end of the Grassmarket was the scene of one of Edinburgh's most notorious mob killings. In April 1736, after the public hanging of smuggler Andrew Wilson turned into a riot, City Guard captain John Porteous ordered his men to fire on the crowd, killing six people. Porteous was convicted of murder, but a royal reprieve from Queen Caroline delayed his execution - and Edinburgh's citizens decided not to wait. On the night of 7 September 1736, a mob of thousands stormed the Tolbooth prison, dragged Porteous out, and marched him down the Lawnmarket and West Bow to the Grassmarket. He was hauled up this close, strung from a dyer's pole using a rope taken from a nearby draper's shop, and lynched within sight of the gallows where he had once commanded the firing squad. The house at the close's entrance carried a stone dated 1671, marking it as one of the older tenements in this stretch of the Old Town.
interesting_fact: The episode became so notorious that Sir Walter Scott used it as the opening set-piece of his 1818 novel The Heart of Midlothian, and the term 'Porteous Mob' entered Scottish history as shorthand for a city administering its own justice when the Crown intervened in a local execution.

title: The Oz Bar
about_site_text: Corrugated-iron cladding and an outback-shed feel announce The Oz Bar the moment you turn onto this corner of Candlemaker Row, just off the Grassmarket - trading here since 1997 and giving Edinburgh's Australian community and expats a proper home-away-from-home. Shelves are cluttered with Australian curios, football jumpers and beach-postcard kitsch under a genuinely ramshackle tin awning. It has outlasted most of the other Australian-themed bars that have come and gone in the city over the years, largely on the strength of screening Aussie Rules and rugby league fixtures live and keeping a menu of proper Australian pub food and beer on tap.
interesting_fact: Candlemaker Row itself is named for the guild of candlemakers banished here after a fire in a candle workshop killed a guild deacon elsewhere in the Old Town - see the Candlemaker Row entry on this walk for the full story. It makes the Oz Bar's very Australian theme sit on one of the most purely Scottish trade-guild streets left in the city.

title: West Bow Well
about_site_text: This carved stone wellhead at the foot of Victoria Street was erected in 1674 by master mason Robert Mylne, working alongside architect William Bruce, as Edinburgh's very first public wellhead, part of the city's earliest piped water supply instigated by Lord Provost Sir Andrew Ramsay. Water was carried down from reservoirs fed by springs in the Pentland Hills, and the West Bow Well became the first stop for the city's water caddies - workers who queued here to fill their kegs before hauling water door to door through the tenements above the Grassmarket. Its square-plan structure carries a semi-circular drinking basin on one face beneath a 19th-century Edinburgh coat of arms, with a smaller ornamental basin and heraldic panel on its other sides.
interesting_fact: The well stopped supplying water in the early 19th century once piped plumbing reached individual buildings, but its 1861 restoration - carried out by sculptor John Rhind and paid for by the Richardson Brothers, merchants of the West Bow - is still recorded on a small iron door: 'The West-Bow Well erected by The Town Council 1674. Repaired and Altered by Richardson Brothers Merchants West Bow 1861.'

title: Museum Context
about_site_text: This three-floor shop on Victoria Street is one of the city's best-known officially licensed Harry Potter retailers, packed with wands, house scarves, robes and collectibles across a warren of small rooms. The building itself has a history that suits its current trade: from 1886 it housed Robert Cresser's brush shop, a Victorian ironmonger-style store selling brooms, brushes and household wares from floor-to-ceiling wooden fittings and dusty stock boxes, for more than 130 years. That original Victorian interior survives largely intact behind the modern merchandise, and its cluttered, old-fashioned character is often cited by visitors and Potter fans as an uncanny match for Ollivanders wand shop in Diagon Alley.
interesting_fact: The shop's top floor has a free photo spot with props and house robes, including a mirror etched with the 'Chamber of Secrets' inscription - a nod to the wider theory, encouraged by J.K. Rowling having written much of the early books nearby, that this curving street inspired Diagon Alley itself.

title: The Enchanted Galaxy
about_site_text: The Enchanted Galaxy sits at the top of Victoria Street and, like its rival Museum Context further down the hill, trades on the street's Diagon Alley reputation - but its name took three attempts, and a lawsuit, to land. Run by the Gold brothers, the shop originally opened as 'The Boy Wizard', a name Warner Bros argued infringed its Harry Potter intellectual property; a rebrand to 'The Great Wizard' drew the same objection, and Warner Bros went as far as taking the Gold brothers to the High Court of England and Wales over it. The owners eventually settled on 'The Enchanted Galaxy', blending magical and sci-fi themes broadly enough to sidestep further disputes while still selling largely Potter-themed merchandise alongside Star Wars, Marvel and other franchise collectibles.
interesting_fact: Where Museum Context leans into cramped, cluttered Victorian atmosphere, The Enchanted Galaxy goes the opposite way - reviewers have compared its clean, brightly lit layout to 'an Apple Store', making the two competing shops, barely 150 metres apart, a study in opposite ways of selling the same theme.

title: Bertie's Proper Fish & Chips
about_site_text: Bertie's occupies a genuinely surprising building for a chip shop: a former church. The site had stood empty for a decade after a serious fire gutted its previous occupant, the Indian restaurant Khushi's, in 2008, before the Vittoria Group - the Crolla family's Edinburgh restaurant business - spent £3 million converting the old St John's church into a three-floor, 300-seat fish and chip restaurant that opened in 2018. The name honours Alberto 'Bertie' Crolla, the group's founder, and the restaurant now sits just a few streets from its sister restaurant Landy's on North Bridge, both built on the same family's decades-long fish-and-chip tradition in the city.
interesting_fact: The building's church origins are still legible in its bones - tall arched windows and a soaring, three-storey-high interior - giving diners eating double-cooked chips and battered haddock a dining room shaped like a nave.

title: Finnegan's Wake
about_site_text: Finnegan's Wake has been Victoria Street's Irish pub since 1994, when it took over the premises of a live-music venue called the Preservation Hall and kept the tradition of nightly bands going. Its interior is built around a large circular bar with small wood-panelled booths around the edge and a raised corner stage where bands still play live Irish music most nights, alongside sport on the screens and Guinness on tap. Its name borrows directly from James Joyce's famously dense, unfinished-feeling final novel, itself named after an old Irish-American comic ballad about a hod-carrier who wakes up mid-funeral - a fittingly playful, slightly literary joke for a pub sitting almost next door to Bertie's converted church.
interesting_fact: The pub sits at 9B Victoria Street, immediately beside Bertie's Fish & Chips at number 9 - two very different Irish/British institutions sharing practically the same doorway on the street's lower curve.

title: John Kay's Shop
about_site_text: This small green-fronted shop at the top of Victoria Street sells prints, postcards and Scottish artworks and mementos, and takes its name from John Kay (1742-1826), one of Edinburgh's most important social chroniclers. Kay worked as a barber in the Old Town before his sketching hobby overtook his trade; in 1785 he took down his barber's pole for good to run a print shop of his own in Parliament Close, where he produced and sold etched caricatures of the city's great and ordinary figures alike. Over nearly 900 etchings between 1785 and 1820, he documented everyone from Enlightenment intellectuals to street vendors, most sketched from nothing more than a passing glance, leaving behind one of the richest visual records of Georgian Edinburgh life.
interesting_fact: The modern shop is a separate business (incorporated in 2017) rather than a surviving continuation of Kay's own print shop, which stood roughly half a mile away in Parliament Close - but its stock of prints, maps and Scottish curiosities makes the name a fitting tribute rather than a coincidence.

title: India Buildings
address: India Buildings, Victoria Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EX
about_site_text: This curved, four-storey Scots Baronial office block was built between 1864 and 1866 to designs by architect David Cousin, its grand interior centred on a domed rotunda ringed by balconies. Its name was likely borrowed from a Liverpool office block of the 1830s, itself named by merchants celebrating the end of the East India Company's monopoly on trade with India - making the building a small piece of Victorian commercial branding transplanted to Edinburgh's Old Town. It originally housed serious institutional tenants, including the British Linen Bank and the Scottish Chamber of Agriculture, fitting for a building built to project financial and civic weight on a street otherwise defined by small shops and closes.
interesting_fact: On 14 January 1906, Indian independence activist Pandurang Mahadev 'Senapati' Bapat read an essay on British rule in India here to an Independent Labour Party meeting, forthright in criticising the constitutional case for empire - a speech that cost him his government scholarship and pushed him toward the radical movements that led him back to India in 1908 as a freedom fighter.

title: George IV Bar
about_site_text: The George IV Bar sits midway along George IV Bridge, the elevated street built in 1827-36 to carry traffic clear over the Cowgate far below, connecting the Old Town's South Side to the New Town - see the George IV Bridge entry on this walk for the story of its construction. Today it's a traditional Scottish public house built around an old horseshoe bar lit by imitation oil lamps, its walls hung with beer and whisky memorabilia and antique mirrors. It carries a genuinely serious whisky selection - over 100 different malts and blends, celebrated at its own George IV Whisky Club tasting nights - alongside regular live music, making it a quieter, more locals-oriented counterpart to the tourist-heavy pubs down in the Grassmarket and on Victoria Street just below.
interesting_fact: The pub's George IV Whisky Club runs regular tasting nights hosted by one of its in-house experts, drawing on a back bar of more than 100 malts and blends - a serious specialist offering tucked into a bridge-top street better known for its tourist pubs a few hundred metres downhill.

title: Augustine United Church
about_site_text: Augustine United Church's congregation traces back to 1802, when Reverend John Aikman founded a church nearby, in what is now the site of the National Museum of Scotland, out of Edinburgh's radical Reformation tradition. The current building on George IV Bridge was built between 1857 and 1861 by architects J J & W H Hay, blending Romanesque, Renaissance and Classical detailing beneath a distinctive projecting central tower long nicknamed the 'bride's-cake' tower for its tiered, ornamental profile, restored in 2005. Named for Augustine of Hippo, the church has kept its founding congregation's progressive, community-facing character, today hosting numerous Christian and community organisations rather than functioning as a conventional single-congregation parish church.
interesting_fact: The congregation's roots lie in one of Edinburgh's most deprived districts, where working families and their livestock once lived crowded beneath the wealthy merchants and academics of the Royal Mile above - a history the church still cites as the root of its long-running social and community engagement.

title: Frankenstein & Bier Keller
about_site_text: This Gothic former church - built in 1859 and originally an Elim Pentecostal church, now a Category A listed building - houses one of Edinburgh's more theatrically themed bars. Upstairs, the horror-themed main bar leans into its own name with Frankenstein's-monster decor inside a genuinely Gothic stone shell of pointed arches and spires, including a mechanical 'birth' of the Monster staged every hour on the hour; downstairs, the Bier Keller recreates a Bavarian beer hall complete with long communal wooden benches, a private bar and a live oompah band on regular nights - an entirely different atmosphere one floor below the horror theming above.
interesting_fact: The building sat abandoned for years after the Elim Pentecostal congregation moved on before its current owners took it on, meaning the pointed arches and spires visible today are the real thing - a genuine former place of worship reused as horror-themed nightlife, not a purpose-built pastiche.

title: Edinburgh Sheriff Court
about_site_text: Edinburgh Sheriff Court has a longer institutional history than its current building suggests. Sheriff court business in the city moved through several homes: an 1816 county hall on the corner of Lawnmarket and George IV Bridge, then a purpose-built Renaissance Revival courthouse designed by David Bryce and completed in 1868, before hearings finally moved to a modern courthouse on Chambers Street - designed by John Kirkwood Wilson and built at a cost of £47 million - which opened to the public in September 1994. The land it now stands on had itself previously been part of Heriot-Watt University, a coincidence repeated a few doors down at the Crown Office, which occupies one of Heriot-Watt's own former college buildings. The office of procurator fiscal that prosecutes cases through this court traces back even further, with the earliest documented references in Scottish records dating to the 1550s - making the basic machinery of local Scottish criminal justice centuries older than any of the buildings that have housed it.
interesting_fact: The Sheriff Court and the adjoining Justice of the Peace Court still share the same ornate iron gateway and postbox-style enquiry point pictured at the entrance, a small formal touch that survives from an era when court buildings were built to visibly project civic authority to everyone passing on the street.

title: Crown Office
about_site_text: The headquarters of the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service - the body that investigates and prosecutes crime across all of Scotland - occupies a building that started life as a college. Built from 1872-74 to designs by David Rhind (with David Cousin and John Lessels), it was originally the Watt Institution and School of Arts, which in 1885 merged with the centuries-old George Heriot Trust to become Heriot-Watt College, the direct ancestor of today's Heriot-Watt University. Its imposing 268-foot Renaissance-influenced facade, borrowing from French chateau architecture, was designed to give a technical college the civic gravity of a bank or a courthouse - gravity the building has kept ever since, just in service of a different institution.
interesting_fact: Heriot-Watt University's own roots run through this one Chambers Street address before the college eventually outgrew it and moved to its present Riccarton campus, meaning Scotland's chief prosecuting authority now works out of what was, in effect, an early ancestor of a modern Scottish university - and, as it happens, just a few doors from the Sheriff Court, whose own Chambers Street building also sits on former Heriot-Watt ground.

title: William Chambers Monument
about_site_text: This statue honours Sir William Chambers (1800-1883), the publisher-turned-Lord-Provost who reshaped this part of the Old Town more than almost anyone else. He and his brother Robert built a printing and publishing empire from a small Peebles bookshop, but it was as Lord Provost from 1865 that Chambers left his biggest mark: pushing through the 1867 Edinburgh Improvement Act, which cleared entire slum closes and cut new streets - including the one that now bears his name - through some of the city's most overcrowded ground. Sculpted by John Rhind on a plinth by H.J. Blanc, the statue was erected in 1891, originally standing in the middle of Chambers Street itself.
interesting_fact: The statue was moved to its current position in 2016, when the pedestrian area was widened to make room for a second, similarly styled statue directly nearby - William Henry Playfair, the architect whose buildings Chambers Street was built to celebrate.

title: William Henry Playfair Monument
about_site_text: Standing a few steps from the William Chambers monument it deliberately echoes, this statue honours William Henry Playfair (1790-1857), the architect behind more of Edinburgh's best-known buildings than perhaps any other single figure - the National Gallery, the Royal Scottish Academy, the National Monument on Calton Hill and Surgeons' Hall among them. Sculpted by Alexander Stoddart and unveiled in 2016, it deliberately mirrors the style, scale and pose of the older Chambers statue nearby, portraying Playfair in period dress with papers in hand, as though caught mid-design.
interesting_fact: The statue was commissioned specifically to give Playfair - whose neoclassical buildings define huge parts of central Edinburgh's skyline - the same kind of permanent public recognition long since given to Chambers, more than 125 years after the earlier statue went up a few metres away.

title: Hotel du Vin & Bistro
about_site_text: This boutique hotel occupies a cluster of former institutional buildings dating back to 1743, which over the centuries served in turn as a poorhouse, an asylum, and later a science laboratory, before Hotel du Vin restored and connected them into a single luxury hotel. Ten of its rooms sit within the original historic buildings, kept deliberately atmospheric, while a newer wing built onto the site matches them in style. The hotel keeps a whisky snug and a specialist wine-tasting room among its features, alongside its bistro and mezzanine bar, trading on the contrast between the building's institutional past and its now thoroughly comfortable present.
interesting_fact: Guests booking the hotel's older rooms are, in effect, staying inside a converted 18th-century asylum - one of several former asylums and poorhouses across Edinburgh's Old Town that have been repurposed for hospitality rather than demolished.

title: The Gilded Saloon
about_site_text: The Gilded Saloon opened in July 2025 as a joint venture between the Gilded Balloon, Paradise Palms and Kelburn Arts, but its name carries real weight in Edinburgh's comedy and arts scene: it's a direct tribute to the original Gilded Saloon, a beloved Cowgate performance bar destroyed in the catastrophic Cowgate fire of December 2002, which also burned down the entire Gilded Balloon venue and ten other Old Town businesses. The new bar, restaurant and 200-capacity performance venue overlooking Bristo Square revives the name more than two decades on, serving craft beer and pub food from local chef Tomas Gormley alongside a full comedy and arts programme.
interesting_fact: The original Gilded Saloon had itself replaced an earlier venue, the 369 Gallery, when that closed in the late 1990s - meaning the current bar carries the memory of a lineage of Cowgate arts venues stretching back decades, not just its immediate 2002-destroyed predecessor.

title: Doctors
about_site_text: This corner building has been serving Forrest Road since 1874, built specifically to house small businesses connected to the old Royal Infirmary, which then stood almost directly opposite. Its two longest-standing tenants both served that hospital trade directly: George Watson, a cabinet and coffin maker, worked from the building from 1884 to 1959, while surgical instrument maker James Gardiner traded there until the early 1960s, eventually closing under pressure from larger manufacturers. After a spell as a barbecue restaurant and then a pub called The Mortar from 1970, the building took on its current name, Doctors, in 1979 - a direct nod to the vanished hospital across the street that had shaped the building's purpose for over a century.
interesting_fact: The pub's name outlived the hospital it referenced by decades - the old Royal Infirmary across the road closed for good when services moved to Little France in 2003, but Doctors, named in its honour, is still trading today.

title: The Kid's Secret Garden
about_site_text: Tucked just off Middle Meadow Walk, this small community garden sprang up spontaneously in 2016 and is still run as a free, volunteer-maintained space for local children and families - built from reclaimed timber and odd, cheerful additions rather than any formal civic design: an open-air piano, a stegosaurus-shaped tent, hand-painted signs and planters assembled by whoever turned up to help. It sits at the point where Middle Meadow Walk - the tree-lined path laid out from 1722 on the drained bed of the old Burgh Loch - opens out toward the Meadows themselves, making it a genuinely grassroots addition to one of Edinburgh's oldest planned green routes rather than part of its original historic design.
interesting_fact: When the University of Edinburgh's Edinburgh Futures Institute reopened at the old Royal Infirmary site nearby in 2024, the redevelopment reached right along Middle Meadow Walk itself - and this garden had to adapt its layout to the new landscaping while keeping its improvised, hand-built character intact, a small grassroots survivor squeezed in beside a multi-million-pound institutional makeover next door.

title: Edinburgh Futures Institute
about_site_text: This grand Scots Baronial building, completed in 1879 to designs by David Bryce, was originally the Old Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh - built on the 'pavilion plan' popularised by nursing pioneer Florence Nightingale, with 600 beds spread across eight separate ward pavilions, one vast ward per floor, deliberately spaced apart for fresh air and reduced cross-infection, and set next to the Meadows for patients recovering. In its day it was considered one of the best-planned hospitals in Britain. It served as Edinburgh's main hospital until services moved to a new site at Little France in 2003, after which the category-A-listed building sat effectively unused for years before the University of Edinburgh undertook a seven-year, multi-million-pound restoration, reopening it in June 2024 as the Edinburgh Futures Institute - a 20,000 square metre home for interdisciplinary research, teaching and business incubation.
interesting_fact: The building's distinctive clock tower, visible for miles across the city, has stood watch over this stretch of Lauriston Place through more than 140 years and two completely different institutional lives - as one of Britain's most advanced Victorian hospitals, and now as a 21st-century university research hub.

title: Simpson Loan
about_site_text: Simpson Loan is one of the main streets running through Quartermile, the large residential and office redevelopment of the former Old Royal Infirmary site, mixing sleek modern glass apartment blocks with the restored Victorian hospital buildings around them. Its name honours Sir James Young Simpson, the Edinburgh professor of midwifery who first demonstrated the anaesthetic properties of chloroform in 1847 and introduced it into obstetric and surgical practice right here at the Royal Infirmary that once stood on this ground - making the street name a direct link between the site's medical history and the development built on top of it.
interesting_fact: Quartermile's street names throughout the development consistently reference figures connected to the old hospital's medical history, of which Simpson Loan is one of the most prominent examples - a rare case of new-build street naming in Edinburgh deliberately preserving a site's institutional memory rather than starting from scratch.

title: Lister Square
about_site_text: Lister Square is the public heart of Quartermile, framed by the glass-and-steel Quartermile One office block and the surrounding cafes and shops of the development. Like Simpson Loan nearby, its name reaches back into the site's medical history: it honours Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery whose techniques - developed in the era when this site was Edinburgh's Royal Infirmary - dramatically cut post-operative infection rates and made modern surgery survivable worldwide. The square now functions as Quartermile's main public gathering space, hosting outdoor seating, events and a mix of leisure and retail units built into the restored and new buildings around it.
interesting_fact: Lister's name appears twice within a few hundred metres of this square - once here in Lister Square, and again a few streets away in the separate Lister Housing Co-operative on Lauriston Place, which was itself part-funded through a trust set up in his memory.

title: George Heriot's School Turrets
about_site_text: These conical corner turrets - properly called bartizans, small corbelled towers flaring out from the wall high up like witches' hats against the sky - are part of George Heriot's School's main quadrangular building, begun in 1628 under master mason William Wallace and completed after his death in 1631. They're a textbook example of a decorative feature that recurs across Edinburgh's grandest historic buildings: originally derived from defensive tower-house design on castles, but adopted purely ornamentally on Renaissance-era civic and institutional buildings like this one to signal status and craftsmanship rather than to serve any defensive purpose. Heriot's own turrets carry ball-finialled lead roofs and, on the chapel turrets specifically, the carved arms of the school's founder, the royal goldsmith George Heriot.
interesting_fact: The same turret style appears on buildings all across the Old and New Town - from tenement stair-towers to grand institutions like this one - making it one of the most immediately recognisable architectural signatures of historic Edinburgh, quite apart from any single building it happens to sit on.

title: Ornate Iron Railings
about_site_text: These spear-topped cast-iron railings, fencing off a sunken basement stairwell on Keir Street, are one of the most common decorative features across Edinburgh's Georgian and Victorian streets - their spearhead finials still catching whatever light Keir Street gets on a grey day. Cast iron became cheap and widely available in Scotland through the 18th and 19th centuries thanks to the country's ironworking industry, and virtually every New Town and tenement-lined Old Town street was fitted with railings like these - both to fence off the sunken 'area' in front of basement windows and doors, and simply to mark property boundaries in an attractive, uniform style. Most surviving examples, this one included, are on category-listed buildings and are protected as part of the character of Edinburgh's UNESCO World Heritage Site.
interesting_fact: Much of Britain's Georgian and Victorian railing stock, unlike this survivor, was cut down and requisitioned in a nationwide scrap-metal drive during the Second World War - though historians have since cast real doubt on how much of it ever reached a munitions factory at all. Some researchers argue much of the iron was the wrong quality for weapons and was simply dumped, making the whole exercise more a boost to public morale than a genuine wartime necessity. Surviving original ironwork like this railing is valued today partly because it escaped that fate.

title: Iron Boot Scraper
about_site_text: Set low into the stone stairs beside the railings at 18 Keir Street, this small cast-iron boot scraper is a fixture once found outside almost every Georgian and Victorian townhouse in Edinburgh. Before the city's streets were consistently paved and drained, mud, horse dung and general filth were unavoidable underfoot, and a boot scraper by the front door let residents and visitors clean their soles before stepping inside onto good carpets and floors. Most were cast in one piece with a flat blade for scraping and a small brush-holder or spike beside it, fixed directly into the stonework of the entrance steps - a small, functional detail now mostly obsolete, easy to walk straight past until you know to look for one, and then somehow impossible to stop noticing outside thousands of Old and New Town doorways.
interesting_fact: Boot scrapers are one of the few genuinely functional (rather than purely decorative) pieces of historic street furniture still surviving in large numbers across Edinburgh, precisely because removing them meant chiselling them out of solid stone steps rather than simply unscrewing them.

title: Flower-Decorated Tenement Steps
about_site_text: Residents of this Keir Street tenement have filled their stone entrance steps with dozens of potted plants and flowers, turning a purely functional stairway into a small blaze of colour against the grey sandstone - one of the street's genuine highlights on an otherwise quiet corner. This kind of communal doorstep gardening is a genuinely widespread tradition across Edinburgh's tenement blocks, where residents typically don't have private gardens of their own - stone steps, window ledges and small shared areas in front of stairwells become the only outdoor space available, and many residents' associations and individual flat-owners take real pride in dressing them with planters, hanging baskets and seasonal flowers.
interesting_fact: Tenement stair 'stair pride' displays like this one are common enough across Edinburgh that they've become an informal part of the city's character - the same stone steps that once needed a boot scraper to keep mud off them now often double as makeshift plant stands.

title: Argyle House - 60s architectural eyesore
about_site_text: Argyle House is Edinburgh's most argued-about building - a hulking 1968 concrete-and-harling office block, designed by Michael Laird & Partners, that sits squarely across West Port in the middle of the Old Town's historic skyline. It went up on the site of John Croall & Son, a long-established garage and Rolls-Royce coachbuilder, after the developer Argyle Securities bought the land in 1961 and then quietly absorbed the neighbouring condemned tenements around it too - ground that had once held Tanner's Close, the notorious lodging house where Burke and Hare murdered their victims in the 1820s, though nothing above ground marks that history today. Its route to approval ran through the city's 1953 Development Plan, which had rezoned the then-decaying West Port and High Riggs area for commercial use - quietly making land that had only ever supported housing suddenly valuable for large-scale office development. The Corporation Planning Committee approved the scheme in September 1966, in a decade when postwar modernisation was consistently prioritised over conservation concerns across British cities, Edinburgh included.
interesting_fact: Even architecture critics sympathetic to the building struggled to defend it - Colin McWilliam tried comparing its scale to Georgian terraces, but still admitted it was 'preposterously large and a potential rival to the Castle rock,' and tellingly, no public opposition to the scheme survives in the historical record, a striking contrast to how fiercely similar proposals are fought today. Despite - or perhaps because of - that reputation as Edinburgh's least-loved building, Argyle House has found a very of-the-moment second life: part of it is now occupied by CodeBase, Scotland's largest tech start-up incubator, putting 21st-century software firms to work inside a slab of 1960s concrete that architecture critics have never forgiven.

title: 6VT Edinburgh City Youth Cafe
about_site_text: 6VT is a charitable youth cafe serving young people across Edinburgh from ages 0 to 26, tucked into the foot of the Vennel just below its famous view up to the Castle - its ground-floor windows usually still lit long after the shops on Forrest Road have closed for the night. Rather than a formal community centre, it operates as a genuine drop-in space: open several evenings a week alongside structured group work, one-to-one support and links to wider services, built specifically so young people have somewhere informal to connect, try new things and get help without it feeling institutional. The name '6VT' comes directly from its address, and the cafe has become a fixture of this stretch of the Old Town, sitting just metres from the historic Flodden Wall remnant the Vennel is famous for.
interesting_fact: The cafe occupies a genuinely tiny footprint for the range of services it runs, relying on the surrounding stonework of the old Flodden and Telfer Walls as part of its own boundary - a modern youth charity operating literally within a 16th-century defensive wall.

title: Brown's Place
about_site_text: This quiet residential square opening off the Vennel takes its name from James Brown, who ran an inn next door in the Grassmarket. When the Flodden Wall - which had marked the edge of the city here since 1513, with the separate burgh of Portsburgh beginning on its far side - was gradually demolished after 1815, following the Union and Napoleon's defeat removed any remaining need for city defences, Brown seized the chance to develop the land behind his inn, very likely reusing stone salvaged from the wall itself. By 1834 the square was being advertised as 'newly built.' It survived a serious threat in the 1960s, when numbers 1-3 stood derelict and the whole area was earmarked for demolition to expand the nearby art college - plans that were ultimately abandoned by decade's end, with those buildings rehabilitated in 1976.
interesting_fact: A residents' association formed in 1986 specifically to restore the square's shared garden, part of which had been concreted over at some point - reclaiming a small green space that Brown himself had built directly on top of the city's old defensive wall.

title: The Black Bull
about_site_text: An L-shaped bar and two small mezzanine levels fill this corner of the Grassmarket, where The Black Bull has traded since at least the early 20th century, part of one of the highest concentrations of historic pubs anywhere in Edinburgh - a market square with written records of trading stretching back to around 1370. Old photographs comparing the pub in 1912 and a century later show the building itself has been rebuilt at some point, even as the pub's name and location have stayed constant. Today it runs as a sports bar, decorated with memorabilia from T&J Bernard, one of Edinburgh's several long-vanished local breweries.
interesting_fact: The pub keeps memorabilia from T&J Bernard, a brewery that no longer exists - a small, deliberate way of keeping Edinburgh's lost brewing history visible inside a pub that has itself already survived at least one full rebuild. T&J Bernard brewed in Edinburgh from the 18th century until 1960, the year the firm was folded into Scottish Brewers - which itself merged with Newcastle Breweries that same year to form Scottish & Newcastle, once one of Britain's biggest brewing groups. The Black Bull's memorabilia is a rare surviving trace of a brewery whose identity was absorbed twice over within a matter of months.

title: Victoria Street's Cobbles
about_site_text: The cobbled setts curving down Victoria Street are a genuine survival of a paving technique once universal across Edinburgh's Old Town, laid using roughly cut rectangular granite blocks (properly called 'setts' rather than true rounded cobbles) bedded into sand and gravel. Streets were paved this way from the 18th century onward because granite setts were durable enough to survive horse-drawn cart traffic and could be re-laid individually when damaged, unlike a continuous surface. Most of Edinburgh's other streets have long since been resurfaced in tarmac for modern traffic, making Victoria Street's intact, curving run of setts - still visibly worn smooth by two centuries of footfall and cartwheels - one of the best-preserved and most photographed stretches of historic paving left in the city.
interesting_fact: The double yellow lines painted directly onto the historic setts are a small, constant tension point for conservation bodies - modern traffic regulation applied directly on top of 19th-century stonework, on a street that's otherwise treated as one of Edinburgh's most protected historic assets.

title: Museum on the Mound
about_site_text: This free museum occupies part of Bank of Scotland's grand early-19th-century headquarters at the top of the Mound - the bank building itself, with its own architects and story, is a stop you'll reach later on this walk. The museum opened in 2006, two years before the global financial crisis it now can't help but be read through, and covers the story of money and banking through historic banknotes (including Scotland's oldest surviving note), an interactive 1820s life-assurance display, exhibits on financial crime and security, and raised maps tracing the Old Town's development since the 1600s.
interesting_fact: The bank's own 1695 founding has an appropriately Edinburgh origin story: rather than launch from a grand hall, the subscription book that raised its founding capital was left for two months in one of the city's taverns, the Cross Keys, where prospective backers could sign up as shareholders over a dram before the venture had even opened for business. Three centuries on, the museum built to tell that story includes a display case stacked with a genuine £1 million in banknotes, and an 18th-century iron money chest solid and heavy enough to explain exactly why the bank was so glad to eventually trust paper instead of coin.

title: Assembly Hall
about_site_text: This neo-Gothic hall, designed by David Bryce in 1858, sits directly east of Edinburgh Castle atop the Mound and has served since 1929 as the meeting place for the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland - the church's annual governing gathering. It was built for the Free Church of Scotland in the wake of the 1843 Disruption, when a large breakaway movement split from the established Church and urgently needed its own theological college, assembly hall and church nearby. One of its most historically significant moments came in 1910, when 1,355 delegates gathered here for the World Missionary Conference, an event widely credited as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement. Between 1999 and 2004 it took on an entirely different role, hosting the newly reconvened Scottish Parliament while the purpose-built Holyrood building was under construction.
interesting_fact: Today, for three weeks every August, this same hall housing Scotland's national church assembly transforms into one of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe's most prestigious venues, hosting circus, comedy, music and dance across three separate performance spaces inside it.

title: Edinburgh City Relief Map
about_site_text: Set into the pavement on the Mound, this bronze high-relief model reproduces central Edinburgh in miniature - from Lothian Road in the west to Regent Road in the east, and from Queen Street in the north down to the Cowgate in the south - with the Castle, Calton Hill, Waverley Station and Princes Street Gardens all rendered in raised bronze detail, alongside raised lettering naming the major streets. It was presented to the City of Edinburgh in 1984 by the staff of the Edinburgh branch of Marks & Spencer to mark the company's centenary, but its real purpose is tactile rather than decorative: the whole point of casting the city in high relief was to let visitors with visual impairments explore the shape and grandeur of Edinburgh's skyline entirely by touch.
interesting_fact: Because it's designed to be touched rather than just looked at, decades of hands tracing the Castle Rock, the Mound and the major streets have left the bronze polished to a bright golden sheen in exactly those spots, while the rest of the map has darkened naturally with age - a map that visibly records where people actually explore it most.

title: The Merchants' Hall
about_site_text: This Category B listed hall on Hanover Street has headquartered the Company of Merchants of the City of Edinburgh since the 19th century, a body whose roots trace back to the trade guilds of the 13th and 14th centuries and was formalised into its modern form by a Royal Charter from Charles II in 1681. It was built to project exactly the values the Company still associates itself with - integrity, commercial acumen and civic accomplishment - and its interior includes a genuinely striking Minstrels' Gallery. The Company's influence reaches well beyond this one hall: it still founded and funds two of Edinburgh's best-known independent schools, George Watson's College and Erskine Stewart's Melville, continuing a charitable and educational role that stretches back through the Company's entire 340-plus-year history.
interesting_fact: The Hall runs a permanent exhibition inside chronicling the Company's full history 'from 1681 to the present day' - meaning this working private hall, still used for events and private hire, is also one of Edinburgh's more discreet, lesser-known small museums.

title: Former TSB Bank, Hanover Street
about_site_text: This imposing neo-Greek bank building, a Category A listed structure, was designed by the architects Oldrieve, Bell and Paterson for the Edinburgh Savings Bank, its steel frame going up in early 1939 and the finished building formally opening on 26 August 1940 - later absorbed into the TSB network whose name still sits carved above its entrance. Its tetrastyle Ionic portico - four full-height fluted columns across the Hanover Street facade - is built from Darney sandstone on a plinth of light grey Creetown granite, with the substructure masonry by G. and R. Cousin of Edinburgh and the superstructure by Jackson, Brown of Giffnock. Decorative roundels above the flanking entrances carry TSB's own arms, a two-towered castle with a closed portcullis, while the arms of Edinburgh, Leith and Musselburgh appear elsewhere on the facade, marking out the three burghs the bank originally served.
interesting_fact: The banking hall was designed on a genuinely double-height scale to project total financial permanence, its steel frame rising just months before the Second World War broke out and the finished building not opening its doors until Edinburgh was a year into the war. The site has since been earmarked for conversion into a pub and restaurant, a change of use that will keep the grand banking hall but end its 85-plus years as a working bank.

title: All Bar One, George Street
about_site_text: Giant-order Corinthian pilasters climb the first and second floors of this cream sandstone corner block, a scale of ornament built to announce a bank rather than a bar. The south range, facing George Street, went up in 1841-42 for the Edinburgh and Leith Bank; David Bryce - working here with William Burn, and responsible for several other George Street banks, including the Union Bank building that's now the Standing Order pub further along this walk - extended it in 1847-48 when the business became the Edinburgh and Glasgow Bank. It later traded for decades as a Clydesdale Bank branch, Category A listed throughout, before the double-height banking hall was repurposed as an All Bar One, giving the modern bar an unusually grand, high-ceilinged interior far larger than a purpose-built pub of the same footprint would ever have.
interesting_fact: The building's position - directly on the crossing of George Street and Hanover Street, two of the New Town's principal axes - meant that whichever bank stood here was making a deliberate statement of prestige simply through its address. That prestige lasted through a long run as a Clydesdale Bank branch, and even now the building isn't purely a bar: in 2021 planning permission was granted to convert its long-empty upper floors into six residential flats, sitting above the drinkers unnoticed by most of them.

title: Stone Basements and Area Wells
about_site_text: The sunken stone-walled gap running beneath the railings at 16 Keir Street is a classic Edinburgh 'area' - a below-street-level space in front of a tenement's basement windows and door, built into virtually every Georgian and Victorian terrace in the city. Areas exist because these buildings' ground floors sit slightly raised above street level, with a basement or 'garden flat' beneath; rather than leaving that basement level buried and windowless, builders left a narrow open trench along the front wall, faced in dressed stone and fenced off with railings, so the basement rooms could get proper daylight and their own street-level door. The stone retaining wall and curving stair down to the basement door, visible here beneath the ironwork, are essentially unchanged from when the tenement was first built - lean over the railing and you're looking at construction details barely touched in two centuries.
interesting_fact: Areas like this one are the reason Edinburgh's New Town and tenement streets needed so much cast ironwork in the first place - the railings weren't purely decorative, they were essential safety barriers stopping pedestrians from stepping straight down into a basement-level drop hidden right at the edge of the pavement.

title: Radisson Blu Hotel
address: The Royal Mile, 80 High St, Edinburgh EH1 1TH, UK
about_site_text: The turreted, sandstone-fronted Radisson Blu sits on the site of Dickson's Close, a narrow medieval alley recorded from at least 1723 that once ran down to the Cowgate. The close was named after the merchant Thomas Dickson and had earlier been known as Aikman's Close and Halyburton's Close, after successive residents going back to the early 1500s. It was swept away when Niddry Street was widened, leaving a conspicuous gap site on the Royal Mile's historic frontage for years - until the hotel that replaced it opened in 1990, designed by Scottish architect Ian Begg. Rather than faking an old tenement or building overtly modern, Begg chose a deliberately "Scottish vernacular" style for the new building - turrets, small windows, thick stone walls - betting that Edinburgh's Old Town character comes from a way of building, not simply from age; the result is one of very few 20th-century buildings on the Mile trying to speak the same architectural language as its centuries-older neighbours. Today, only the old street sign survives from what stood here before, mounted above a doorway on the building.
interesting_fact: One of Dickson's Close's most notable residents was the artist David Allan, nicknamed the 'Scottish Hogarth' for his satirical engravings and illustrations - he's buried across town in Old Calton Burial Ground.

title: Carrubber's Close
about_site_text: Carrubber's Close takes its name from James Hay of Carruber, a 15th-century landowner who held ground and a coal yard here. In 1736 the poet Allan Ramsay opened a playhouse at the foot of the close as Scotland's first purpose-built theatre, defying strict Presbyterian opposition to stage drama in the city - opposition that won out within the year, forcing the theatre to close. The building later passed through several religious congregations, becoming known as the Whitefield Chapel after evangelist George Whitefield preached there.
interesting_fact: Long before Ramsay's playhouse, this close held a secret Episcopalian chapel, worshipped in under threat of prosecution after Stewart-era attempts to impose bishops on a Presbyterian city. One attendee, a medical student at Edinburgh University in the 1750s named Samuel Seabury, later returned home and was consecrated the first ever American Episcopal bishop. After the old theatre building was eventually demolished, the site turned to religion again: it became home to the Carrubbers Christian Mission, whose current hall - funded by American evangelist D.L. Moody in 1883 - still stands in the close today.

title: North Bridge Arcade
address: 7 North Bridge, Arcade, Edinburgh EH1 1QL, UK
about_site_text: Glass overhead throws coloured light down through a stained-glass rotunda ceiling, its gold and turquoise mosaic giving this covered Victorian arcade a starlit glow even on a grey Edinburgh afternoon. Built in 1899-1902 to designs by Dunn & Findlay, linking North Bridge with Cockburn Street, it went up after the Scotsman newspaper's owners, John Ritchie & Co, bought the wider site from the city in 1898 as part of a larger redevelopment that also produced the Scotsman Hotel and Steps next door. It's one of only five surviving arcades of its kind left in Scotland, its original shopfronts still fitted with bowed plate glass beneath coffered ceilings.
interesting_fact: The arcade sits within the wider complex once known as the Scotsman Buildings, and its entrance carries genuine Victorian sculpture: an allegorical figure by William Birnie Rhind above the doorway, a figure of Peace by Frederick Schenk, and figures of Mercury modelled - like Michelangelo's Night and Day - by Joseph Hayes.

title: Bishop's Close
address: 129 High St, Bishop's Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1SG, UK
about_site_text: Bishop's Close is named for Bishop's Land, the grand townhouse of Archbishop John Spottiswood, who died here in 1639, and later home to Bishop Thomas Sydserf. By the 19th century the tenement had filled with ordinary Old Town families, and from the 1880s onward it became home to Jewish families fleeing persecution in Eastern Europe. Among the earliest recorded was the Emmanuel family, furriers who had arrived from England in 1841 - Ezekiel and Rachel Emmanuel and their three sons, one of the households that built Edinburgh's small but growing Jewish community through the century.
interesting_fact: The close sits sandwiched directly between two pubs, The Mitre Bar and the Royal Mile Tavern - The Mitre's very name is a nod to the bishop's headgear, tying the two neighbouring sites together.

title: The Mitre Bar
about_site_text: The Mitre Bar takes its name - and its sign - from the site's earlier history: in 1615 a fine tenement here belonged to Archbishop John Spottiswood, Bishop of St Andrews, whose episcopal headgear the tavern still nods to over the door. The original building burned down in 1814 and was rebuilt as the pub that stands today, now part of the Nicholson's collection of historic Edinburgh pubs.
interesting_fact: The bishop whose mitre gives the pub its name wasn't universally loved in life: after backing Charles I's unpopular prayer-book reforms, Archbishop Spottiswood fled Edinburgh in fear for his life during the riots of 1637, and was later deposed from his post in absence on charges that included sacrilege and adultery - accusations widely regarded at the time as a Covenanter smear rather than proven fact. Local legend has since given him an even stranger afterlife: it holds that the bishop's own throne lies buried beneath the bar, and that his ghost still walks the premises.

title: Bailie Fyfe's Close
about_site_text: Bailie Fyfe's Close is named after Gilbert Fyfe, a merchant and city magistrate (a 'bailie') who lived here between 1677 and 1686. The close stood directly in the path of the Great Fire of Edinburgh, which broke out on the night of 15 November 1824 just around the corner in Old Assembly Close and swept through this stretch of the High Street, destroying much of what stood here at the time.
interesting_fact: The 1824 fire burned for five days, destroyed dozens of buildings across the full width of the Old Town between the High Street and Cowgate, and left over 400 people homeless - one of the worst disasters in the city's history.

title: The Nutcracker Christmas Shop
about_site_text: Baubles, tartan decorations and traditional wooden nutcrackers spill from every shelf of this narrow High Street shopfront, one of the Royal Mile's few shops dedicated entirely to Christmas and open year-round rather than just in December. It's a family-run operation, a satellite of a flagship store and workshop based in Crieff, Perthshire, drawing browsing tourists past its window displays whatever the season.
interesting_fact: Permanent Christmas shops like this one are a Royal Mile tradition in their own right - Edinburgh's festive trade has become a year-round draw for visitors, not just a winter one.

title: Stevenlaw's Close
about_site_text: Stevenlaw's Close takes its name from Stephen Law, a flesher - a butcher - made a burgess of Edinburgh in 1501, his property here recorded a decade later as lying west of a plot on Peebles Wynd. The name wore down over the centuries, from 'Stenelawis clois' in 1593 to 'Steven Laws Closs' on a 1647 map, before settling into today's spelling. The narrow close cuts steeply down from the High Street to the Cowgate between high tenement walls, a classic Old Town 'close' built to pack maximum housing into minimum street frontage.
interesting_fact: One notorious former resident was James 'Daft Jamie' Wilson, a well-known Old Town figure who became one of the victims of the West Port murderers Burke and Hare, who killed to supply cadavers for anatomical dissection.

title: New Assembly Close
about_site_text: New Assembly Close took its name when Edinburgh's fashionable dancing assembly, a magnet for the city's high society, moved here from Old Assembly Close in 1736, remaining until 1784. The building later housed the Edinburgh Assembly Rooms, the King's Arms Tavern, and even the Edinburgh Wax Museum, before the Commercial Bank built its head office on the site in 1814.
interesting_fact: The 18th-century Assembly was run by female managers and often doubled as a charitable fundraiser for the city's hospitals - a rare example of women holding formal organisational control over Edinburgh's high society. Two centuries later the close took a stranger turn: Edinburgh Wax Museum operated here from 1976 until March 1989, its ground and first-floor galleries devoted to heroes of Scottish history while, upstairs, a second-floor 'Castle Dracula' theatre catered to visitors after something scarier. At its peak it drew around 230,000 visitors a year, making it one of the city's biggest tourist draws before the building was converted into legal offices.

title: Netherbow Wellhead
about_site_text: Two grotesque bronze masks glare out from this carved stone wellhead, one facing east and one west - faithful replicas of originals that have long since worn away. Sir William Bruce designed it and master mason Robert Mylne built it in 1675, part of Old Town Edinburgh's first piped drinking water supply, carried three miles from the Comiston Springs into storage tanks on Castlehill and out to public wellheads like this one.
interesting_fact: The wellhead fell out of daily use once Victorian housing modernisation brought indoor plumbing to Old Town tenements, but it was restored to working order - with running water again - by the Edinburgh Old Town Renewal Trust in 1997.

title: Old Assembly Close
about_site_text: Old Assembly Close was originally called Little's Close, after the brothers Clement and William Little, before Edinburgh's dancing assembly - which began in 1723 - gave it its present name. The great hall here hosted the city's high society balls until the assembly moved to New Assembly Close in 1736, and the original hall was later destroyed in the Great Fire of 1824, which started in an engraver's workshop in this very close.
interesting_fact: The 1824 fire began when a pot of overheated linseed oil in James Kirkwood's engraving workshop set a stack of paper alight - within hours the flames had spread along the High Street rooftops, fanned by a southwesterly wind. The blaze that started here went on to burn for five days, destroy the Assembly Hall and roughly twenty tenements across the Old Town, and kill thirteen people - one of the worst disasters in the city's history, and part of the reason Edinburgh set up a dedicated, professional fire brigade under James Braidwood later that same decade.

title: Borthwick's Close
about_site_text: One of the many narrow closes running off the High Street near St Giles' and Parliament Square, this one is said to take its name from Lord Borthwick, thought to have built a house here around 1450 to be close to the old Scottish Parliament as a sitting advocate - the Borthwick family later marrying into royal and noble circles on both sides of the border. Like its neighbours, the close was built to squeeze maximum tenement housing into a tight sliver of Old Town street frontage, its precise history since largely lost to time.
interesting_fact: Closes like this one were sealed at night by a locked gate at the street end - hence the name 'close' - a security measure for the crowded, largely self-contained communities living up the shared stairs above.

title: Statue of James Braidwood
about_site_text: This bronze statue in Parliament Square honours James Braidwood (1800-1861), who in 1824 became the first Master of Engines of Edinburgh's fire brigade - the world's first municipal fire service. Braidwood introduced protective helmets and uniforms and pioneered the then-radical idea of training firefighters to enter burning buildings rather than simply spraying water from outside.
interesting_fact: Braidwood later became head of the London Fire Engine Establishment and died fighting a warehouse fire on Tooley Street in 1861, aged 61, when a collapsing wall killed him - the statue was unveiled in 2008, funded by a former Lothian & Borders Firemaster. News of his death triggered a public outpouring rarely seen outside royalty: his funeral procession stretched a mile and a half through London, while the Thames-side warehouse fire that killed him burned on for two more weeks after he died fighting it.

title: The Supreme Courts
about_site_text: Behind Parliament Square's unassuming frontage, this is where Scotland's supreme courts still sit today: the Court of Session, the country's highest civil court, and the High Court of Justiciary, its highest criminal court, spread across more than 700 rooms behind the historic facade. The building itself is Parliament House, completed in 1639 as the seat of the pre-Union Scottish Parliament - see Parliament House for the story of its construction. Its most striking feature is inside: the Great Window at the south end of Parliament Hall, added in 1868 from around 8,000 pieces of painted and stained glass, depicting King James V presenting the charter that founded the Court of Session in 1532, above portraits and busts of the judges who have sat here since.
interesting_fact: Unlike most supreme courts, the public can simply walk in: courtrooms here are generally open to anyone who wants to sit in the public gallery and watch a case, with the Court of Session's Inner House sittings now livestreamed too - a level of openness few countries extend to their highest courts.

title: Charles II Statue
about_site_text: This lead equestrian statue of Charles II, erected in 1685 - the year of his death - is believed to be the oldest statue in Edinburgh and possibly the oldest lead equestrian statue in Britain. It depicts the king in Roman military dress, carrying a baton as a symbol of imperial authority, on a pedestal carved from Craigleith stone by Robert Mylne, the King's Master Mason.
interesting_fact: Charles II's own path to the throne ran through Edinburgh: after his father's execution in 1649, the Scottish Parliament proclaimed him king, but Cromwell crushed his forces at the Battle of Worcester in 1651, forcing him into exile until the monarchy's restoration in 1660.

title: Roxburgh's Close
about_site_text: Roxburgh's Close carries a grander name than its history really supports: it's often assumed to honour an Earl of Roxburghe, but the close actually takes its name from John Roxburgh, a working cook recorded as its owner in 1635 - probably the same John Roxburgh made a burgess of the city in 1605. Before that it went by at least two other names in the space of a few decades, Cant's Close and then Cruick's Close, for a resident called William Crockie - a reminder that these closes were renamed almost as often as they changed hands. Much later, the tenements separating it from its neighbour were demolished to create the more open Roxburgh Court seen today.
interesting_fact: The 'Earl of Roxburghe' story is a guess that stuck - the real namesake was just a cook who happened to own property here. It's a pattern repeated up and down the Royal Mile: most closes are named for a long-forgotten resident tradesman or merchant, not the aristocrat visitors often assume.

title: Bank of Scotland
address: Bank of Scotland Private Banking, The Mound, Edinburgh EH1 1YZ, UK
about_site_text: Bank of Scotland's headquarters has crowned the top of the Mound since 1806, when architects Robert Reid and Richard Crichton - both former pupils of Robert Adam - completed a domed Georgian villa on land the bank bought from the city in 1800. David Bryce substantially enlarged the building in 1862, adding the grand central dome and domed wings that give the skyline its present silhouette.
interesting_fact: Founded by Act of the Scottish Parliament in 1695 - just a year after the Bank of England - Bank of Scotland is one of the oldest banks in the world still trading under its original name, and its Mound headquarters remains the registered Scottish office of Lloyds Banking Group today. It marked its 300th birthday in 1995 by putting Sir Walter Scott's face on every note in a special tercentenary series, having already absorbed two rivals along the way, the Union Bank of Scotland in 1955 and the British Linen Bank in 1971.

title: Wardrop's Court
address: Wardrop Court, Lawnmarket, Edinburgh EH1 2NY, UK
about_site_text: Wardrop's Court was formed behind the Lawnmarket in the 1890s, on the site of the older Middle Baxter's Close, after a wave of tenement demolition swept through the area. Builder John Wardrop put up a new tenement here and gave the resulting court and its archway his own name. Above the entrance arch, a pair of carved dragon brackets keep watch - one set carved around 1890 by J. S. Gibson, the other added in 1911 by a sixteen-year-old apprentice, Arthur Geddes, working under the craftsman Alec Miller. The open courtyard itself was laid out on the instructions of town planner Sir Patrick Geddes, part of his wider push to bring light and air back into Edinburgh's crowded Old Town.
interesting_fact: The court sits immediately beside Lady Stair's Close and Makars' Court, part of the same cluster of Old Town redevelopment carried out as the Lawnmarket was remodelled in the late 19th century. One detail from that rebuild stands out above the entrance arch: the 1911 dragon brackets were carved by a teenager, Arthur Geddes, just sixteen years old when he made them, working under Alec Miller, a sculptor closely associated with the Arts and Crafts movement - a piece of apprentice work that has been weathering quietly on the Lawnmarket ever since.

title: Author's Phrases in the Flagstones
address: Lady Stair's Cl & Makars' Ct, Edinburgh EH1 2LP, UK
about_site_text: The literary quotations carved into Makars' Court's paving stones (see Makars' Court, right next door, for the story of how the project began) keep growing: among the more than one hundred names now underfoot is Dame Muriel Spark, whose line 'the transfiguration of the commonplace' - from The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie - was added after her death in 2006, alongside a set of eleven stones unveiled in 1998 spanning the full range of Scotland's literary languages, from the medieval poet Robert Henryson through to Sorley MacLean, one of the great 20th-century Gaelic poets. Each new inscription is still chosen by committee and unveiled at its own small annual ceremony.
interesting_fact: New names are still being added most years - recent arrivals include the Gaelic songwriter Mairi Mhor nan Oran and the 18th-century poet Donnchadh Ban Mac an t-Saoir - so this isn't a fixed monument but a literary map still being drawn, stone by stone, in Gaelic, Scots, English and Latin.

title: Scottish War Poets Memorial
address: Lady Stair's Cl & Makars' Ct, Edinburgh EH1 2LP, UK
about_site_text: This hand-carved Celtic cross in light grey granite, its shaft decorated with deep Celtic knotwork and a stone sword in relief, was unveiled in Makars' Court in November 2018 to commemorate Scotland's First World War poets. It was installed jointly by Edinburgh Napier University, the University of Aberdeen, the Scottish Poetry Library, and the National Library of Scotland, among other partners.
interesting_fact: The memorial's inscription is a line of verse: 'Sweet be their sleep now wherever they're lying, far though they be from the hills of their home' - a tribute to Scottish soldier-poets who died far from home in the trenches.

title: Milne's Court
about_site_text: Milne's Court, built in 1692 by Robert Milne, master mason to the king, was the first open courtyard of its kind in Edinburgh - a deliberate break from the cramped, enclosed closes surrounding it. The original west range was demolished in 1883, but the University of Edinburgh restored the north and south blocks and rebuilt the east range between 1966 and 1970, turning the court into student accommodation.
interesting_fact: Milne's Court set the template that later, grander courtyards like James' Court and Riddle's Court would follow - proof that even in the crowded 17th-century Old Town, there was appetite for a bit more light and air.

title: James' Court
about_site_text: James' Court was built from 1727 by James Brownhill, from whom it takes its name, and quickly became one of Edinburgh's most fashionable addresses - philosopher David Hume lived here before moving to the New Town, and diarist James Boswell later took over Hume's old flat. The buildings behind Gladstone's Land, some dating to the 16th century, still convey the crowded feel of the 18th-century Old Town.
interesting_fact: James Boswell entertained Samuel Johnson here during Johnson's 1773 visit to Edinburgh, the very trip that produced Johnson's 'A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland'. The court that survives today isn't quite the one Hume and Boswell knew: much of it, including the building that had held Hume's old flat, burned down in a fire in 1857 and was rebuilt, so the crowded closes visitors walk through now are largely a Victorian reconstruction of the 18th-century original.

title: The Jolly Judge
about_site_text: Tucked below street level just off the Lawnmarket, the Jolly Judge is a traditional basement pub known for its low beamed ceilings and roaring log fire - a world away from the busier tourist bars further down the Royal Mile. Its location close to the Sheriff Court and High Court once made it a favourite haunt of the city's legal community.
interesting_fact: The Jolly Judge has become something of a CAMRA institution: as well as being named Edinburgh Pub of the Year in 2023 and 2024, it has picked up the branch's Cider Pub of the Year award eight years running, missing out only in 2021 when Covid cancelled the competition - recognition for a pub that deliberately keeps the music off to stay a genuinely quiet place to drink.

title: Susannah Alice Stephen Memorial
