about_site_text: This memorial seat, topped with a bronze sculpture of a parakeet and garden trug by sculptor Frances Pelly, sits in James' Court in honour of Susannah Alice Stephen (1960-1997), a landscape designer who co-founded the Scottish Society of Garden Designers before her death in a diving accident off the Galapagos Islands. She chose this spot deliberately, knowing that pioneering town planner Patrick Geddes - a hero of hers for bringing green space into Edinburgh's Old Town - had once lived in James' Court himself.
interesting_fact: The memorial is inscribed with the line 'Keep your face towards the sun and the shadows will fall behind you', a fitting motto for a landscape designer who spent her career finding light and green space within the dense, shadowed closes of the Old Town.

title: The Ensign Ewart
about_site_text: This Lawnmarket pub, trading in some form since at least 1680, was renamed in 1938 in honour of Ensign Charles Ewart of the Royal Scots Greys, who captured the eagle standard of the French 45th Regiment of the Line at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. The name was chosen the same year Ewart's remains were reburied with full honours at Edinburgh Castle.
interesting_fact: A large painting of the Battle of Waterloo hangs inside, alongside Scottish military memorabilia - the pub sits only a few hundred metres from Ewart's actual grave on the Castle esplanade.

title: Boswell's Court
about_site_text: Boswell's Court on Castlehill dates from the 17th century and takes its name not from the famous diarist James Boswell but from his uncle, Dr John Boswell, a physician who lived here. James did visit his uncle at this address in October 1762, and a plaque on the building - now home to the Witchery restaurant - also claims that James Boswell and Samuel Johnson dined here around 1770.
interesting_fact: The stair entrance still carries a carved lintel bearing a merchant's mark and the initials 'T' and 'L', thought to belong to an earlier owner, Thomas Lowthian.

title: Ramsay Lane
about_site_text: Ramsay Lane climbs steeply from the Royal Mile up toward the Castle esplanade, named for the poet Allan Ramsay, whose distinctive octagonal house - nicknamed 'the goose-pie house' for its unusual shape - once stood at its head. The lane connects Castlehill to Ramsay Garden, the striking Arts and Crafts tenement development built around Ramsay's old home in the 1890s.
interesting_fact: Ramsay Garden was one of the first projects of town planner Patrick Geddes, who saw restoring housing on the Castle slopes as a way to bring the professional classes back to live in the Old Town.

title: Castle Rock Hostel
about_site_text: Behind a solid Victorian facade, this Johnston Terrace building started life as a school and teacher training college before becoming Castle Rock Hostel in 1997. Its interiors lean fully into a medieval theme, with pointed arches, faux tapestries, heraldic shields, and suits of armour lining the stairs, all within sight of the Castle esplanade just above.
interesting_fact: The hostel now hosts around 40,000 overnight guests a year and underwent a major renovation that added a dramatic new staircase to open up extra accommodation in the attic, while keeping the historic exterior intact.

title: St Columba's by the Castle
about_site_text: Battlemented and built from recycled royal stone, St Columba's by the Castle rose in 1846-47 in Early English Gothic style to designs by architect John Henderson, using stone salvaged from the demolished palace of Mary of Guise on the Royal Mile. It went up specifically to serve the poor of a rapidly emptying Old Town, as Edinburgh's wealthier residents decamped for the New Town and left the tenements below the Castle overcrowded; its layout reflects the reforming ideas of the Oxford Movement within the Scottish Episcopal Church, and a day school beneath the church once educated up to 200 local children.
interesting_fact: The church's east window, blocked up for decades, was eventually filled in 1959 with a striking mural of 'Christ Enthroned' by artist John Busby.

title: Fiddler's Arms
about_site_text: At the western tip of the Grassmarket, in the shadow of Edinburgh Castle, the Fiddler's Arms sits on ground that hosted Edinburgh's weekly horse and cattle market for close to 500 years, cattle driven in down the Cowgate until trading finally stopped here in 1911. The wholesale trade running through the neighbouring West Bow once dealt in iron, pitch, tar, hemp and other heavy goods bound for warehouses down in Leith - a working, market-town identity the pub still leans into today.
interesting_fact: True to its name, the pub still leans into a folk-music identity, with regular traditional Scottish sessions - a nod to a Grassmarket long associated with market traders, drovers, and travelling entertainers.

title: West Port Garden
about_site_text: West Port Garden was created in 1909 by pioneering town planner Patrick Geddes as one of several small green spaces he carved into the crowded Old Town, specifically to give slum children a place to experience nature. His daughter Norah, a landscape gardener, laid out this terraced, roughly 930-square-yard plot on the steep slope between West Port and the College of Art, and it officially opened in June 1910.
interesting_fact: In its early decades the garden doubled as a genuine community hub rather than just a green space - hosting a boxing club run by soldiers from the Castle, knitting classes for girls, scouting for boys, and even student training in kindergarten methods. Over a century later it's still community-run, now overseen by the Grassmarket Residents Association, and continues to host local people doing therapeutic gardening and growing their own food.

title: Portsburgh Square
about_site_text: Portsburgh Square is a pocket of turn-of-the-century social housing tucked behind the Grassmarket, its balconied, pastel-painted tenement blocks rising directly beneath the sheer face of Castle Rock. Built around 1900 to designs by the City Engineer's Department, the quadrangular block followed the model-dwelling principles pioneered decades earlier by Prince Albert, with concrete balconies on cast-iron columns and shoulder-arched stair entrances at each corner. The square takes its name from the old Burgh of Portsburgh, an independent burgh that grew up outside Edinburgh's city walls near the West Port before being absorbed into the city in the 19th century.
interesting_fact: Standing in the square gives one of the most dramatic close-up views of Edinburgh Castle anywhere in the city, with the volcanic crag rising almost directly overhead.

title: Salvation Army Womens Hostel
about_site_text: This Art Nouveau-detailed building on West Port was built in 1910-11 to designs by Glasgow architect John Hamilton as a Salvation Army hostel for homeless and vulnerable women, its foundation stone laid by a senior Salvation Army officer on 6 February 1911. Its red sandstone and ogee-roofed corner tower give it a distinctly Glasgow character - an unusual western import sitting in the middle of Edinburgh's Old Town - and carved lettering reading 'THE SALVATION ARMY WOMENS HOSTEL' still runs across the facade above the entrance.
interesting_fact: The building has since been converted into backpacker accommodation, now trading as Kick Ass Hostels, though its original carved signage remains as a visible reminder of over a century of sheltering the city's most vulnerable residents.

title: Granny's Green Steps
about_site_text: Granny's Green Steps climb from the Grassmarket up to Johnston Terrace, cutting through what was once a communal drying green - 'Granny's Green' - used by the wives of soldiers from the Castle's married quarters to hang out their washing in the 19th century. Despite the old-fashioned name, the steps themselves are a modern addition, rebuilt in 2001.
interesting_fact: The 'Granny' in the name almost certainly isn't a specific historical figure - the steps take their name from the shared drying green they once cut through, not from any one named resident. It's an easy detail to get backwards: some guides still repeat an older theory that the steps were named after one particular woman, when the better-supported explanation is a communal green, not a person.

title: Quaker Meeting House
address: 7 Victoria Terrace, above, Victoria St, Edinburgh EH1 2JL, UK
about_site_text: This Italian Gothic building on Victoria Terrace was built in 1865-66 by architects Paterson and Shiells as a chapel for the United Original Secession Church. Once that congregation of 'Auld Seceders' returned to the Kirk, the building was sold to the Boys' Brigade in 1956, becoming 'Kirk House', headquarters of the Edinburgh Battalion, in a 1960 conversion by the noted architectural practice of Basil Spence. The Religious Society of Friends converted it into Edinburgh's Quaker Meeting House in 1987, giving the city's Quaker community - which had first formed a small central Edinburgh meeting back in 1924 - a permanent, fully accessible home.
interesting_fact: Before settling here, Edinburgh's Central Meeting spent almost fifty years, from 1938 to 1987, gathering in a building on Stafford Street in the New Town.

title: The Albanach
about_site_text: Bare stone walls and a hush of muted colour set The Albanach apart the moment you duck in from the crowds on the Royal Mile. Its Gaelic name - meaning 'Scottish' or 'Highlander' - is no idle branding: the High Street bar stocks over 330 different malt whiskies. Behind the pub's front room, a quieter restaurant serves modern Scottish food, giving the building a split identity - buzzing whisky bar facing the street, calmer dining room tucked away from it.
interesting_fact: With over 330 malts behind the bar, the Albanach's whisky list is among the largest on a street already saturated with whisky bars aimed at tourists - a serious, connoisseur-grade collection sitting behind a modern Scottish food menu that gets comparatively little of the attention on this stretch of the Mile.

title: The Advocate
about_site_text: The Advocate sits on Hunter Square right beside St Giles' Cathedral, its name a nod to the legal profession clustered nearby around Parliament House. Converted into a pub in the 1990s, it reopened after a refit in May 2025 and still draws a daytime crowd of lawyers on their lunch break alongside the usual Old Town foot traffic.
interesting_fact: The pub can seat over 200 people and runs live music through the week - acoustic sets on Sunday nights, livelier entertainment on Fridays - a scale that's easy to miss from its fairly modest Hunter Square frontage.

title: Malt Shovel Inn
about_site_text: The Malt Shovel occupies a building dating to around 1800 on Cockburn Street, itself cut through the Old Town in the 1850s. Inside, the pub keeps its period character - corniced ceilings, dark woodwork, and stained glass - across three connected rooms.
interesting_fact: The Malt Shovel was named among the last of Edinburgh's 'proper old-school' Old Town pubs in a 2024 roundup of the city's classic boozers, its dark wood snugs and stained glass largely untouched by decades of modernisation - it still keeps a rotating line-up of Scottish cask ales alongside more than fifty malt whiskies on the shelf.

title: The Piper's Rest
about_site_text: Warm light spills from one of Hunter Square's most eye-catching frontages at The Piper's Rest, tucked just behind the Tron Kirk. The pub serves Scottish food - haggis, Cullen skink, steak pie - alongside a solid range of malt whiskies, local gins, and craft beers, in a space relaunched after a major refurbishment in January 2020. Live music runs seven nights a week, mixing traditional Scottish tunes with more contemporary covers.
interesting_fact: The pub's golden bagpiper figures displayed in its window cases give it one of the more eye-catching frontages on Hunter Square, visible from the top of the square day or night.

title: The Scotsman's Lounge
about_site_text: The Scotsman's Lounge has been pouring pints on this stretch of Cockburn Street since 1860, making it one of the oldest continuously trading pubs in the Old Town. Old photographs of pipers line the walls, live musicians take the small stage most evenings, and the bar stocks a large range of malt whiskies, all just a couple of minutes' walk from the Royal Mile.
interesting_fact: The ceiling itself has become an informal visitors' book: it's papered with hand-signed banknotes left by customers from all over the world, a tradition built up pint by pint over more than a century and a half.

title: Sir Chris Hoy Gold Post Box (Hanover Street)
about_site_text: This pillar box at the foot of Hanover Street, on the corner with Princes Street, is the second of Edinburgh's two gold post boxes honouring Sir Chris Hoy. Royal Mail painted it gold in August 2012 to mark his gold medal in the men's team sprint, won alongside Philip Hindes and Jason Kenny - a different medal from the keirin gold that earned the city's other gold box in Hunter Square. A hometown collecting two gold boxes was unusual under the nationwide scheme, since most gold medallists only ever earned their city one; Hoy's second gold in the same Games meant Edinburgh became one of the few places with a pair.
interesting_fact: The team sprint final was itself a piece of Olympic drama: Hindes crashed on the opening lap of the first-round heat, triggering a restart under a rule permitting a rerun after any first-lap fall - a decision some observers suspected was tactical, though officials ruled it accidental. On the restart, Hoy, Hindes and Kenny broke their own qualifying world record, stopping the clock at 42.600 seconds. This box sits a short walk from the New Town streets where Hoy grew up before his track career began at Meadowbank Velodrome, just a few miles east.

title: Harvey Nichols Edinburgh
about_site_text: Harvey Nichols opened on the east side of St Andrew Square in 2002, built to designs by Edinburgh-based CDA Architects - the same practice behind the neighbouring Multrees Walk development and Edinburgh Bus Station. At five storeys and around 100,000 square feet, it was, at the time of opening, the largest Harvey Nichols store outside London, part of a wave of investment that transformed this corner of the New Town from a quiet Georgian square into the city's most upscale shopping quarter. Multrees Walk, the pedestrian street of luxury boutiques linking the square to the older St James Centre, followed the year after in 2003.
interesting_fact: The top floor houses the Forth Floor restaurant and bar, whose external terrace looks north over the Firth of Forth - the estuary the store is named after, sharing its view with the much older Melville Monument, its Doric column standing at the square's centre. St Andrew Square itself dates to the 1760s, the very first phase of James Craig's New Town plan, and was originally Edinburgh's most fashionable residential address; its early residents included the philosopher David Hume, whose townhouse there predates Harvey Nichols' glass-and-stone facade by well over two centuries.

title: Milnes Bar
about_site_text: Milnes Bar opened at 35 Hanover Street in 1910 as a spirit merchants' shop before growing into a full public house by the 1950s. It was during those same decades that it earned its enduring nickname, the "Poets' Pub" - the gathering place at the centre of the Scottish Literary Renaissance, drawing figures including Hugh MacDiarmid, Sorley MacLean and Norman MacCaig. MacDiarmid, whose 1926 poem A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle helped launch that revival in Scots-language verse, called Milnes his favourite howff, and the bar was redecorated in his memory in 1985 with photographs and a painted sign marking the connection.
interesting_fact: The bar's basement snug was nicknamed the "Little Kremlin" by its regulars, only half-jokingly, for the intensity of the political arguments and poetic manifestos traded there. MacDiarmid's own Milnes-fuelled reputation later found its way into fiction: Alasdair Gray's 1984 novel 1982, Janine draws directly on his legendary sessions at the bar. A century on from its 1910 opening, Milnes still trades as a pub barely a hundred metres from the gold-painted post box on Hanover Street that marks Sir Chris Hoy's team sprint gold - one of only two such boxes in the city, the other standing across town in Hunter Square.

title: Browns Restaurant
about_site_text: Browns occupies 131-133 George Street, a pair of category B-listed townhouses built between 1780 and 1790 as part of the New Town's original George Street terrace, with alterations carried out by the architect John Bryce in 1883. The building has a genuinely distinguished architectural pedigree: William Burn kept his office at No.131 from 1822, and after 1844 the celebrated Scottish architect David Bryce - designer of Fettes College and the Royal Infirmary - worked from the same address. No.133 later passed through very different uses, including a spell as the Leicester Permanent Building Society's offices and, more recently, a hairdressers, before its current life as part of Browns' brasserie.
interesting_fact: No.133's most notable resident predates all of that commercial history: the portrait painter Sir Henry Raeburn, whose likenesses of Sir Walter Scott and the skating Reverend Robert Walker rank among Scotland's best-known images, lived there for a time, as did the novelist and illustrator Catherine Sinclair. Raeburn's own studio still stands nearby on York Place - easy to imagine him passing this same George Street frontage, now filled with Browns' pavement tables, on his way between the two.

title: St Andrew Square
about_site_text: This wasn't meant to be Edinburgh's financial quarter - it was supposed to be its grandest address. James Craig's 1767 plan put a church here, mirroring Charlotte Square at the New Town's far end, but banker Sir Lawrence Dundas outbid the city and built Dundas House for himself in 1774. Where one banker led, others followed, and by the century's end this had become Scotland's banking and insurance headquarters - a role the buildings ringing you still play today. For over 200 years the gardens at the centre stayed locked, private to residents and nearby offices only, finally opening to the public for the first time in April 2008.
interesting_fact: This calm garden square was a battleground for three nights running. In June 1792, City Guardsmen firing pistols into the air while toasting the King's birthday curdled into full civil unrest - stoked by food shortages, grievances over the corn laws, and a public seething at Henry Dundas's stranglehold on Scottish politics - and by the third night the mob had reached St Andrew Square itself. They surrounded the Lord Provost's house on the square's south-east corner, smashed every window, and tried to burn the place down with ripped-up sentry boxes while his wife and daughters sheltered inside; only marines marched up from Leith broke the siege. The Lord Provost, Sir James Stirling, came through it well enough to be made a baronet a few weeks later for how he'd handled it.

title: George Street
about_site_text: Everything about this street was built to impress. George Street sits on the New Town's central ridge, a full storey above Princes Street and Queen Street on either side, so that from up here you can see clear across the Forth to Fife in one direction and the Pentland Hills in the other. James Craig's 1767 grid made it the spine of the whole development, running dead straight between St Andrew Square behind you and Charlotte Square three-quarters of a mile ahead - named for King George III, with the two squares at either end named for his wife and, informally, himself.
interesting_fact: Every name along this street is a loyalty oath. James Craig laid out the New Town barely twenty years after Culloden, when Edinburgh - a city that had opened its gates to Bonnie Prince Charlie's army in 1745 - still needed to prove itself thoroughly, publicly Hanoverian. So the spine of the whole development took the reigning king's own name, flanked by his wife on Queen Street behind you and his son on Frederick Street ahead, with St Andrew and St George anchoring the two end squares as a nod to the very Union the Jacobites had tried to break. The address worked almost too well: within a couple of generations, the grand private townhouses lining George Street had been bought out wholesale by banks and insurance offices, and "the most fashionable street in Edinburgh" became its financial high street instead.

title: Charlotte Square
about_site_text: James Craig's original 1767 plan named this square after King George III and gave it the same footprint as St Andrew Square at the New Town's other end - a matching bookend, symmetrical right down to the name. It was renamed Charlotte Square in 1786, for the King's queen, to stop confusion with a different George Square over in the Old Town. Robert Adam won the commission for its unifying design in 1791, his last major work before his death the following year - one long palace-like frontage on the north side, disguising what's actually a row of separate townhouses behind it, an idea barely tried in Scotland before this.
interesting_fact: No. 22 Charlotte Square, 1810: Dame Helen Cumming Gordon pulled her mixed-race granddaughter Jane out of a nearby girls' boarding school over rumors that its two headmistresses, Marianne Woods and Jane Pirie, were having an affair — then told the rest of New Town society to do the same. The school emptied within days. Woods and Pirie sued for defamation and technically won, but Cumming Gordon fought the verdict all the way to the House of Lords; by the time her appeal was dismissed nine years later, each woman had barely £500 left after legal costs. Lillian Hellman later turned the case into her play The Children's Hour.

title: Princes Street
about_site_text: Here's the oddity: Edinburgh's most famous street has buildings running down only one side of it. James Craig's 1767 plan left the north side of Princes Street open on purpose, so residents - and later, everyone - would keep an unbroken view south across the valley to the Old Town and the Castle on its crag. That valley used to be underwater, the old Nor Loch, drained as the New Town went up, and its bed became Princes Street Gardens - still open ground today for exactly the reason Craig intended.
interesting_fact: 1767, before the street even existed: James Craig's official New Town plan named it "St Giles Street," after Edinburgh's own patron saint. King George III vetoed it on sight — to him, St Giles meant the notorious London slum of that name, not a Scottish saint. Sir John Pringle wrote to the Lord Provost with the fix: name it instead for the King's eldest son, Prince George, Duke of Rothesay, later King George IV. The apostrophe in "Prince's Street" quietly dropped out of use by the 1830s, but the royal snub behind the name stuck.

title: Royal Mile
about_site_text: You won't find 'Royal Mile' on a single street sign - it's a Victorian nickname, coined in the late 19th century, for a chain of streets that has no official name of its own. Walking downhill from the Castle to Holyroodhouse, the same road changes its name four times: Castlehill, then Lawnmarket, then High Street - the stretch you're on now - then Canongate. The name comes from the royal processional route once ridden between the two, and the distance really does work out to almost exactly one mile.
interesting_fact: Daniel Defoe, touring Scotland in the 1720s, called it "perhaps the largest, longest, and finest street for buildings and number of inhabitants, not only in Britain, but in the World" - which is a strange compliment once you know why the street he was praising also housed some of Europe's worst overcrowding. Walled in and too wary of English invasion to build outward, Old Town builders went up instead: tenements along the Royal Mile eventually reached 11 storeys or more, sometimes called the world's first skyscrapers, built to cram tens of thousands of people into the same cramped medieval footprint.

title: Grassmarket
about_site_text: This long, flat hollow beneath the Castle rock has been a marketplace since 1477, when a weekly market for hay, cattle and grain was first licensed here - a trade that carried on, remarkably, until 1911. But it's better known today for what happened at its east end: from 1660 until the last hanging in 1784, this was Edinburgh's public execution ground, watched by crowds that could number in the thousands.
interesting_fact: By the early 20th century the square had earned a very different nickname: 'Little Italy'. Waves of Italian immigrants settled around the Grassmarket from the 1880s onward, working as street musicians and organ-grinders before many turned to selling ice cream from carts, calling out 'Gelati, ecco un poco' - 'ice cream, here's a little' - to passing crowds, which earned them the affectionate nickname 'Hokey Pokey men'.

title: Chambers Street
about_site_text: This whole street didn't exist before 1871 - it was cut straight through a warren of slum housing under the Edinburgh Improvement Act of 1867, the same clearance that swept away three entire 18th-century squares nearby. It's named after the man who pushed the Act through: publisher and Lord Provost William Chambers, of the Chambers's dictionary and encyclopaedia firm, who used his position to remake this whole corner of the Old Town around a single grand purpose - housing Scotland's national museum.
interesting_fact: Inside the museum this street was built to house is one of Edinburgh's strangest unsolved mysteries: in June 1836, boys hunting rabbits on Arthur's Seat found a hidden niche holding seventeen tiny wooden coffins, each carved in pine and containing a miniature figure dressed in hand-stitched clothes. Nobody has ever worked out who made them or why - though one persistent theory ties them to Burke and Hare, whose own killing spree had scandalised the city just a few years earlier. Only eight of the original seventeen coffins survive today, and they're still on public display in the National Museum of Scotland, a short walk from where you're standing.

title: Cowgate
about_site_text: Everything about the Cowgate sits below the Royal Mile in more than one sense - literally lower down the valley, and for most of its history, socially lower too. Its name is exactly what it sounds like: this was once 'Via Vaccarum', the route drovers used to bring cattle down from the fields south and east of the city to the market at the Grassmarket, back when driving livestock through the main streets above was against the law.
interesting_fact: By the 19th century the drovers were long gone, but the Cowgate's reputation had only got worse: as Edinburgh's wealthy decamped to the elegant New Town, their old High Street tenements were carved up into single-room flats and left to the city's poorest, and the valley filled with Irish immigrants fleeing the Great Famine of the 1840s alongside Highlanders driven from their land by the Clearances. So many settled here, clustered around St Patrick's Church at the street's eastern end, that the whole area became known as 'Little Ireland' - a name that stuck for the rest of the century, even as sectarian tension and anti-Irish prejudice ran high in the same overcrowded closes the drovers had once walked their cattle through.
